content.title: Schema

content.text:
| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| material_systems | str | Host materials and chemistries studied (e.g., Si, GaN, MgO, perovskites, alloys), and whether multiple hosts are used. |
| defect_types | str | Defect/dopant types considered (vacancy, interstitial, substitutional dopant, antisite, Frenkel pair, defect complex) and whether complexes are included. |
| charge_state_handling | str | How charged defects/charge states are represented or handled (explicit charge label, electron chemical potential/Fermi level features, background charge correction, electrostatic descriptors, none/neutral only). |
| target_properties | str | Defect-influenced properties predicted (e.g., defect formation energy, charge transition levels, migration barriers, diffusion coefficients, local strain/relaxation, electronic levels, phonon scattering rates, lattice thermal conductivity or its degradation). |
| representation_strategy_name | str | Name/label of the main representation/featurization strategy (e.g., defect-centered graph, atom-centered local descriptor, SOAP, bispectrum/SNAP, symmetry functions, Voronoi/coordination features, Coulomb matrix variants, sparse defect representation, charge-aware embedding, foundation-potential embedding). |
| representation_strategy_description | str | Concise description of what is encoded and how (e.g., graph constructed around defect, radius cutoff, inclusion of pristine reference, difference features, global crystal context, periodic images, local subgraph extraction). |
| defect_centering_or_reference | str | Whether the representation is defect-centered and/or uses a pristine reference (e.g., encode defect neighborhood only; encode full supercell; encode delta features between defective and pristine; uses host-only baseline). |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | str | If local descriptors are used, extract key details: neighbor cutoff, angular/radial basis, invariances/equivariance, whether species are included and how (one-hot, continuous embeddings). |
| graph_model_architecture | str | If a graph model is used: model name/architecture (CGCNN, MEGNet, SchNet, DimeNet, GemNet, NequIP, MACE, Allegro, PaiNN, equivariant MPNN), and key settings if reported (equivariance, edge features, interaction blocks). |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | str | Any use of pretrained models/foundation interatomic potentials to generate embeddings or initialize networks (what model, what pretraining data/task, how embeddings are extracted or transferred). |
| data_regime_and_dataset | str | Dataset name/source and size (number of defective structures, defect types, number of hosts), data generation method (DFT, MD, experiments), and whether data are scarce/low-shot. |
| transferability_evidence | str | Evidence/results about transfer across hosts/chemistries (e.g., train on some materials, test on unseen materials; cross-chemistry splits; out-of-distribution evaluation) including any numerical results. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | str | Evidence/results about performance vs dataset size (learning curves, few-shot results, active learning, sample efficiency claims), with numbers if available. |
| evaluation_protocol | str | Train/validation/test split strategy (random, by composition, by host material, by defect type, by charge state), cross-validation, and any leakage-avoidance steps. |
| baselines_and_ablations | str | Reported comparisons between representations/featurizations (e.g., with/without defect-centering, with/without charge features, full-supercell vs local subgraph, descriptor vs GNN) and key ablation outcomes. |
| performance_metrics | str | Numerical predictive performance with metric and units where relevant (MAE/RMSE/R2 for energies in eV, barriers in eV, conductivity in W/mK, scattering rates), including per-task breakdown if given. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | str | How the ML outputs connect to phonon scattering or lattice thermal conductivity degradation (direct prediction of kappa; prediction of scattering rates; surrogate for BTE/Callaway; coupling to phonon calculations; use of relaxation time approximation), including assumptions. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | str | Authors' stated reasons why a representation helps (e.g., captures local symmetry breaking, long-range electrostatics, charge localization, strain fields, size-mismatch, chemical trends, invariance/equivariance benefits). |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | str | Reported negative results, limitations, or edge cases (e.g., poor generalization to new chemistries, issues with charge states, sensitivity to supercell size, inability to capture long-range fields, data bias). |
| recommended_best_practices | str | Any explicit recommendations for practitioners on defect/dopant representations, dataset construction, evaluation for transferability, or handling charged defects/complexes. |

artifacts.description: Please build theories about which representation and featurization strategies for point defects and dopants in crystalline materials (e.g., defect-centered graph encodings, local-environment descriptors, sparse defect representations, charge-aware embeddings, learned embeddings from foundation interatomic potentials) most improve machine learning prediction of defect-influenced material properties, and why. For additional context: we are especially interested in transferability across host materials and chemistries, data efficiency given scarce defect datasets, handling of charged defects and defect complexes, and downstream prediction of phonon scattering and lattice thermal conductivity degradation caused by defects, motivated by thermal management applications.

s2_metadata.abstract: The Materials Genome Initiative (MGI) has streamlined the materials discovery effort by leveraging generic traits of materials, with focus largely on perfect solids. Defects such as impurities and perturbations, however, drive many attractive functional properties of materials. The rich tapestry of charge, spin, and bonding states hosted by defects are not accessible to elements and perfect crystals, and defects can thus be viewed as another class of “elements” that lie beyond the periodic table. Accordingly, a Defect Genome Initiative (DGI) to accelerate functional defect discovery for energy, quantum information, and other applications is proposed. First, major advances made under the MGI are highlighted, followed by a delineation of pathways for accelerating the discovery and design of functional defects under the DGI. Near‐term goals for the DGI are suggested. The construction of open defect platforms and design of data‐driven functional defects, along with approaches for fabrication and characterization of defects, are discussed. The associated challenges and opportunities are considered and recent advances towards controlled introduction of functional defects at the atomic scale are reviewed. It is hoped this perspective will spur a community‐wide interest in undertaking a DGI effort in recognition of the importance of defects in enabling unique functionalities in materials.

tldr.text: This study highlights a consistent potential energy surface (PES) softening effect in three uMLIPs and finds that the PES softening behavior originates from a systematic underprediction error of the PES curvature, which derives from the biased sampling of near-equilibrium atomic arrangements in uMLIP pre-training datasets.

s2_metadata.abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have introduced a new paradigm for atomic simulations. Recent advancements have seen the emergence of universal MLIPs (uMLIPs) that are pre-trained on diverse materials datasets, providing opportunities for both ready-to-use universal force fields and robust foundations for downstream machine learning refinements. However, their performance in extrapolating to out-of-distribution complex atomic environments remains unclear. In this study, we highlight a consistent potential energy surface (PES) softening effect in three uMLIPs: M3GNet, CHGNet, and MACE-MP-0, which is characterized by energy and force under-prediction in a series of atomic-modeling benchmarks including surfaces, defects, solid-solution energetics, phonon vibration modes, ion migration barriers, and general high-energy states. We find that the PES softening behavior originates from a systematic underprediction error of the PES curvature, which derives from the biased sampling of near-equilibrium atomic arrangements in uMLIP pre-training datasets. We demonstrate that the PES softening issue can be effectively rectified by fine-tuning with a single additional data point. Our findings suggest that a considerable fraction of uMLIP errors are highly systematic, and can therefore be efficiently corrected. This result rationalizes the data-efficient fine-tuning performance boost commonly observed with foundational MLIPs. We argue for the importance of a comprehensive materials dataset with improved PES sampling for next-generation foundational MLIPs.

s2_metadata.abstract: Quantifying charge-state transition energy levels of impurities in semiconductors is critical to understanding and engineering their optoelectronic properties for applications ranging from solar photovoltaics to infrared lasers. While these transition levels can be measured and calculated accurately, such efforts are time-consuming and more rapid prediction methods would be beneficial. Here, we significantly reduce the time typically required to predict impurity transition levels using multi-fidelity datasets and a machine learning approach employing features based on elemental properties and impurity positions. We use transition levels obtained from low-fidelity (i.e., local-density approximation or generalized gradient approximation) density functional theory (DFT) calculations, corrected using a recently proposed modified band alignment scheme, which well-approximates transition levels from high-fidelity DFT (i.e., hybrid HSE06). The model fit to the large multi-fidelity database shows improved accuracy compared to the models trained on the more limited high-fidelity values. Crucially, in our approach, when using the multi-fidelity data, high-fidelity values are not required for model training, significantly reducing the computational cost required for training the model. Our machine learning model of transition levels has a root mean squared (mean absolute) error of 0.36 (0.27) eV vs high-fidelity hybrid functional values when averaged over 14 semiconductor systems from the II-VI and III-V families. As a guide for use on other systems, we assessed the model on simulated data to show the expected accuracy level as a function of bandgap for new materials of interest. Finally, we use the model to predict a complete space of impurity charge-state transition levels in all zinc blende III-V and II-VI systems.

s2_metadata.abstract: The presence of defects strongly influences semiconductor behavior. However, predicting the electronic properties of defective materials at finite temperatures remains computationally expensive even with density functional theory due to the large number of atoms in the simulation cell and the multitude of thermally accessible configurations. Here, we present a neural network-based framework to investigate the electronic properties of defective semiconductors at finite temperatures efficiently. We develop an active learning approach that integrates two advanced equivariant graph neural networks: MACE for atomic energies and forces and DeepH-E3 for the electronic Hamiltonian. Focusing on representative point defects in GaAs, we demonstrate computational accuracy comparable to density functional theory at a fraction of the computational cost, predicting the temperature-dependent band gap of defective GaAs directly from larger scale molecular dynamics trajectories with an accuracy of few tens of meV. Our results highlight the potential of equivariant neural networks for accurate atomic-scale predictions in complex, dynamically evolving materials.

s2_metadata.abstract: Point defects in solid-state materials are now routinely simulated using large supercell structures, requiring efficient quantum mechanical solutions. Data-driven and machine learning (ML) models trained on computational data can enable rapid defect property predictions and high-throughput screening. In this article, we provide an overview of prominent efforts to accelerate defect simulations using these approaches. We begin by discussing the motivations for data-driven techniques in defect modeling, and describe efforts over the past decade to use descriptor-based models for rapid screening of defect properties—most notably in oxides. In particular, we discuss case studies where surrogate models and interatomic potentials were trained on density functional theory (DFT) data, leading to predictions with quantum mechanical accuracies at a fraction of the cost. In addition to geometry relaxation and formation energy predictions, these interatomic potentials are capable of predicting phonon modes and vibrational free energies to yield defect energetics at finite temperatures—representing a key frontier for computational defect research. We finish with a discussion on how to connect these approaches and their outputs with experimental data, and provide an outlook on this burgeoning subfield. s2_metadata.abstract:
Understanding phonon transport properties in defect-laden AlN is important for their device applications. Here, we construct a machine-learning potential to describe phonon transport with accuracy in pristine and defect-laden AlN, following the template of Behler-Parrinello-type neural network potentials (NNPs) but extending them to consider multiple charge states of defects. The high accuracy of our NNP in predicting second- and third-order interatomic force constants is demonstrated through calculations of phonon bands, three-phonon anharmonic, phonon-isotope and phonon-defect scattering rates, and thermal conductivities. In particular, our NNP accurately describes the difference in phonon-related properties among various native defects and among different charge states of the defects. They reveal that the phonon-defect scattering rates induced by VN3+ are the largest, followed by VAl3−, and that VN1+ is the least effective scatterer. This is further confirmed by the magnitude of the respective depressions of the thermal conductivity of AlN. Our findings reveal the significance of the contribution from structural distortions induced by defects to the elastic scattering rates. The present work shows the usefulness of our NNP scheme to cost-efficiently study phonon transport in partially disordered crystalline phases containing charged defects.

s2_metadata.abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) can now reproduce the energy, forces and stresses of bulk materials with high accuracy compared to first-principles calculations. The description of imperfections, where coordination environments and electron counts deviate from those found in pristine reference structures, remains a challenge. We find that the current generation of foundation MLIPs do not describe the defect physics of the semiconductor Sb2Se3. We introduce global defect charge embeddings that distinguish the bonding characteristics of different charge states. We further employ a multi-fidelity approach that combines low-cost (semi-local exchange-correlation functional) reference data with high-quality (non-local hybrid functional) energies and forces that describe well the subtleties of the defect energy landscape. The resulting defect-capable force fields can find stable structural configurations and predict defect thermodynamics in quantitative agreement with direct quantum mechanical calculations, at a fraction of the computational cost.

s2_metadata.abstract: Point defects critically influence the properties of materials and devices, yet density functional theory (DFT) remains computationally demanding for defect supercell calculations. Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) offer high efficiency but require extensive datasets. MLIPs trained only on defect configurations in small supercells exhibit systematic energy errors in larger supercells, demonstrating limited transferability. Here, we present a machine learning Hamiltonian (MLH) model-based method for calculating total energies and atomic forces in defect supercells with linear-scaling computational cost, enabling efficient structural relaxation and accurate formation energy predictions. We take oxygen vacancies in amorphous SiO$_2$ as an example and train the MLH model on defect configurations in 95-atom supercells, with the training data derived from 120 self-consistent field calculations and 12 structural relaxations. The MLH model enables efficient structural relaxations for host (defect-free) and defect systems in larger supercells, avoiding the systematic energy errors observed in MLIPs. The cancellation of energy errors between host and defect systems yields accurate formation energy predictions, with deviations from DFT below 50 meV. The proposed method holds significant potential for defect simulations in complex materials.

This review provides a comprehensive review of ML/DL methods to enhance 2D materials research via the optimization of synthesis conditions, interpretation of complex data sets, and the use of generative adversarial networks and variational autoencoders for innovative material design and image processing tasks. s2_metadata.abstract: The presence of point defects, such as vacancies, plays an important role in materials design. Here, we explore the extrapolative power of a graph neural network (GNN) to predict vacancy formation energies. We show that a model trained only on perfect materials can also be used to predict vacancy formation energies (Evac) of defect structures without the need for additional training data. Such GNN-based predictions are considerably faster than density functional theory (DFT) calculations and show potential as a quick pre-screening tool for defect systems. To test this strategy, we developed a DFT dataset of 530 Evac consisting of 3D elemental solids, alloys, oxides, semiconductors, and 2D monolayer materials. We analyzed and discussed the applicability of such direct and fast predictions. We applied the model to predict 192 494 Evac for 55 723 materials in the JARVIS-DFT database. Our work demonstrates how a GNN-model performs on unseen data.

s2_metadata.abstract: Graphene, its derivatives such as graphene oxide and reduced graphene oxide, and related carbon nanostructures including carbon nanotubes, possess exceptional mechanical, thermal, and electronic properties. These features make them highly attractive for applications ranging from energy storage and filtration to flexible electronics and biomedical systems. Molecular simulation methods, including atomistic molecular dynamics, coarse grained modeling, and dissipative particle dynamics, have become essential tools for investigating the behavior of these materials at multiple length and time scales. This review presents recent advances in the modeling of graphene-based systems, highlighting how different simulation techniques are employed to explore mechanical deformation, defect evolution, thermal transport, and interfacial behavior. Special attention is given to the development of coarse-grained models, the role of force field selection, and the integration of machine learning to improve computational efficiency and predictive accuracy. Future directions include the use of high-performance computing, artificial intelligence assisted simulations, and scalable frameworks for large scale modeling. Overall, molecular simulations continue to play a critical role in the rational design and optimization of graphene-derived materials for advanced technological applications.

s2_metadata.abstract: Point defects in semiconductors dictate their electronic and optical properties. Vacancies, interstitials, substitutional defects, and defect complexes can form in the semiconductor lattice and significantly impact its performance in applications such as solar absorption, light emission, electronics, and catalysis. Understanding the nature and energetics of point defects is essential for the design and optimization of next-generation semiconductor technologies. Here, we provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of research on point defects in semiconductors, focusing on the application of density functional theory (DFT) and machine learning (ML) in accelerating the prediction and understanding of defect properties. DFT has been instrumental in accurately calculating defect formation energies, charge transition levels, and other defect-related properties such as carrier recombination rates and lifetimes, and ion migration barriers. ML techniques, particularly neural networks, have emerged as powerful tools for enabling rapid prediction of defect properties at DFT-accuracy in order to overcome the expense of using large supercells and advanced functionals. We begin this article with a discussion of different types of point defects and complexes, their impact on semiconductor properties, and the experimental and DFT approaches typically used for their characterization. Through multiple case studies, we explore how DFT has been successfully applied to understand defect behavior across a variety of semiconductors, and how ML approaches integrated with DFT can efficiently predict defect properties and facilitate the discovery of new materials with tailored defect behavior. Overall, the advent of ‘DFT+ML’ promises to drive advancements in semiconductor technology, catalysis, and renewable energy applications, paving the way for the development of high-performance semiconductors which are defect-tolerant or have desirable dopability.

s2_metadata.abstract: Defects dictate the properties of many functional materials. To understand the behaviour of defects and their impact on physical properties, it is necessary to identify the most stable defect geometries. However, global structure searching is computationally challenging for high-throughput defect studies or materials with complex defect landscapes, like alloys or disordered solids. Here, we tackle this limitation by harnessing a machine-learning surrogate model to qualitatively explore the structural landscape of neutral point defects. By learning defect motifs in a family of related metal chalcogenide and mixed anion crystals, the model successfully predicts favourable reconstructions for unseen defects in unseen compositions for 90% of cases, thereby reducing the number of first-principles calculations by 73%. Using CdSe_ x Te_1− x alloys as an exemplar, we train a model on the end member compositions and apply it to find the stable geometries of all inequivalent vacancies for a range of mixing concentrations, thus enabling more accurate and faster defect studies for configurationally complex systems.

s2_metadata.abstract: Ion migration in semiconductor devices is facilitated by the presence of point defects and has a major influence on electronic and optical properties. It is important to understand and identify ways to mitigate photoinduced and electrically induced defect-mediated ion migration in semiconductors. In this Perspective, we discuss the fundamental mechanisms of defect-mediated ion migration and diffusion as understood through atomistic simulations. The discussion covers a variety of case studies from the literature, with a special focus on metal halide perovskites, important materials for solar absorption and related optoelectronic applications. Tuning the perovskite composition and dimensionality and applying systematic strains are identified as ways to suppress phase segregation and ion migration. This Perspective delves into first-principles modeling approaches for defect migration and diffusion, presenting detailed case studies on the diffusion of defects and dopants in CdTe, hydrogen impurities in halide perovskites, and halogen migration in hybrid perovskites and emphasizing the importance of organic cations. The discussion further extends to accelerating the prediction of migration pathways and barriers through machine learning approaches, particularly the application of crystal-graph neural networks. By combining theoretical insights with practical case studies, this Perspective aims to provide an understanding of defect-mediated ion migration and suggestions for next-generation semiconductor discovery while considering ion migration suppression as one of many design objectives.

s2_metadata.abstract: We review recent machine learning (ML) approaches for point defects in non-metallic materials, with an emphasis on defect formation energies. Existing studies largely fall into two categories: direct ML models that predict defect energies from local structural representations, and ML potentials that approximate the defect-containing potential energy surface. We summarize key achievements as well as persistent bottlenecks, emphasizing that dataset quality often dominates practical model performance. We further identify charged-defect formation energies as a central frontier, where Fermi-level alignment, finite-size corrections, and long-range electrostatics must be handled carefully and consistently to enable meaningful comparisons and transferable predictions across different materials.

s2_metadata.abstract: Defects are ubiquitous in solids and strongly influence materials' mechanical and functional properties. However, non-destructive characterization and quantification of defects, especially when multiple types coexist, remain a long-standing challenge. Here we introduce DefectNet, a foundation machine learning model that predicts the chemical identity and concentration of substitutional point defects with multiple coexisting elements directly from vibrational spectra, specifically phonon density-of-states (PDoS). Trained on over 16,000 simulated spectra from 2,000 semiconductors, DefectNet employs a tailored attention mechanism to identify up to six distinct defect elements at concentrations ranging from 0.2% to 25%. The model generalizes well to unseen crystals across 56 elements and can be fine-tuned on experimental data. Validation using inelastic scattering measurements of SiGe alloys and MgB$_2$ superconductor demonstrates its accuracy and transferability. Our work establishes vibrational spectroscopy as a viable, non-destructive probe for point defect quantification in bulk materials, and highlights the promise of foundation models in data-driven defect engineering.

tldr.text: This work proposes a machine-learning charge density route for predicting defect formation energies with higher data efficiency and shows that charge-density learning enables more robust cross-size transfer than direct energy-force fitting and that mixed-size data design can substantially reduce the cost of defect prediction.

s2_metadata.abstract: First-principles defect calculations are often limited by the cost of the large supercells required to suppress image interactions. Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) provide another alternative, but training defect MLIPs typically requires thousands of structures and weeks of data generation. Since charge density is the key to density-functional-theory (DFT), we propose a machine-learning charge density (MLCD) route for predicting defect formation energies with higher data efficiency. We optimize the training set by integrating small supercells of varying sizes for better extrapolation, allocating their proportions based on spatial charge-density analysis. With only 96 supercells containing 16--96 atoms as the dataset, MLCD accurately predicts the formation energies of four intrinsic defects in 360-atom supercells, with defect-wise mean absolute error below 0.05 eV. In contrast, MLIPs trained on the same dataset can err by more than 1 eV. These results show that charge-density learning enables more robust cross-size transfer than direct energy-force fitting and that mixed-size data design can substantially reduce the cost of defect prediction.

s2_metadata.abstract: First-principles computations reliably predict the energetics of point defects in semiconductors but are constrained by the expense of using large supercells and advanced levels of theory. Machine learning models trained on computational data, especially ones that sufficiently encode defect coordination environments, can be used to accelerate defect predictions. Here, we develop a framework for the prediction and screening of native defects and functional impurities in a chemical space of group IV, III–V, and II–VI zinc blende semiconductors, powered by crystal Graph-based Neural Networks (GNNs) trained on high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) data. Using an innovative approach of sampling partially optimized defect configurations from DFT calculations, we generate one of the largest computational defect datasets to date, containing many types of vacancies, self-interstitials, anti-site substitutions, impurity interstitials and substitutions, as well as some defect complexes. We applied three types of established GNN techniques, namely crystal graph convolutional neural network, materials graph network, and Atomistic Line Graph Neural Network (ALIGNN), to rigorously train models for predicting defect formation energy (DFE) in multiple charge states and chemical potential conditions. We find that ALIGNN yields the best DFE predictions with root mean square errors around 0.3 eV, which represents a prediction accuracy of 98% given the range of values within the dataset, improving significantly on the state-of-the-art. We further show that GNN-based defective structure optimization can take us close to DFT-optimized geometries at a fraction of the cost of full DFT. The current models are based on the semi-local generalized gradient approximation-Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional but are highly promising because of the correlation of computed energetics and defect levels with higher levels of theory and experimental data, the accuracy and necessity of discovering novel metastable and low energy defect structures at the PBE level of theory before advanced methods could be applied, and the ability to train multi-fidelity models in the future with new data from non-local functionals. The DFT-GNN models enable prediction and screening across thousands of hypothetical defects based on both unoptimized and partially optimized defective structures, helping identify electronically active defects in technologically important semiconductors.

s2_metadata.abstract: Point defects dictate the properties of many functional materials. The standard approach to modelling the thermodynamics of defects relies on a static description, where the change in Gibbs free energy is approximated by the internal energy. This approach has a low computational cost, but ignores contributions from atomic vibrations and structural configurations that can be accessed at finite temperatures. We train a machine learning force field (MLFF) to explore dynamic defect behaviour using Te+1i and V+2Te in CdTe as exemplars. We consider the different entropic contributions (e.g., electronic, spin, vibrational, orientational, and configurational) and compare methods to compute the defect free energies, ranging from a harmonic treatment to a fully anharmonic approach based on thermodynamic integration. We find that metastable configurations are populated at room temperature and thermal effects increase the predicted concentration of Te+1i by two orders of magnitude — and can thus significantly affect the predicted properties. Overall, our study underscores the importance of finite-temperature effects and the potential of MLFFs to model defect dynamics at both synthesis and device operating temperatures.

s2_metadata.abstract: We developed a framework for predicting the energies and ground state configurations of native point defects, extrinsic dopants and impurities, and defect complexes across zinc blende-phase Cd/Zn-Te/Se/S compounds, important for CdTe-based solar cells. This framework, named DeFecT-FF, is powered by high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) computations and crystal graph-based machine learning force field (MLFF) models trained on the DFT data. The Cd/Zn-Te/Se/S chemical space is chosen because alloying at Cd or Te sites is a promising avenue to tailor the electronic and defect properties of the CdTe absorber layer to potentially improve solar cell performance. The sheer number of defect configurations achievable when considering all possible singular defects and their combinations, symmetry-breaking operations, and defect charge states, as well as the expense of running large supercell calculations, makes this an ideal problem for developing accurate and widely-applicable force field models. Here, we introduce our dataset of structures and energies from HSE06 geometry optimization, including bulk and alloyed supercells with and without defects. Data were gradually expanded using active learning and accurate MLFF models were trained to predict energies and atomic forces across different charge states. Via accelerated prediction and screening, we identified many new low energy defect configurations and obtained high-fidelity defect formation energy diagrams using HSE06 calculations with spin-orbit coupling. The DeFecT-FF framework has been released publicly as an online tool on the nanoHUB platform, allowing users to upload any crystallographic information file, generate defects of interest, and compute defect formation energies as a function of Fermi level and chemical potential conditions, thus bypassing expensive DFT calculations.

extracted_data.name_full: Multi-fidelity (MBA-corrected) ML with elemental + one-hot features using Gradient Boosting Regression
extracted_data.brief_description: A machine-learning pipeline that predicts impurity charge-state transition levels by training a gradient-boosting regressor on a large dataset of low-fidelity (LDA/GGA) DFT transition levels corrected by a Modified Band Alignment (MBA) scheme, using only elemental properties and one-hot encoded impurity-position and charge-state features (no structural/graph descriptors).
extracted_data.citation_title: Machine Learning for Impurity Charge-State Transition Levels in Semiconductors from Elemental Properties Using Multi-Fidelity Datasets
extracted_data.material_systems: II-VI Cd-based systems (CdS, CdSe, CdTe, alloys) and binary III-V zincblende semiconductors (AlP, AlAs, AlSb, GaP, GaAs, GaSb, InP, InAs, InSb) — multiple hosts (14 systems used for training/validation; full prediction space extends to 18 binary zincblende systems and 63 impurity elements).
extracted_data.defect_types: Substitutional impurities/dopants (impurity charge-state transition levels); explicit defect complexes are not reported as included (only single-impurity sites considered; 5 defect sites enumerated), vacancies/antisites/ Frenkel pairs/complexes not treated.
extracted_data.charge_state_handling: Explicit charge-state label is included as a feature; DFT targets include charged-defect energies computed with supercells and Freysoldt–Neugebauer–Van de Walle (FNV) finite-size electrostatic charge corrections; Fermi-level/chemical potential enters implicitly via the charge-transition-level target but is not an explicit continuous feature beyond the charge label.
extracted_data.target_properties: Impurity charge-state transition energy levels (charge transition levels) relative to band edges (i.e., defect transition energies in eV).
extracted_data.representation_strategy_name: Elemental + one-hot impurity-position and charge-state feature vector (sparse tabular representation)
extracted_data.representation_strategy_description: Handcrafted tabular feature vector composed of elemental properties (ionization energies, electronegativity, electrical conductivity, etc.), one-hot encoding of impurity lattice site/position, and explicit impurity charge-state as a categorical/ numerical feature; no atomistic local structural descriptors, no atom-centered radial/angular basis, and no graph/neural message-passing representation. Targets are MBA-corrected low-fidelity DFT values.
extracted_data.defect_centering_or_reference: Not defect-centered in a geometric/graph sense — representation encodes the impurity identity, its site (one-hot), and charge state but does not encode an explicit defect-centered local atomic graph or delta features between defective and pristine geometries; the DFT target implicitly references the defective supercell (MBA-corrected), but the input features are non-geometric elemental/site encodings.
extracted_data.local_environment_descriptor_details: No explicit local-environment descriptors (no neighbor cutoff, no angular/radial basis functions, no SOAP/SOAP-like or symmetry-function features). Species information entered via elemental scalar properties (continuous) and one-hot site encoding; categorical charge-state feature included. No invariance/equivariance architectural details because no atomistic local descriptors/GNN were used.
extracted_data.graph_model_architecture: None — model is a non-graph ensemble regressor (Gradient Boosting Regression).
extracted_data.pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings: None reported — no use of pretrained/foundation interatomic potentials or pretrained neural embeddings; features are directly elemental descriptors and one-hot encodings.
extracted_data.data_regime_and_dataset: Training/validation dataset: 2910 low-fidelity (LDA or GGA) impurity transition levels corrected with MBA used as ML targets; 896 of these systems additionally have high-fidelity HSE06 calculations (used for testing/benchmarking). Data generated with DFT (VASP) on 64-atom supercells with spin polarization and ionic relaxation; dataset covers <10% of the enumerated full impurity/charge-space (full space ≈ 34,524 possible transition levels). Dataset is moderate-sized but not huge; authors describe potential scarcity for some subregions.
extracted_data.transferability_evidence: Cross-validation and multi-fidelity results: 10-fold cross validation (with nested CV for hyperparameter/feature selection) used throughout. Evidence that training on the larger MBA-corrected low-fidelity dataset yields better prediction of HSE06-level transition levels than training directly on smaller HSE06 sets: ML predicted MBA -> HSE06 RMSE = 0.36 eV (better than direct ML->HSE06 RMSE = 0.42 eV). Synthetic tests assessing classification performance across band gaps show better applicability for larger-gap hosts (e.g., systems with band gaps ≳1 eV have F1 > 75% for 'in-gap' classification). No explicit leave-one-chemistry-out OOD numerical split reported, but 10-fold CV over pooled data is used; authors additionally simulated performance on hypothetical band gaps.
extracted_data.data_efficiency_evidence: Feature-learning curve: performance plateaus after ≈15 top-ranked features. Data learning curve: adding ≈1500 more low-fidelity points (≈50% more) is estimated to reduce MAE/RMSE by ~50 meV if trend persists. Multi-fidelity approach shown to be more data-efficient than training on a smaller high-fidelity set: larger MBA-corrected low-fidelity dataset produces lower error in predicting HSE06-level values than direct ML on limited HSE06 data (quantified RMSE improvement from 0.42 eV to 0.36 eV).
extracted_data.evaluation_protocol: 10-fold cross-validation for main performance reporting; nested 10-fold CV inside each top-level training set for hyperparameter optimization and feature selection to avoid information leakage. Comparison to HSE06 performed on 896-system subset with HSE06 calculations. Synthetic sampling used to assess classification metrics vs band gap. No explicit by-composition holdout (e.g., leave-one-host-out) reported.
extracted_data.baselines_and_ablations: Baselines: (1) MBA-corrected low-fidelity vs HSE06 (RMSE 0.24 eV), (2) direct ML predicting HSE06 (RMSE 0.42 eV), (3) ML predicting MBA then comparing to HSE06 (this work) (RMSE 0.36 eV). Ablations/analyses: feature-importance ranking used to select top 15 features (performance plateaus beyond 15); latent-variable transfer-learning (predict low-fidelity then use as feature to predict HSE06) was tested and improved over direct ML->HSE06 but did not outperform the MBA-target multi-fidelity approach. No ablation comparing atomistic local descriptors or graph representations because such representations were not used.
extracted_data.performance_metrics: Reported errors for predicted charge-state transition levels (energies in eV): MBA vs HSE06 RMSE = 0.24 eV (benchmark); ML predicted HSE06 (direct) RMSE = 0.42 eV; ML predicted MBA vs MBA RMSE = 0.27 eV; ML predicted MBA vs HSE06 RMSE = 0.36 eV; corresponding MAE for ML predicted MBA vs HSE06 = 0.27 eV. Precision/recall/F1 presented for classification of 'in-gap' / half-gap / third-gap occupancy as functions of host band gap (synthetic and resampled evaluation).
extracted_data.phonon_or_thermal_transport_link: No connection — the paper does not predict phonon scattering rates or lattice thermal conductivity degradation, nor does it couple ML predictions to phonon transport models; phonon/thermal transport is not addressed.
extracted_data.interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims: Authors argue that simple elemental properties plus impurity site and charge-state encodings capture dominant chemical trends determining transition levels, and that using a much larger (but corrected) low-fidelity dataset via MBA yields better effective high-fidelity predictions (improved transferability/data efficiency) than training on a smaller high-fidelity set. They note that errors arise mainly from physics not captured by semilocal DFT (e.g., incorrect localization) which MBA cannot fix.
extracted_data.failure_modes_and_limitations: Model limitations reported: poorer quantitative accuracy for low band-gap materials (errors of ≈0.36 eV can flip shallow vs deep defect classification); cases where LDA/GGA fail to capture electronic localization produce large discrepancies not corrected by MBA and cause outliers; lack of structural/local-environment encoding may limit capture of relaxation/local-strain effects; dataset covers <10% of combinatorial space and does not include defect complexes; symmetry constraints were not explicitly broken in relaxations which may miss local minima; no explicit handling of long-range electrostatics beyond FNV corrections and charge label.
extracted_data.recommended_best_practices: Use MBA-corrected large low-fidelity datasets to train ML models when high-fidelity data are scarce; include explicit impurity charge-state and impurity-site one-hot features plus relevant elemental properties (ionization energy, electronegativity, conductivity, etc.); use FNV corrections for charged-defect DFT targets; perform nested CV (hyperparameter selection within outer CV) to avoid leakage; select a compact set (~15) of physically-meaningful features via importance ranking; assess applicability as a function of host band gap (classification metrics) before trusting fine-grained predictions; include HSE06/high-fidelity calculations where possible for validation and to identify localization failures.

extracted_data.name_full: MACE (equivariant message-passing) machine-learning force field trained separately for each system/supercell
extracted_data.brief_description: An equivariant message-passing ML force field (MACE) trained on DFT energies/forces/stresses of full supercells (bulk and defective charged supercells) to model defect potential-energy surfaces and enable MD/TI-based free-energy calculations of charged point defects.
extracted_data.material_systems: CdTe host (bulk), point defects in CdTe (Te_i^{+1}, V_Te^{+2}), elemental Te (multiple solid phases and liquid); multiple systems were modelled but all within Cd/Te chemistry (no cross-chemistry transfer experiments reported).
extracted_data.defect_types: Point defects: interstitial (Te_i^{+1}) and vacancy (V_Te^{+2}); charged defects were modelled explicitly in supercells. No substitutional dopants, Frenkel pairs or explicit defect complexes beyond charged single-defect supercells are reported.
extracted_data.charge_state_handling: Charged defects were modelled by training separate MLFFs on charged-defect supercells (e.g., distinct models for Te_i^{+1} and V_Te^{+2}); formation energies include a posteriori charged-defect finite-size corrections (Kumagai-Oba eFNV) and Fermi-level contributions in the thermodynamic formalism. No explicit charge label feature vector or electron-density embedding is reported; charge handled by separate datasets/models per charge state and by standard charged-supercell corrections in analysis.
extracted_data.target_properties: Defect formation free energies g_f(T) (decomposed into vibrational, orientational, structural/configurational, electronic and spin entropies), potential energy surfaces (energies and barriers), energy/force/stress predictions for MD, phonons/vibrational free energies (bulk validation), anharmonic free energies via thermodynamic integration, defect migration/hopping barriers and associated rates. No direct ML prediction of phonon scattering rates or lattice thermal conductivity (kappa) degradation was performed.
extracted_data.representation_strategy_name: Equivariant atomic message-passing MLFF (MACE) operating on full supercells with ZBL short-range correction
extracted_data.representation_strategy_description: MACE represents the system as atoms with local atomic environments within a cutoff and performs equivariant message passing to predict per-system total energy, forces and stresses. Short-range Ziegler–Biersack–Littmark (ZBL) pair repulsion is included. Models are trained on full-supercell DFT energies/forces/stresses for bulk and for each defect/charge-state supercell separately.
extracted_data.defect_centering_or_reference: Full-supercell representation (the MLFF learns the total energy of the defective supercell directly). The authors emphasize training separate models per system (bulk, defect charge states, reservoir element Te) rather than training a single joint model; they also warn against training only on defect configurations if the model will be used to compute absolute energies for larger supercells.
extracted_data.local_environment_descriptor_details: Cutoff radius = 5 Å; correlation order = 3; angular resolution = 3; species included explicitly (Cd, Te); architecture uses 256 invariant messages (per the MACE settings reported). ZBL pair repulsion term added for short-range repulsion. No explicit one-hot or continuous pretrained elemental embedding is reported beyond MACE's internal treatment of species.
extracted_data.graph_model_architecture: MACE (equivariant message-passing architecture) with 2 message-passing layers, 256 invariant messages, correlation order 3, angular resolution 3, cutoff 5 Å; Huber loss with weighted energy/force/stress terms during training; training used reference energies defined relative to isolated Cd and Te atoms. (MACE is an equivariant MPNN; specific equivariance / tensor order details are those of MACE as used here.)
extracted_data.pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings: None reported — MACE models were trained from-scratch on DFT-generated datasets for each system; no pretrained/foundation interatomic potential embeddings or transfer of pretrained network weights is described.
extracted_data.data_regime_and_dataset: DFT-generated datasets created with VASP on-the-fly MD (structure similarity kernel) using heating runs (NPT, 100 K up to >840 K), plus compressed/expanded cells (0.9–1.1 volume) for quasiharmonic sampling. Independent datasets & models for: bulk CdTe (2x2x2 conventional supercell, 64 atoms), Te_i^{+1} supercell, V_Te^{+2} supercell, elemental Te (multiple phases including liquid). Test sets: NPT MD at 300, 550, 900 K with five independent 24 ps runs per temperature; 100–300 sampled configs per temperature were re-evaluated with DFT for MAE/RMSE calculation. Exact total dataset sizes (number of training structures) are not enumerated in the main text (learning-curve details are in SI).
extracted_data.transferability_evidence: Evidence of limited transferability across modelling choices: authors report that training separate models per system (bulk and defect datasets) yields higher accuracy than a single joint model trained on all systems; they also report that models trained only on defect configurations (i.e., excluding bulk training) can show systematic errors in total energies when applied to larger supercells than those used for training, indicating poor transfer to different system sizes. No experiments training on one chemistry and testing on another were performed.
extracted_data.data_efficiency_evidence: No quantitative few-shot/fine-tuning experiments reported in main text. Authors state that defect-only training gives higher accuracy for defective supercells of the same atom count but warns about systematic errors for larger supercells; learning curves for Te_i^{+1} are mentioned to be in the Supporting Information but no main-text numbers are given. Training used ~150–200 epochs with 10% validation; no explicit small-data performance numbers reported in main text.
extracted_data.evaluation_protocol: Validation: 10% of dataset used as validation during training. Test: MD-generated trajectories (NPT) at 300, 550, 900 K; five independent 24 ps runs at each temperature; 100–300 equally-spaced configurations sampled per run and recalculated with DFT for test MAE/RMSE. Training/validation/test splits are time/trajectory-based sampling; no composition- or charge-state-based cross-validation beyond separate models per system. Finite-size charged-defect corrections (Kumagai-Oba eFNV) are applied in formation-energy analysis to avoid supercell-charge artifacts.
extracted_data.baselines_and_ablations: Architectural/representation comparisons reported: (i) independent per-system MACE models vs a single joint model — independent models were more accurate; (ii) defect-only training vs models including bulk — defect-only training yields higher accuracy for same-size defective supercells but causes systematic energy errors when applied to larger supercells (advised against). No explicit ablation removing equivariance or changing cutoff is reported in main text. For thermodynamics, the authors compare harmonic, quasiharmonic, and fully anharmonic (TI) approaches — this is for free-energy methodology rather than ML representation ablation.
extracted_data.performance_metrics: Test MAE/RMSE reported (Table I) for energies, forces, stresses on test sets: CdTe energy MAE=0.3 meV/atom (RMSE 0.4), force MAE=13 meV/Å (RMSE 17), stress MAE=0.2 meV/Å^3 (RMSE 0.3); Te_i^{+1} energy MAE=0.5 meV/atom (RMSE 0.7), force MAE=21 meV/Å (RMSE 30), stress MAE=0.2 meV/Å^3 (RMSE 0.3); V_Te^{+2} energy MAE=0.4 meV/atom (RMSE 0.6), force MAE=18 meV/Å (RMSE 24), stress MAE=0.2 meV/Å^3 (RMSE 0.3); Te (elemental) energy MAE=1.6 meV/atom (RMSE 2.3), force MAE=73 meV/Å (RMSE 102) attributed to inclusion of liquid phase. For thermodynamic integration, they aimed for TI error sigma_mu < 0.25 meV/atom (~20 meV/supercell) and used multiple independent TI runs to estimate uncertainty.
extracted_data.phonon_or_thermal_transport_link: MLFFs were validated against phonons and used to compute harmonic/quasiharmonic vibrational free energies and fully anharmonic free energies via non-equilibrium thermodynamic integration (TI), enabling temperature-dependent defect formation free energies; authors computed anharmonicity scores (FHI-vibes) for pristine and defective systems. However, the paper does not present direct ML predictions of phonon scattering rates or lattice thermal conductivity degradation (kappa). Instead, the MLFF provides accurate vibrational/anharmonic free energies and dynamical sampling (MD) that could be used as inputs to further phonon-scattering or BTE-based calculations, but such coupling to kappa prediction was not performed here.
extracted_data.interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims: Authors state that learning the defect energy surface with an MLFF (MACE) reduces cost and enables long-time/large-scale sampling of defect dynamics and anharmonic contributions; separate per-system training improves accuracy because defect and bulk configurational spaces differ; including compressed/expanded volumes is necessary to capture quasiharmonic thermal expansion; including ZBL improves short-range repulsion handling. They argue the MLFF captures local symmetry-breaking, metastability and anharmonicity important for defect entropies and dynamics.
extracted_data.failure_modes_and_limitations: Reported limitations: (i) models trained only on defect configurations may produce systematic energy errors when applied to different system sizes (lack of transfer across supercell sizes); (ii) more challenging systems (e.g., liquid phases) show higher errors (Te liquid shows larger force errors); (iii) computational cost remains high for fully anharmonic TI and long MD (need many and long MD runs); (iv) electronic-entropy estimates require accurate electronic structure — the MLFF does not replace the need for higher-level electronic structure for electronic entropy; (v) no explicit long-range electrostatic descriptor or embedding was used—charged-defect analysis relies on standard charged-supercell corrections rather than an ML-incorporated electrostatic feature, which could limit capturing long-range fields if that were required.
extracted_data.recommended_best_practices: Authors' recommendations and methodological prescriptions: (1) train separate MLFFs for bulk, each charged-defect supercell and reservoir phases to maximise accuracy; (2) avoid training only on defect configurations if the model will be used to compute absolute energies for larger supercells (include bulk data); (3) include compressed/expanded volumes to enable quasiharmonic sampling; (4) include liquid/phase-relevant configurations if reservoir phases melt near target temperatures; (5) include ZBL short-range repulsion and validate phonons and vibrational free energies; (6) use ShakeNBreak (or similar) to identify metastable defect configurations for structural/configurational entropy estimation; (7) apply finite-size charged-defect corrections (eFNV/Kumagai-Oba) when computing formation energies from supercell energies; (8) ensure TI switching/equilibration times and number of independent runs are sufficient to drive TI standard error below ~0.25 meV/atom (≈20 meV/supercell) for reliable g_f differences.

extracted_data.name_full: Atomistic Line Graph Neural Network applied to full supercell energy-per-atom prediction
extracted_data.brief_description: Use of a pretrained ALIGNN energy-per-atom model (trained on perfect bulk structures) applied directly to full defect supercells to predict vacancy formation energies via E_defect - E_perfect + mu, without any defect-specific training.
extracted_data.citation_title: A Deep-learning Model for Fast Prediction of Vacancy Formation in Diverse Materials
extracted_data.material_systems: Diverse: 3D elemental solids, metallic alloys, oxides, nitrides, and 2D monolayers; pretrained on 55,723 bulk solids (JARVIS-DFT); tested on DFT vacancy dataset of 508 entries and applied to 55,723 materials to produce 192,494 vacancy predictions.
extracted_data.defect_types: Vacancies only (single-atom vacancies); neutral defects only; no interstitials, substitutionals, antisites, Frenkel pairs, or defect complexes included.
extracted_data.charge_state_handling: None — study explicitly restricted to neutral vacancies; charged defects and charge-state handling not included.
extracted_data.target_properties: Vacancy formation energy (E_vacancy) computed as E_defect - E_perfect + chemical potential (mu).
extracted_data.representation_strategy_name: Full-supercell atomistic graph (ALIGNN) with energy-per-atom prediction
extracted_data.representation_strategy_description: Represent the entire (periodic) supercell as an atomistic graph: atom nodes with atomic-property features and edges representing bonds/distances; use ALIGNN line-graph construction (bond-distance nodes and bond-angle edges) to predict total/energy-per-atom for both defect and pristine supercells, then form the vacancy formation energy as a difference plus chemical potential.
extracted_data.defect_centering_or_reference: Not defect-centered: entire supercell graph including the missing-atom site (node removed) is encoded. A pristine reference energy per atom from a perfect cell is used and the formation energy is computed as a delta between predicted defect and perfect energies (plus mu).
extracted_data.local_environment_descriptor_details: Node features: 9 per-atom features (electronegativity, group number, covalent radius, valence electrons, first ionization energy, electron affinity, block, atomic volume, and related atomic-property features reported). Edge features: interatomic bond distances expanded with radial basis functions, up to an 8 Å cutoff and using 12 nearest neighbours; line-graph encodes bond-angles. Species are encoded via continuous atomic-property features rather than one-hot.
extracted_data.graph_model_architecture: ALIGNN (Atomistic Line Graph Neural Network) using edge-gated graph convolutions; uses both bond-distance edge features and bond-angle information through a line-graph construction; implemented in PyTorch and DGL. Not an explicitly equivariant MPNN (uses distance/angle features).
extracted_data.pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings: Yes — used a pretrained ALIGNN energy-per-atom model trained on JARVIS-DFT OptB88vdW energy-per-atom data for 55,723 perfect materials; model weights used without further fine-tuning on defect data.
extracted_data.data_regime_and_dataset: Pretraining dataset: JARVIS-DFT bulk energy-per-atom (55,723 solids). Defect test DFT dataset: 508 charge-neutral vacancy entries (elemental solids, alloys, oxides, 2D monolayers) generated with OptB88vdW DFT and relaxed. Predicted large-scale dataset: 192,494 vacancy formation energies for 55,723 materials. Defect dataset is small (508), i.e., low-shot/sparse for defect-specific learning.
extracted_data.transferability_evidence: Direct transfer from model trained only on perfect bulk structures to defect energetics demonstrated: ALIGNN predictions correlate with DFT vacancies (MAE 1.51 eV) and improve with a global scissor-shift to MAE 1.0 eV. Subset performance: Elements MAE 1.53 -> 1.2 eV (after shift), Oxides 2.3 -> 1.4 eV, 2D monolayers 1.9 -> 1.2 eV. Authors note better transfer for oxides and 2D semiconducting/insulating systems versus elemental/metals due to local message passing and bonding differences.
extracted_data.data_efficiency_evidence: Authors varied the amount of bulk pretraining data used (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, 100% of energy-per-atom training set) and reported corresponding vacancy-prediction MAEs: 1.20 eV, 1.22 eV, 1.11 eV, 1.05 eV, and 1.00 eV respectively, showing improved defect prediction with larger bulk pretraining sets (evidence that more diverse perfect-structure training improves defect transfer).
extracted_data.evaluation_protocol: Pretrained ALIGNN model (trained on bulk JARVIS-DFT) used without defect fine-tuning. Test set: independently computed DFT vacancy dataset of 508 entries. ALIGNN predicted energies for both defect and perfect structures; vacancy formation energies calculated via Eq. 2 using chemical potentials from JARVIS. No cross-validation on defect data (no defect-training). Comparison metrics reported as MAE versus DFT. Defect structures passed to ALIGNN were generated by deleting an atom at a unique Wyckoff position without relaxing atomic positions (while DFT defect energies were computed with relaxation).
extracted_data.baselines_and_ablations: Comparisons: (1) Original ALIGNN predictions vs DFT, (2) ALIGNN + scissor-shift heuristic (+1.3 eV) to reduce systematic underestimation, (3) literature ML models trained on defect-specific datasets (reported MAEs 0.40 eV and 0.67 eV) mentioned as specialized baselines. Ablation: effect of pretraining dataset size on defect MAE (20–100% experiments). No ablation explicitly comparing defect-centered vs full-supercell encodings or inclusion/exclusion of angle features.
extracted_data.performance_metrics: Vacancy formation energy MAE (vs DFT): overall original ALIGNN MAE = 1.51 eV; with global scissor-shift (add 1.3 eV) MAE = 1.00 eV. Subsets (original -> scissor-shift MAE): Elements 1.53 -> 1.2 eV; Oxides 2.30 -> 1.4 eV; 2D monolayers 1.90 -> 1.2 eV. Pretrained ALIGNN energy-per-atom model (reported from ref.) MAE = 0.037 eV for energy-per-atom prediction on perfect structures.
extracted_data.phonon_or_thermal_transport_link: None — the paper does not attempt to predict phonon scattering rates or lattice thermal conductivity degradation, nor to connect ML defect energetics to phonon transport models.
extracted_data.interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims: Authors suggest ALIGNN captures a transferable functional form for energies via local message passing and angle information; message-passing locality may favor insulating/less-bonded systems (oxides, 2D) over metallic systems with delocalized electrons and many bonds. They argue increasing diversity/size of perfect-structure pretraining data should improve defect transferability.
extracted_data.failure_modes_and_limitations: Explicit limitations: only charge-neutral vacancies considered; finite supercell size effects; ALIGNN tends to systematically underestimate vacancy formation energies (necessitating a scissor-shift); poorer accuracy for elemental solids/alloys (metallic systems) relative to oxides/2D; defect structures used unrelaxed for ALIGNN prediction whereas DFT defect energies are relaxed (mismatch); no treatment of charged defects, defect complexes, or long-range electrostatics/background-charge corrections; relatively small DFT defect dataset (508) limits evaluation.
extracted_data.recommended_best_practices: Authors recommend leveraging pretrained total-energy models trained on large, diverse perfect-structure datasets to rapidly screen defect energetics, increasing the diversity/size of perfect-structure training sets to improve transfer, and being aware of limitations: explicitly handle/compute charged defects separately, consider supercell-size effects, and validate via DFT for high-value candidates; a simple heuristic correction (global scissor-shift) may reduce systematic bias.

extracted_data.name_full: Atomistic Line Graph representation (ALIGNN) featurization
extracted_data.brief_description: The ALIGNN featurization constructs an atomistic graph with atomic-property node features and distance-based edge features, augmented by a line-graph that encodes bond-angle information, enabling message passing that incorporates both radial and angular structural information.
extracted_data.citation_title: A Deep-learning Model for Fast Prediction of Vacancy Formation in Diverse Materials
extracted_data.material_systems: Applied across a broad set of crystalline materials in this paper (bulk solids and 2D), and pretrained on 55,723 JARVIS-DFT bulk entries.
extracted_data.defect_types: Used in this work to represent vacancy-containing supercells (single neutral vacancies); ALIGNN itself is a general crystal representation not limited to vacancies.
extracted_data.charge_state_handling: No explicit charge-aware features in the representation described; charged-defect handling was not performed in this study.
extracted_data.target_properties: Originally used to predict total energy / energy per atom; in this paper used to produce vacancy formation energies via energy differences.
extracted_data.representation_strategy_name: Atomistic line-graph featurization (distance + angle features) with atomic-property node embeddings
extracted_data.representation_strategy_description: Nodes = atoms with continuous atomic-property features (9 properties). Edges = bond/distances encoded with radial basis functions up to 8 Å and limited to 12 nearest neighbors. A line graph is constructed where bond-distances become nodes and bond-angles serve as line-graph edges; message passing updates both node and edge/line-graph features.
extracted_data.defect_centering_or_reference: Full-structure encoding (entire supercell) rather than extracting a strictly local, defect-centered subgraph. Vacancy formation energy uses predicted energies for both defective and pristine full cells as the reference.
extracted_data.local_environment_descriptor_details: Key settings: radial basis expansion of interatomic distances, cutoff 8 Å, 12-NN neighbor list; atomic species encoded via 9 continuous atomic-property features (no one-hot), angles included through line graph; invariances: uses distance and angle features so representation is invariant to translation/rotation via scalar geometric descriptors (no explicit equivariant vector/tensor features reported).
extracted_data.graph_model_architecture: ALIGNN architecture (atomistic graph + line graph) with edge-gated graph convolution and propagation functions; implemented in PyTorch + DGL. The model uses both node and edge updates and incorporates angle information via the line graph.
extracted_data.pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings: ALIGNN model used here was pretrained for energy-per-atom prediction on JARVIS-DFT; the same pretrained representation/weights were used directly for defect energy inference.
extracted_data.data_regime_and_dataset: ALIGNN pretrained on 55,723 JARVIS-DFT bulk entries (OptB88vdW energies). In this work the representation is evaluated on a defect DFT set of 508 neutral vacancies.
extracted_data.transferability_evidence: ALIGNN representation/weights trained on perfect crystals transferred to predicting defect energetics (vacancies) with moderate accuracy (MAE 1.51 eV before correction), showing representation-level transfer from pristine to defective structures.
extracted_data.data_efficiency_evidence: Increasing the amount of bulk data used to train the ALIGNN energy model improves downstream vacancy-prediction MAE (reported for 20–100% of bulk training data); no few-shot defect fine-tuning experiments reported.
extracted_data.evaluation_protocol: Pretrained ALIGNN energy model trained on bulk energies, then applied unchanged to defective and pristine supercell graphs to compute formation energies; testing performed against an independent DFT vacancy dataset of 508 entries.
extracted_data.baselines_and_ablations: Reported ablation-like experiment: effect of varying the fraction of bulk training data on vacancy prediction MAE. No direct ablations isolating the contribution of angle features, RBF cutoff, or node-feature sets reported in this paper.
extracted_data.performance_metrics: Indirect performance reported through vacancy-formation MAE when using the pretrained ALIGNN energy predictions (overall MAE 1.51 eV; energy-per-atom ALIGNN reported elsewhere MAE 0.037 eV).
extracted_data.phonon_or_thermal_transport_link: None — no explicit use of ALIGNN representation for phonon-scattering or thermal-transport predictions in this work.
extracted_data.interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims: Authors argue that including bond-angle information via the line graph and atomic-property features helps capture local energetic contributions; locality of message passing favors systems with more localized bonding (insulators/oxides/2D) over delocalized metallic systems.
extracted_data.failure_modes_and_limitations: Representation lacks explicit charge-aware descriptors and long-range electrostatics treatment; performance degraded on metallic/delocalized systems; no tests on charged defects or defect complexes; prediction used unrelaxed defective geometries which can mismatch relaxed DFT energetics.
extracted_data.recommended_best_practices: Use large, diverse bulk datasets for ALIGNN pretraining if the goal is transfer to defect energetics; include angular information and atomic-property features; validate predictions for metals and charged defects separately as the representation lacks explicit long-range/charge handling.
