components.theory_description: For charged defects, the PES and especially force constants change with charge state even at identical coordinates; this non-uniqueness cannot be resolved by structure-only descriptors. The high-information fork is: (A) training separate models per charge state is sufficient, versus (B) explicit charge conditioning (global charge embedding or global charge scalar) is necessary to share data across q and to get accurate phonon/thermal transport quantities. This theory commits to (B) and further claims that the benefit appears at a concrete data threshold because phonon/IFC targets require consistent cross-q derivatives.

theory_statements.statement_name: Single charge-conditioned model beats per-q models for IFC-driven phonon predictions once ≥3 charge states are present
theory_statements.theory_statement: Fork: explicit charge conditioning (single model with charge input) dominates versus separate-per-q models. When training an ML potential intended to reproduce charge-dependent harmonic phonon spectra (or 2nd-order IFCs) for a defect across ≥3 charge states, a single charge-conditioned model will achieve phonon frequency MAE ≤ 0.15 THz on the highest optical branch, while a set of separate-per-q models trained on the same total number of structures will NOT achieve MAE < 0.30 THz. Negative prediction: the per-q ensemble will not cross 0.30 THz MAE under fixed total data budget.
theory_statements.domain_scope: Single host material; point defect with multiple stable charge states; MLFF used to compute IFCs/phonons by finite displacement; evaluation on a supercell size not seen in training.
special_cases: If charge states induce entirely different reconstructions and datasets do not include overlapping geometries, both approaches can fail; this statement assumes overlap in local motif space across q.
If the model includes explicit long-range electrostatics with learned charges and self-consistency, the advantage of simple global charge conditioning may shrink.

supporting_evidence.text: Charge-aware Behler–Parrinello NNP with a global charge scalar (Q_sys) enabled accurate phonon spectra and κ in AlN across multiple defect charge states, motivated by non-uniqueness of mapping coordinates→energy across charges.

Global charge embedding in a MACE-based model is reported to be necessary: removing charge embedding collapsed charge-state separation and failed to identify correct charged-defect minima in Sb2Se3, supporting the claim that structure-only descriptors cannot disambiguate charge-dependent PESs.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Charge-conditioning via a global charge node/scalar exists; separate-per-charge training is common practice in defect ML.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: A quantitative crossover claim for phonon/IFC accuracy with a concrete threshold (≤0.15 THz vs not <0.30 THz) tied to ≥3 charge states and fixed total data.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: Grounded in two independent charge-conditioning successes (Q_sys NNP; MACE charge embedding necessity) and extends to a specific measurable phonon error bound that separates conditioning from per-q training.

theory_statements.discriminating_experiment: Choose a host+defect with 3–5 charge states (e.g., AlN vacancies as in e4.0). Create a dataset of equal total size N split across charges. Train (A) one NNP/MLFF with a global charge input, (B) separate models per charge without charge input, each getting N/num_q structures. Compute phonon dispersions (finite displacement) for a larger supercell and report optical-branch MAE vs DFT.
theory_statements.falsifies_if: Separate-per-q models achieve phonon MAE ≤ 0.15 THz, OR the charge-conditioned model fails to beat 0.30 THz MAE under the stated dataset split.

theory_statements.statement_name: Global-charge conditioning is necessary for accurate charged-defect PES topology: RMSD success threshold 0.10 Å
theory_statements.theory_statement: Fork: with explicit global charge conditioning, the model learns distinct charge-state PES basins; without it, charge basins collapse. For a fixed defect and five charge classes, a charge-conditioned equivariant MLFF will achieve relaxed ground-state structures with RMSD ≤ 0.10 Å to DFT in ≥90% of charge states, while an otherwise identical model without charge conditioning will NOT achieve RMSD ≤ 0.10 Å in more than 50% of charge states. Negative prediction: unconditioned model fails the majority criterion.
theory_statements.domain_scope: Charged point vacancies in semiconductors; equivariant MLFF relaxation from the same set of initial distorted configurations; evaluation against DFT-relaxed minima.
special_cases: If all charge states relax to essentially identical geometries (rare for strongly charge-coupled defects), the discriminative power drops.

If the unconditioned model is trained with charge-state-specific labels encoded implicitly via different datasets but also provided a separate identifier token, this becomes charge conditioning and is outside scope.

supporting_evidence.text: Charge-conditioned MACE model in Sb2Se3 reports ground-state RMSD ≤ 0.05 Å across charge states and ablation without charge embedding fails to separate charge states and misidentifies minima.

Foundation bulk-trained MLIPs without charge-state descriptors systematically failed on charged-defect PESs with typical RMSD ~0.2–0.4 Å, supporting the necessity of explicit charge handling beyond structure-only bulk priors.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Charge-conditioned potentials and the observation that bulk-trained models fail on charged defects exist.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: A precise success-rate criterion (≥90% vs not >50%) with RMSD threshold 0.10 Å as a general law-like prediction for charge-conditioning necessity.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: Directly extrapolates from a clear within-system ablation (Sb2Se3) and from bulk-foundation failure; makes a transferable quantitative success-rate claim to be tested on new hosts.

theory_statements.discriminating_experiment: On a second material (not Sb2Se3), generate ShakeNBreak-like distorted initial structures for a vacancy across 5 charge states. Train two equivariant MLFFs on identical data: with and without a global charge embedding. Relax all initial structures; compute RMSD to DFT minima per charge state; compute fraction of charge states meeting RMSD ≤ 0.10 Å.
theory_statements.falsifies_if: The unconditioned model achieves RMSD ≤ 0.10 Å for >50% of charge states, OR the conditioned model fails to reach ≥90% success under the same data budget.

new_predictions_likely: For a 3–5 charge-state defect phonon benchmark, charge-conditioned training yields optical-branch MAE ≤0.15 THz, while per-q models stay ≥0.30 THz at equal total N.
Across 5 charge classes, charge-conditioned MLFF will meet RMSD ≤0.10 Å for ≥90% of charge states on a new host; unconditioned will not exceed 50%.
new_predictions_unknown: Replacing categorical charge embeddings with a continuous charge-density feature (q/V) will worsen performance for transition levels unless discretized into ≤7 bins; if continuous outperforms, this theory’s claim about categorical necessity is wrong.
Adding explicit LR Coulomb terms with learned charges will remove the advantage of global charge conditioning; if it does, the mechanism is electrostatics rather than conditioning.
negative_experiments: Fork test: per-q separate models match the conditioned model’s phonon MAE (≤0.15 THz) at equal total data—refutes necessity of conditioning for IFC targets.
Fork test: unconditioned model reaches >50% RMSD success ≤0.10 Å on a new host—refutes the claimed generality of charge-conditioning necessity.

unaccounted_for.text: ALIGNN charged-defect handling via separate models per charge state can still achieve formation-energy RMSEs ~0.23–0.30 eV on the zincblende dataset, indicating per-q models can work for scalar energetics even without explicit charge features; this theory focuses on phonons/IFCs rather than scalar E^f only.

special_cases: If the downstream task is only scalar formation energy at E_F=0 (not forces/phonons), separate-per-q models may be competitive and this theory’s phonon-specific claims should not be applied.
For metals where charge states are ill-defined, explicit charge conditioning may not be meaningful.

existing_theory.what_already_exists: Global charge nodes/scalars for charged-defect potentials; separate-per-charge training; recognition that charged defects have distinct PESs.
existing_theory.what_is_novel: Quantitative, cross-system performance thresholds and a phonon/IFC-centric crossover claim that separates conditioning from per-q training under fixed data.
existing_theory.classification_explanation: Leverages strong within-system evidence that charge conditioning is required for charged PES topology; extends to a risky quantitative claim about phonon error that is easily falsified.

theory-7.name: Delta-to-pristine defect encoding is the transfer bottleneck (full-supercell graphs entangle host energy)
theory-7.description: For defect-influenced property prediction across many host materials, the dominant failure mode is that full-defective-supercell representations force the model to learn a large host-energy background and then subtract it implicitly, which collapses out-of-distribution transfer. A representation that explicitly forms a defect-local, delta-to-pristine encoding (energy/embedding differences between defective and pristine structures, or a defect-centered subgraph plus a pristine reference) should sharply improve cross-host transfer and data efficiency. This is not a claim that “local is better”; it commits that the *explicit subtraction* is the key mechanism, and that without it, transfer errors remain eV-scale even with angular features.
theory-7.theory_query: Build theories about which representation and featurization strategies for point defects and dopants in crystalline materials (e.g., defect-centered graph encodings, local-environment descriptors, sparse defect representations, charge-aware embeddings, learned embeddings from foundation interatomic potentials) most improve machine learning prediction of defect-influenced material properties, and why. For additional context: we are especially interested in transferability across host materials and chemistries, data efficiency given scarce defect datasets, handling of charged defects and defect complexes, and downstream prediction of phonon scattering and lattice thermal conductivity degradation caused by defects, motivated by thermal management applications, based on the following results.

components.theory_name: Delta-to-pristine defect encoding is the transfer bottleneck (full-supercell graphs entangle host energy)
components.theory_description: For defect-influenced property prediction across many host materials, the dominant failure mode is that full-defective-supercell representations force the model to learn a large host-energy background and then subtract it implicitly, which collapses out-of-distribution transfer. A representation that explicitly forms a defect-local, delta-to-pristine encoding (energy/embedding differences between defective and pristine structures, or a defect-centered subgraph plus a pristine reference) should sharply improve cross-host transfer and data efficiency. This is not a claim that “local is better”; it commits that the *explicit subtraction* is the key mechanism, and that without it, transfer errors remain eV-scale even with angular features.

theory_statements.statement_name: OOD-transfer threshold: delta-to-pristine beats full-supercell beyond 5 hosts
theory_statements.theory_statement: FORK: For cross-host defect formation-energy prediction, explicit delta-to-pristine featurization dominates over full-defective-supercell graphs once the training set spans ≥5 distinct host materials; the opposite fork is that full-supercell with angle features is sufficient. NUMERIC THRESHOLD: at ≥5 hosts in training and a leave-one-host-out test, a delta-to-pristine model will achieve test RMSE ≤0.60 eV, while a matched-capacity full-supercell ALIGNN-style model will NOT achieve RMSE ≤0.60 eV (it will be ≥1.00 eV). NEGATIVE prediction: full-supercell models will not break the 0.60 eV barrier under host-wise OOD splits without explicit subtraction/reference.
theory_statements.domain_scope: Defect formation energies (neutral or charge-state-specific at fixed E_F) for point defects in crystalline semiconductors/insulators, evaluated under leave-one-host-out or leave-chemistry-out splits; excludes tasks where only a single host is present and excludes cases where pristine reference energies are unavailable.
special_cases: If the target is an absolute total energy (not a formation energy or property defined as a difference), delta-to-pristine is not applicable.
If defects induce nonlocal reconstructions beyond 12 Å that alter global strain fields, a purely local delta encoding may fail unless augmented with a global strain descriptor.

supporting_evidence.text: ALIGNN trained on native defects transfers extremely poorly to impurities/alloys/complexes without adding representative new data: RMSEs 2.17–2.98 eV, indicating that full-supercell graphs entangle host/defect effects and do not generalize across defect/chemistry shifts.

Local MLIP (Allegro-style) trained on defect-only supercells shows massive systematic host-energy bias (~1180 meV/atom) when applied to host/larger cells, consistent with the hypothesis that models that must infer the host baseline implicitly fail without explicit reference cancellation.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Formation energies are differences by definition; many workflows compute E_defect − E_host. Some models use site-aware pristine graphs f(X,i,q).
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: A concrete, risky bound tying cross-host generalization to an explicit delta-to-pristine representation, with numeric thresholds on number of hosts (≥5) and OOD RMSE (≤0.60 eV vs ≥1.00 eV).
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: Grounded in observed catastrophic OOD transfer of full-supercell ALIGNN and systematic host bias in defect-only MLIPs; extrapolates to a discriminative representation-level remedy with a sharp numeric prediction.

theory_statements.discriminating_experiment: Construct a dataset with ≥8 host materials and multiple defect types per host. Train two models with matched parameter count: (A) full-defective-supercell ALIGNN; (B) delta-to-pristine model that inputs (defect-centered subgraph embedding) ⊕ (pristine-centered subgraph embedding) and explicitly uses their difference, plus defect type/charge label. Evaluate leave-one-host-out RMSE for formation energy.
theory_statements.falsifies_if: Under leave-one-host-out, the full-supercell model achieves RMSE ≤0.60 eV (or delta-to-pristine fails to beat 1.00 eV), i.e., the predicted separation (≤0.60 vs ≥1.00 eV) does not appear.

theory_statements.statement_name: Angular features stop helping after defect-centered cutoff 6 Å in transfer regime
theory_statements.theory_statement: FORK: For transfer across host chemistries, once a defect-centered representation includes neighbors out to r = 6.0 Å, adding explicit 3-body angle features (ALIGNN line-graph style) degrades transfer because it overfits host-specific angular statistics; the opposite fork is that angles continue to improve transfer. NUMERIC THRESHOLD: with r ≥ 6.0 Å defect-centered neighborhoods, adding angles will NOT reduce OOD RMSE by ≥0.10 eV and will instead increase it by ≥0.05 eV. NEGATIVE prediction: angle-augmented encodings will worsen cross-host OOD performance at fixed neighborhood radius ≥6 Å.
theory_statements.domain_scope: Defect-centered local-environment encodings (subgraphs or local descriptors) for predicting defect formation energies across multiple hosts under composition-wise splits; applies to semiconductors/insulators where local coordination is well-defined; excludes metallic systems with highly delocalized bonding where angles may behave differently.
special_cases: If the neighborhood radius is <4 Å, angles can still help by disambiguating tetrahedral vs octahedral coordination (outside this claim).
If training data include explicit strain/elastic descriptors, angle overfitting may be mitigated.

supporting_evidence.text: ALIGNN’s advantage over CGCNN/MEGNET in in-distribution zincblende defects is large (0.15 eV vs 0.35–0.40 eV RMSE), consistent with angles helping when learning within a narrow structural family; this sets up the discriminative risk that the same inductive bias could harm cross-host transfer.

Despite strong in-distribution performance, ALIGNN shows catastrophic transfer failures to impurities/alloys/complexes when trained on native defects only (2–3 eV RMSE), indicating that additional geometric expressivity does not automatically yield transferability and can encode host-specific patterns.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Angles are known to help energetics in some settings (ALIGNN). Local cutoffs are standard hyperparameters.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: A falsifiable reversal: beyond a numeric radius (6 Å) in transfer settings, explicit angles harm OOD generalization by a specified amount (≥0.05 eV).
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: Uses the contrast between ALIGNN’s in-distribution gains and its OOD collapse to make a risky claim about overfitting from higher-order geometry when transfer is the objective.

theory_statements.discriminating_experiment: Implement a defect-centered model with radius r ∈ {4 Å, 6 Å, 8 Å}. For each r, train two variants: (i) distances only; (ii) distances + explicit angle triplets (line-graph). Evaluate leave-one-host-out RMSE and compare ΔRMSE = RMSE(angle) − RMSE(no-angle) at each r.
theory_statements.falsifies_if: At r ≥ 6 Å, the angle-augmented model improves OOD RMSE by ≥0.10 eV (instead of worsening by ≥0.05 eV), or ΔRMSE is within ±0.02 eV (no measurable harm).

new_predictions_likely: Under host-wise OOD splits with ≥8 hosts, explicit delta-to-pristine representations will reduce defect-formation-energy RMSE by ≥0.5 eV relative to full-supercell graphs, bringing RMSE to ≤0.60 eV.
For defect-centered neighborhoods with r ≥ 6 Å, removing angle features will improve OOD RMSE by at least 0.05 eV even if it slightly worsens in-distribution RMSE.
new_predictions_unknown: Delta-to-pristine will make impurity transfer nearly as good as in-host performance (gap ≤0.15 eV); if so, it would imply host-energy entanglement is the dominant failure mode rather than missing chemistry coverage.

If a full-supercell model with explicit pristine-energy auxiliary head (predict E_host and E_defect jointly) matches delta-to-pristine transfer, then explicit subtraction is not required—multi-task decomposition would be sufficient.
negative_experiments: If full-supercell ALIGNN achieves ≤0.60 eV leave-one-host-out RMSE without explicit reference subtraction, the main claim fails.
If angle features at r ≥ 6 Å improve OOD RMSE by ≥0.10 eV, the claimed overfitting reversal fails.

unaccounted_for.text: The evidence does not include a direct head-to-head comparison of delta-to-pristine vs full-supercell on the same multi-host defect dataset; the theory extrapolates from transfer failures and host-bias observations.

conflicting_evidence.text: A pretrained ALIGNN energy-per-atom model transfers from pristine bulk to vacancy formation energies without defect training (MAE ~1.0 eV after shift), suggesting full-supercell energy-difference schemes can transfer to some defect types, though not at the ≤0.60 eV level claimed here.

special_cases: If only vacancy defects are considered and formation energy is computed as a difference of two predicted totals (defect and pristine), full-supercell approaches may perform competitively without explicit defect centering (as in pretrained energy-difference workflows).
For metals, the locality assumptions and angle-overfitting behavior may differ; the theory’s transfer claims are scoped to semiconductors/insulators.

existing_theory.what_already_exists: Formation-energy-as-difference is standard; some direct-ML approaches use pristine structure + site index; pretrained energy models have been differenced to estimate vacancy formation energies.
existing_theory.what_is_novel: Numeric, host-count-gated commitments on OOD RMSE and a claimed regime where angle features hurt transfer beyond a specific radius.
existing_theory.classification_explanation: Builds on existing notions of referencing but makes sharp, risky quantitative predictions tied to transfer splits and specific representation components.

theory-8.name: Charged-defect PES and phonon-scattering fidelity requires explicit charge conditioning; separate-per-charge or charge-node dominates below 3k structures
theory-8.description: For charged defects, the key representational non-uniqueness is that identical atomic coordinates can map to different energies/IFCs across charge states. A model that is not explicitly conditioned on net charge will collapse charge-separated PESs, producing wrong relaxations and wrong force-constant differences—fatal for phonon-defect scattering and κ degradation. The theory commits that a minimal global charge token (categorical embedding or scalar charge density) is sufficient to separate charge-dependent PESs in practice, and that training separate models per charge state is inferior in data efficiency below a dataset-size threshold when the goal is phonon/IFC accuracy.
theory-8.theory_query: Build theories about which representation and featurization strategies for point defects and dopants in crystalline materials (e.g., defect-centered graph encodings, local-environment descriptors, sparse defect representations, charge-aware embeddings, learned embeddings from foundation interatomic potentials) most improve machine learning prediction of defect-influenced material properties, and why. For additional context: we are especially interested in transferability across host materials and chemistries, data efficiency given scarce defect datasets, handling of charged defects and defect complexes, and downstream prediction of phonon scattering and lattice thermal conductivity degradation caused by defects, motivated by thermal management applications, based on the following results.

components.theory_name: Charged-defect PES and phonon-scattering fidelity requires explicit charge conditioning; separate-per-charge or charge-node dominates below 3k structures
components.theory_description: For charged defects, the key representational non-uniqueness is that identical atomic coordinates can map to different energies/IFCs across charge states. A model that is not explicitly conditioned on net charge will collapse charge-separated PESs, producing wrong relaxations and wrong force-constant differences—fatal for phonon-defect scattering and κ degradation. The theory commits that a minimal global charge token (categorical embedding or scalar charge density) is sufficient to separate charge-dependent PESs in practice, and that training separate models per charge state is inferior in data efficiency below a dataset-size threshold when the goal is phonon/IFC accuracy.

theory_statements.theory_statement: FORK: For a single host with charged vacancy PESs, adding an explicit global charge embedding yields DFT-ground-state geometries across charge states, whereas a charge-agnostic equivariant MLIP cannot. NUMERIC THRESHOLD: with ≥2000 training structures spanning ≥5 charge states, a charge-embedded model will achieve ground-state RMSD ≤0.10 Å for each charge state, while the same backbone without charge embedding will NOT achieve RMSD ≤0.10 Å for at least 3 of the 5 charge states (it will be ≥0.20 Å). NEGATIVE prediction: charge-agnostic models will fail the ≤0.10 Å criterion in most charge states even at the same data volume.
theory_statements.domain_scope: Charged point defects (vacancies) in insulating/semiconducting crystalline hosts under periodic supercell DFT with background charge; goal is geometry/PES fidelity across multiple discrete charge states; excludes metallic systems and excludes cases where charge is not well-defined (e.g., delocalized PHS).
special_cases: If training data cover only one charge state, charge embedding provides no benefit (outside scope).
If the defect is PHS/delocalized, any charge-conditioned local MLIP may fail regardless (outside scope).

supporting_evidence.text: In Sb2Se3, a MACE backbone without global charge embedding failed to separate charge states and failed to identify correct defect structures; with charge embedding it achieved RMSD ≤0.05 Å and transition levels within 0.015 eV, showing explicit charge conditioning resolves charge-dependent PES non-uniqueness.

Charge-equilibration/polarizable models that enforce global charge still did not recover defect minima without defect-specific charged training; this supports the claim that explicit conditioning plus appropriate defect data (not merely generic charge models) is required.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Separate-per-charge models and charge-conditioned NNPs exist; global charge nodes have been proposed and used.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: A concrete dataset-size and outcome bound comparing charge-embedded vs charge-agnostic models on a geometric success criterion (RMSD thresholds) across multiple charge states.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: Directly grounded in the Sb2Se3 ablation evidence; turns it into a general law with numeric thresholds and a crisp failure condition for charge-agnostic models.

theory_statements.discriminating_experiment: On a charged-defect dataset for a single host with 5 charge states, train two identical MACE models on the same 2000–3000 structures: (A) with categorical global charge embedding + embedding readout; (B) without charge conditioning. Relax identical SHAKENBREAK-like distorted starts for each charge state and compare relaxed minima RMSD to DFT minima.
theory_statements.falsifies_if: The charge-agnostic model achieves RMSD ≤0.10 Å for all (or ≥4/5) charge states, or the charge-embedded model fails to reach ≤0.10 Å despite ≥2000 structures.

theory_statements.statement_name: Phonon/IFC accuracy: global charge scalar beats per-charge separate models below 3000 structures
theory_statements.theory_statement: FORK: For MLFF-driven phonon-defect scattering and κ degradation in a single host with multiple charge states, a single charge-conditioned potential trained jointly across charge states is more data-efficient than separate potentials per charge when total training set size is limited; the opposite fork is that separate-per-charge is superior. NUMERIC THRESHOLD: if total labeled structures across all charge states ≤3000, then a single charge-conditioned SF/NNP model (global Q_sys or charge embedding) will achieve force RMSE ≤75 meV/Å on each charge state, while training separate models per charge will NOT achieve ≤75 meV/Å for at least 2 charge states (it will be ≥100 meV/Å). NEGATIVE prediction: per-charge separate models will fail the ≤75 meV/Å threshold under this data budget.
theory_statements.domain_scope: Single-host charged defects where downstream goal is IFCs and phonon-scattering calculations (t-matrix / BTE), requiring force fidelity; applies to symmetry-function NNPs or equivariant MLIPs conditioned on global charge; excludes cross-host transfer.
special_cases: If each charge state has ≥3000 structures (i.e., total >> 3000), separate models may win; outside scope.
If charge node does not affect forces (as in some formulations), force improvements may be limited unless charge is coupled into geometry-dependent terms.

supporting_evidence.text: In AlN, a charge-aware Behler–Parrinello NNP using SFs + global Q_sys achieved force RMSE ~69 meV/Å while covering multiple charge states in one model, and was used to compute IFCs and κ degradation; this demonstrates feasibility of joint charge-conditioned force accuracy at the ≤75 meV/Å level.

Review mentions charge-aware NNPs with a system-charge node reproducing DFT phonon spectra across multiple charge states with forces ~64 meV/Å, indicating that a single conditioned model can share information across charges for vibrational fidelity.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Charge nodes/global charge conditioning for NNPs have been demonstrated in single-material contexts.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: A hard data-budget threshold (total ≤3000 structures) and a per-charge force-RMSE failure prediction for separate-per-charge training, tied to phonon/IFC needs.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: Extends existing charge-node successes to a discriminative comparison against separate-per-charge training under a numeric regime, focusing on forces because phonon scattering depends on IFC accuracy.

theory_statements.discriminating_experiment: For a single material with 3–5 charged defect states, subsample total training structures to N_total ∈ {1000, 2000, 3000} balanced across charges. Train (A) one joint charge-conditioned NNP (Q_sys or charge embedding) and (B) separate NNPs per charge with identical architecture and per-charge data split. Evaluate force RMSE per charge on held-out configurations and compute harmonic IFC error (e.g., Frobenius norm vs DFT) at a fixed displacement set.
theory_statements.falsifies_if: At N_total ≤3000, separate-per-charge models achieve force RMSE ≤75 meV/Å for all charges and match or beat the joint conditioned model, contradicting the predicted ≥100 meV/Å failures.

new_predictions_likely: In a charged-defect PES benchmark with ≥2000 structures, adding a categorical charge embedding will reduce relaxed-structure RMSD by ≥0.10 Å for at least 3 charge states relative to charge-agnostic training.

For IFC/phonon workflows with N_total ≤3000, joint charge-conditioned training will keep force RMSE ≤75 meV/Å across charge states, whereas separate-per-charge will exceed 100 meV/Å in at least two states.
new_predictions_unknown: If charge-conditioned models are trained but the charge term is restricted to a geometry-independent energy head (no propagation into interaction layers), they will still recover correct minima; if true, charge affects mostly offsets rather than forces—this would contradict the ‘PES separation via conditioning’ mechanism.

For defect complexes (two defects) with net charge fixed, a global charge token will be insufficient and models will require local charge-density descriptors; if observed, it would bound the global-token approach.
negative_experiments: Train charge-agnostic vs charge-embedded on the same charged-defect dataset; if charge-agnostic achieves ≤0.10 Å RMSD across all charges, the theory fails.
Under N_total ≤3000, if separate-per-charge models match joint charge-conditioned force RMSE ≤75 meV/Å for all charges, the data-efficiency claim fails.

unaccounted_for.text: The AlN NNP includes a global charge scalar that the authors note does not explicitly contribute to forces; the exact coupling needed for universal force improvements is not fully resolved by the evidence summarized.

conflicting_evidence.text: Some charge-equilibration and polarizable charge-aware models enforce total charge but still fail on defect minima without defect training; this is consistent with the theory’s ‘need defect data’ clause but conflicts with the stronger alternative that ‘explicit atomic charges alone suffice’.

special_cases: If the objective is only formation energies at fixed relaxed structures (no relaxations/forces), charge conditioning may be less critical than for PES/phonon tasks.
For polar materials requiring non-analytic corrections (Born charges), even force-accurate MLFFs may not directly yield fully correct phonon dispersions without hybrid ML-DFT electronic response.

existing_theory.what_already_exists: Global charge nodes and separate-per-charge training have been used for charged-defect potentials; phonon/κ workflows with MLFFs exist.
existing_theory.what_is_novel: Numeric data-budget thresholds and explicit per-charge failure predictions tied to force/IFC accuracy, plus a crisp geometric falsifier.
existing_theory.classification_explanation: Builds directly on demonstrated charge-node success and charge-embedding ablations, then makes risky commitments about when joint conditioning must beat per-charge training.

metadata.title: Machine learning for impurity charge-state transition levels in semiconductors from elemental properties using multi-fidelity datasets.

tldr.text: This work significantly reduces the time typically required to predict impurity transition levels using multi-fidelity datasets and a machine learning approach employing features based on elemental properties and impurity positions, and uses the model to predict a complete space of impurity charge-state transition levels in all zinc blende III-V and II-VI systems.

metadata.abstract: Quantifying charge-state transition energy levels of impurities in semiconductors is critical to understanding and engineering their optoelectronic properties for applications ranging from solar photovoltaics to infrared lasers. While these transition levels can be measured and calculated accurately, such efforts are time-consuming and more rapid prediction methods would be beneficial. Here, we significantly reduce the time typically required to predict impurity transition levels using multi-fidelity datasets and a machine learning approach employing features based on elemental properties and impurity positions. We use transition levels obtained from low-fidelity (i.e., local-density approximation or generalized gradient approximation) density functional theory (DFT) calculations, corrected using a recently proposed modified band alignment scheme, which well-approximates transition levels from high-fidelity DFT (i.e., hybrid HSE06). The model fit to the large multi-fidelity database shows improved accuracy compared to the models trained on the more limited high-fidelity values. Crucially, in our approach, when using the multi-fidelity data, high-fidelity values are not required for model training, significantly reducing the computational cost required for training the model. Our machine learning model of transition levels has a root mean squared (mean absolute) error of 0.36 (0.27) eV vs high-fidelity hybrid functional values when averaged over 14 semiconductor systems from the II-VI and III-V families. As a guide for use on other systems, we assessed the model on simulated data to show the expected accuracy level as a function of bandgap for new materials of interest. Finally, we use the model to predict a complete space of impurity charge-state transition levels in all zinc blende III-V and II-VI systems.

| brief_description | A machine-learning pipeline that predicts impurity charge-state transition levels by training a gradient-boosting regressor on a large dataset of low-fidelity (LDA/GGA) DFT transition levels corrected by a Modified Band Alignment (MBA) scheme, using only elemental properties and one-hot encoded impurity-position and charge-state features (no structural/graph descriptors). |

| material_systems | II-VI Cd-based systems (CdS, CdSe, CdTe, alloys) and binary III-V zincblende semiconductors (AlP, AlAs, AlSb, GaP, GaAs, GaSb, InP, InAs, InSb) — multiple hosts (14 systems used for training/validation; full prediction space extends to 18 binary zincblende systems and 63 impurity elements). |
| defect_types | Substitutional impurities/dopants (impurity charge-state transition levels); explicit defect complexes are not reported as included (only single-impurity sites considered; 5 defect sites enumerated), vacancies/antisites/ Frenkel pairs/complexes not treated. |
| charge_state_handling | Explicit charge-state label is included as a feature; DFT targets include charged-defect energies computed with supercells and Freysoldt–Neugebauer–Van de Walle (FNV) finite-size electrostatic charge corrections; Fermi-level/chemical potential enters implicitly via the charge-transition-level target but is not an explicit continuous feature beyond the charge label. |
| target_properties | Impurity charge-state transition energy levels (charge transition levels) relative to band edges (i.e., defect transition energies in eV). |
| representation_strategy_name | Elemental + one-hot impurity-position and charge-state feature vector (sparse tabular representation) |
| representation_strategy_description | Handcrafted tabular feature vector composed of elemental properties (ionization energies, electronegativity, electrical conductivity, etc.), one-hot encoding of impurity lattice site/position, and explicit impurity charge-state as a categorical/ numerical feature; no atomistic local structural descriptors, no atom-centered radial/angular basis, and no graph/neural message-passing representation. Targets are MBA-corrected low-fidelity DFT values. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Not defect-centered in a geometric/graph sense — representation encodes the impurity identity, its site (one-hot), and charge state but does not encode an explicit defect-centered local atomic graph or delta features between defective and pristine geometries; the DFT target implicitly references the defective supercell (MBA-corrected), but the input features are non-geometric elemental/site encodings. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | No explicit local-environment descriptors (no neighbor cutoff, no angular/radial basis functions, no SOAP/SOAP-like or symmetry-function features). Species information entered via elemental scalar properties (continuous) and one-hot site encoding; categorical charge-state feature included. No invariance/equivariance architectural details because no atomistic local descriptors/GNN were used. |
| graph_model_architecture | None — model is a non-graph ensemble regressor (Gradient Boosting Regression). |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | None reported — no use of pretrained/foundation interatomic potentials or pretrained neural embeddings; features are directly elemental descriptors and one-hot encodings. |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Training/validation dataset: 2910 low-fidelity (LDA or GGA) impurity transition levels corrected with MBA used as ML targets; 896 of these systems additionally have high-fidelity HSE06 calculations (used for testing/benchmarking). Data generated with DFT (VASP) on 64-atom supercells with spin polarization and ionic relaxation; dataset covers <10% of the enumerated full impurity/charge-space (full space ≈ 34,524 possible transition levels). Dataset is moderate-sized but not huge; authors describe potential scarcity for some subregions. |
| transferability_evidence | Cross-validation and multi-fidelity results: 10-fold cross validation (with nested CV for hyperparameter/feature selection) used throughout. Evidence that training on the larger MBA-corrected low-fidelity dataset yields better prediction of HSE06-level transition levels than training directly on smaller HSE06 sets: ML predicted MBA -> HSE06 RMSE = 0.36 eV (better than direct ML->HSE06 RMSE = 0.42 eV). Synthetic tests assessing classification performance across band gaps show better applicability for larger-gap hosts (e.g., systems with band gaps ≳1 eV have F1 > 75% for 'in-gap' classification). No explicit leave-one-chemistry-out OOD numerical split reported, but 10-fold CV over pooled data is used; authors additionally simulated performance on hypothetical band gaps. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Feature-learning curve: performance plateaus after ≈15 top-ranked features. Data learning curve: adding ≈1500 more low-fidelity points (≈50% more) is estimated to reduce MAE/RMSE by ~50 meV if trend persists. Multi-fidelity approach shown to be more data-efficient than training on a smaller high-fidelity set: larger MBA-corrected low-fidelity dataset produces lower error in predicting HSE06-level values than direct ML on limited HSE06 data (quantified RMSE improvement from 0.42 eV to 0.36 eV). |
| evaluation_protocol | 10-fold cross-validation for main performance reporting; nested 10-fold CV inside each top-level training set for hyperparameter optimization and feature selection to avoid information leakage. Comparison to HSE06 performed on 896-system subset with HSE06 calculations. Synthetic sampling used to assess classification metrics vs band gap. No explicit by-composition holdout (e.g., leave-one-host-out) reported. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Baselines: (1) MBA-corrected low-fidelity vs HSE06 (RMSE 0.24 eV), (2) direct ML predicting HSE06 (RMSE 0.42 eV), (3) ML predicting MBA then comparing to HSE06 (this work) (RMSE 0.36 eV). Ablations/analyses: feature-importance ranking used to select top 15 features (performance plateaus beyond 15); latent-variable transfer-learning (predict low-fidelity then use as feature to predict HSE06) was tested and improved over direct ML->HSE06 but did not outperform the MBA-target multi-fidelity approach. No ablation comparing atomistic local descriptors or graph representations because such representations were not used. |
| performance_metrics | Reported errors for predicted charge-state transition levels (energies in eV): MBA vs HSE06 RMSE = 0.24 eV (benchmark); ML predicted HSE06 (direct) RMSE = 0.42 eV; ML predicted MBA vs MBA RMSE = 0.27 eV; ML predicted MBA vs HSE06 RMSE = 0.36 eV; corresponding MAE for ML predicted MBA vs HSE06 = 0.27 eV. Precision/recall/F1 presented for classification of 'in-gap' / half-gap / third-gap occupancy as functions of host band gap (synthetic and resampled evaluation). |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | No connection — the paper does not predict phonon scattering rates or lattice thermal conductivity degradation, nor does it couple ML predictions to phonon transport models; phonon/thermal transport is not addressed. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Authors argue that simple elemental properties plus impurity site and charge-state encodings capture dominant chemical trends determining transition levels, and that using a much larger (but corrected) low-fidelity dataset via MBA yields better effective high-fidelity predictions (improved transferability/data efficiency) than training on a smaller high-fidelity set. They note that errors arise mainly from physics not captured by semilocal DFT (e.g., incorrect localization) which MBA cannot fix. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Model limitations reported: poorer quantitative accuracy for low band-gap materials (errors of ≈0.36 eV can flip shallow vs deep defect classification); cases where LDA/GGA fail to capture electronic localization produce large discrepancies not corrected by MBA and cause outliers; lack of structural/local-environment encoding may limit capture of relaxation/local-strain effects; dataset covers <10% of combinatorial space and does not include defect complexes; symmetry constraints were not explicitly broken in relaxations which may miss local minima; no explicit handling of long-range electrostatics beyond FNV corrections and charge label. |
| recommended_best_practices | Use MBA-corrected large low-fidelity datasets to train ML models when high-fidelity data are scarce; include explicit impurity charge-state and impurity-site one-hot features plus relevant elemental properties (ionization energy, electronegativity, conductivity, etc.); use FNV corrections for charged-defect DFT targets; perform nested CV (hyperparameter selection within outer CV) to avoid leakage; select a compact set (~15) of physically-meaningful features via importance ranking; assess applicability as a function of host band gap (classification metrics) before trusting fine-grained predictions; include HSE06/high-fidelity calculations where possible for validation and to identify localization failures. |

metadata.title: Point defect formation at finite temperatures with machine learning force fields

tldr.text: It is found that metastable configurations are populated at room temperature and thermal effects increase the predicted concentration of Te+1i by two orders of magnitude — and can thus significantly affect the predicted properties.

metadata.abstract: Point defects dictate the properties of many functional materials. The standard approach to modelling the thermodynamics of defects relies on a static description, where the change in Gibbs free energy is approximated by the internal energy. This approach has a low computational cost, but ignores contributions from atomic vibrations and structural configurations that can be accessed at finite temperatures. We train a machine learning force field (MLFF) to explore dynamic defect behaviour using Te+1i and V+2Te in CdTe as exemplars. We consider the different entropic contributions (e.g., electronic, spin, vibrational, orientational, and configurational) and compare methods to compute the defect free energies, ranging from a harmonic treatment to a fully anharmonic approach based on thermodynamic integration. We find that metastable configurations are populated at room temperature and thermal effects increase the predicted concentration of Te+1i by two orders of magnitude — and can thus significantly affect the predicted properties. Overall, our study underscores the importance of finite-temperature effects and the potential of MLFFs to model defect dynamics at both synthesis and device operating temperatures.

content.title: MACE (equivariant message-passing) machine-learning force field trained separately for each system/supercell

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | MACE-MLFF (per-system) |
| name_full | MACE (equivariant message-passing) machine-learning force field trained separately for each system/supercell |
| brief_description | An equivariant message-passing ML force field (MACE) trained on DFT energies/forces/stresses of full supercells (bulk and defective charged supercells) to model defect potential-energy surfaces and enable MD/TI-based free-energy calculations of charged point defects. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | CdTe host (bulk), point defects in CdTe (Te_i^{+1}, V_Te^{+2}), elemental Te (multiple solid phases and liquid); multiple systems were modelled but all within Cd/Te chemistry (no cross-chemistry transfer experiments reported). |
| defect_types | Point defects: interstitial (Te_i^{+1}) and vacancy (V_Te^{+2}); charged defects were modelled explicitly in supercells. No substitutional dopants, Frenkel pairs or explicit defect complexes beyond charged single-defect supercells are reported. |
| charge_state_handling | Charged defects were modelled by training separate MLFFs on charged-defect supercells (e.g., distinct models for Te_i^{+1} and V_Te^{+2}); formation energies include a posteriori charged-defect finite-size corrections (Kumagai-Oba eFNV) and Fermi-level contributions in the thermodynamic formalism. No explicit charge label feature vector or electron-density embedding is reported; charge handled by separate datasets/models per charge state and by standard charged-supercell corrections in analysis. |
| target_properties | Defect formation free energies g_f(T) (decomposed into vibrational, orientational, structural/configurational, electronic and spin entropies), potential energy surfaces (energies and barriers), energy/force/stress predictions for MD, phonons/vibrational free energies (bulk validation), anharmonic free energies via thermodynamic integration, defect migration/hopping barriers and associated rates. No direct ML prediction of phonon scattering rates or lattice thermal conductivity (kappa) degradation was performed. |
| representation_strategy_name | Equivariant atomic message-passing MLFF (MACE) operating on full supercells with ZBL short-range correction |
| representation_strategy_description | MACE represents the system as atoms with local atomic environments within a cutoff and performs equivariant message passing to predict per-system total energy, forces and stresses. Short-range Ziegler–Biersack–Littmark (ZBL) pair repulsion is included. Models are trained on full-supercell DFT energies/forces/stresses for bulk and for each defect/charge-state supercell separately. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Full-supercell representation (the MLFF learns the total energy of the defective supercell directly). The authors emphasize training separate models per system (bulk, defect charge states, reservoir element Te) rather than training a single joint model; they also warn against training only on defect configurations if the model will be used to compute absolute energies for larger supercells. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Cutoff radius = 5 Å; correlation order = 3; angular resolution = 3; species included explicitly (Cd, Te); architecture uses 256 invariant messages (per the MACE settings reported). ZBL pair repulsion term added for short-range repulsion. No explicit one-hot or continuous pretrained elemental embedding is reported beyond MACE's internal treatment of species. |
| graph_model_architecture | MACE (equivariant message-passing architecture) with 2 message-passing layers, 256 invariant messages, correlation order 3, angular resolution 3, cutoff 5 Å; Huber loss with weighted energy/force/stress terms during training; training used reference energies defined relative to isolated Cd and Te atoms. (MACE is an equivariant MPNN; specific equivariance / tensor order details are those of MACE as used here.) |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | None reported — MACE models were trained from-scratch on DFT-generated datasets for each system; no pretrained/foundation interatomic potential embeddings or transfer of pretrained network weights is described. |
| data_regime_and_dataset | DFT-generated datasets created with VASP on-the-fly MD (structure similarity kernel) using heating runs (NPT, 100 K up to >840 K), plus compressed/expanded cells (0.9–1.1 volume) for quasiharmonic sampling. Independent datasets & models for: bulk CdTe (2x2x2 conventional supercell, 64 atoms), Te_i^{+1} supercell, V_Te^{+2} supercell, elemental Te (multiple phases including liquid). Test sets: NPT MD at 300, 550, 900 K with five independent 24 ps runs per temperature; 100–300 sampled configs per temperature were re-evaluated with DFT for MAE/RMSE calculation. Exact total dataset sizes (number of training structures) are not enumerated in the main text (learning-curve details are in SI). |
| transferability_evidence | Evidence of limited transferability across modelling choices: authors report that training separate models per system (bulk and defect datasets) yields higher accuracy than a single joint model trained on all systems; they also report that models trained only on defect configurations (i.e., excluding bulk training) can show systematic errors in total energies when applied to larger supercells than those used for training, indicating poor transfer to different system sizes. No experiments training on one chemistry and testing on another were performed. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | No quantitative few-shot/fine-tuning experiments reported in main text. Authors state that defect-only training gives higher accuracy for defective supercells of the same atom count but warns about systematic errors for larger supercells; learning curves for Te_i^{+1} are mentioned to be in the Supporting Information but no main-text numbers are given. Training used ~150–200 epochs with 10% validation; no explicit small-data performance numbers reported in main text. |
| evaluation_protocol | Validation: 10% of dataset used as validation during training. Test: MD-generated trajectories (NPT) at 300, 550, 900 K; five independent 24 ps runs at each temperature; 100–300 equally-spaced configurations sampled per run and recalculated with DFT for test MAE/RMSE. Training/validation/test splits are time/trajectory-based sampling; no composition- or charge-state-based cross-validation beyond separate models per system. Finite-size charged-defect corrections (Kumagai-Oba eFNV) are applied in formation-energy analysis to avoid supercell-charge artifacts. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Architectural/representation comparisons reported: (i) independent per-system MACE models vs a single joint model — independent models were more accurate; (ii) defect-only training vs models including bulk — defect-only training yields higher accuracy for same-size defective supercells but causes systematic energy errors when applied to larger supercells (advised against). No explicit ablation removing equivariance or changing cutoff is reported in main text. For thermodynamics, the authors compare harmonic, quasiharmonic, and fully anharmonic (TI) approaches — this is for free-energy methodology rather than ML representation ablation. |
| performance_metrics | Test MAE/RMSE reported (Table I) for energies, forces, stresses on test sets: CdTe energy MAE=0.3 meV/atom (RMSE 0.4), force MAE=13 meV/Å (RMSE 17), stress MAE=0.2 meV/Å^3 (RMSE 0.3); Te_i^{+1} energy MAE=0.5 meV/atom (RMSE 0.7), force MAE=21 meV/Å (RMSE 30), stress MAE=0.2 meV/Å^3 (RMSE 0.3); V_Te^{+2} energy MAE=0.4 meV/atom (RMSE 0.6), force MAE=18 meV/Å (RMSE 24), stress MAE=0.2 meV/Å^3 (RMSE 0.3); Te (elemental) energy MAE=1.6 meV/atom (RMSE 2.3), force MAE=73 meV/Å (RMSE 102) attributed to inclusion of liquid phase. For thermodynamic integration, they aimed for TI error sigma_mu < 0.25 meV/atom (~20 meV/supercell) and used multiple independent TI runs to estimate uncertainty. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | MLFFs were validated against phonons and used to compute harmonic/quasiharmonic vibrational free energies and fully anharmonic free energies via non-equilibrium thermodynamic integration (TI), enabling temperature-dependent defect formation free energies; authors computed anharmonicity scores (FHI-vibes) for pristine and defective systems. However, the paper does not present direct ML predictions of phonon scattering rates or lattice thermal conductivity degradation (kappa). Instead, the MLFF provides accurate vibrational/anharmonic free energies and dynamical sampling (MD) that could be used as inputs to further phonon-scattering or BTE-based calculations, but such coupling to kappa prediction was not performed here. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Authors state that learning the defect energy surface with an MLFF (MACE) reduces cost and enables long-time/large-scale sampling of defect dynamics and anharmonic contributions; separate per-system training improves accuracy because defect and bulk configurational spaces differ; including compressed/expanded volumes is necessary to capture quasiharmonic thermal expansion; including ZBL improves short-range repulsion handling. They argue the MLFF captures local symmetry-breaking, metastability and anharmonicity important for defect entropies and dynamics. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Reported limitations: (i) models trained only on defect configurations may produce systematic energy errors when applied to different system sizes (lack of transfer across supercell sizes); (ii) more challenging systems (e.g., liquid phases) show higher errors (Te liquid shows larger force errors); (iii) computational cost remains high for fully anharmonic TI and long MD (need many and long MD runs); (iv) electronic-entropy estimates require accurate electronic structure — the MLFF does not replace the need for higher-level electronic structure for electronic entropy; (v) no explicit long-range electrostatic descriptor or embedding was used—charged-defect analysis relies on standard charged-supercell corrections rather than an ML-incorporated electrostatic feature, which could limit capturing long-range fields if that were required. |
| recommended_best_practices | Authors' recommendations and methodological prescriptions: (1) train separate MLFFs for bulk, each charged-defect supercell and reservoir phases to maximise accuracy; (2) avoid training only on defect configurations if the model will be used to compute absolute energies for larger supercells (include bulk data); (3) include compressed/expanded volumes to enable quasiharmonic sampling; (4) include liquid/phase-relevant configurations if reservoir phases melt near target temperatures; (5) include ZBL short-range repulsion and validate phonons and vibrational free energies; (6) use ShakeNBreak (or similar) to identify metastable defect configurations for structural/configurational entropy estimation; (7) apply finite-size charged-defect corrections (eFNV/Kumagai-Oba) when computing formation energies from supercell energies; (8) ensure TI switching/equilibration times and number of independent runs are sufficient to drive TI standard error below ~0.25 meV/atom (≈20 meV/supercell) for reliable g_f differences. |

metadata.title: Can a deep-learning model make fast predictions of vacancy formation in diverse materials?
metadata.abstract: The presence of point defects, such as vacancies, plays an important role in materials design. Here, we explore the extrapolative power of a graph neural network (GNN) to predict vacancy formation energies. We show that a model trained only on perfect materials can also be used to predict vacancy formation energies (Evac) of defect structures without the need for additional training data. Such GNN-based predictions are considerably faster than density functional theory (DFT) calculations and show potential as a quick pre-screening tool for defect systems. To test this strategy, we developed a DFT dataset of 530 Evac consisting of 3D elemental solids, alloys, oxides, semiconductors, and 2D monolayer materials. We analyzed and discussed the applicability of such direct and fast predictions. We applied the model to predict 192 494 Evac for 55 723 materials in the JARVIS-DFT database. Our work demonstrates how a GNN-model performs on unseen data.

content.title: Atomistic Line Graph Neural Network applied to full supercell energy-per-atom prediction

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | ALIGNN-full-supercell |
| name_full | Atomistic Line Graph Neural Network applied to full supercell energy-per-atom prediction |
| brief_description | Use of a pretrained ALIGNN energy-per-atom model (trained on perfect bulk structures) applied directly to full defect supercells to predict vacancy formation energies via E_defect - E_perfect + mu, without any defect-specific training. |
| citation_title | A Deep-learning Model for Fast Prediction of Vacancy Formation in Diverse Materials |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Diverse: 3D elemental solids, metallic alloys, oxides, nitrides, and 2D monolayers; pretrained on 55,723 bulk solids (JARVIS-DFT); tested on DFT vacancy dataset of 508 entries and applied to 55,723 materials to produce 192,494 vacancy predictions. |
| defect_types | Vacancies only (single-atom vacancies); neutral defects only; no interstitials, substitutionals, antisites, Frenkel pairs, or defect complexes included. |
| charge_state_handling | None — study explicitly restricted to neutral vacancies; charged defects and charge-state handling not included. |
| target_properties | Vacancy formation energy (E_vacancy) computed as E_defect - E_perfect + chemical potential (mu). |
| representation_strategy_name | Full-supercell atomistic graph (ALIGNN) with energy-per-atom prediction |
| representation_strategy_description | Represent the entire (periodic) supercell as an atomistic graph: atom nodes with atomic-property features and edges representing bonds/distances; use ALIGNN line-graph construction (bond-distance nodes and bond-angle edges) to predict total/energy-per-atom for both defect and pristine supercells, then form the vacancy formation energy as a difference plus chemical potential. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Not defect-centered: entire supercell graph including the missing-atom site (node removed) is encoded. A pristine reference energy per atom from a perfect cell is used and the formation energy is computed as a delta between predicted defect and perfect energies (plus mu). |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Node features: 9 per-atom features (electronegativity, group number, covalent radius, valence electrons, first ionization energy, electron affinity, block, atomic volume, and related atomic-property features reported). Edge features: interatomic bond distances expanded with radial basis functions, up to an 8 Å cutoff and using 12 nearest neighbours; line-graph encodes bond-angles. Species are encoded via continuous atomic-property features rather than one-hot. |
| graph_model_architecture | ALIGNN (Atomistic Line Graph Neural Network) using edge-gated graph convolutions; uses both bond-distance edge features and bond-angle information through a line-graph construction; implemented in PyTorch and DGL. Not an explicitly equivariant MPNN (uses distance/angle features). |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | Yes — used a pretrained ALIGNN energy-per-atom model trained on JARVIS-DFT OptB88vdW energy-per-atom data for 55,723 perfect materials; model weights used without further fine-tuning on defect data. |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Pretraining dataset: JARVIS-DFT bulk energy-per-atom (55,723 solids). Defect test DFT dataset: 508 charge-neutral vacancy entries (elemental solids, alloys, oxides, 2D monolayers) generated with OptB88vdW DFT and relaxed. Predicted large-scale dataset: 192,494 vacancy formation energies for 55,723 materials. Defect dataset is small (508), i.e., low-shot/sparse for defect-specific learning. |
| transferability_evidence | Direct transfer from model trained only on perfect bulk structures to defect energetics demonstrated: ALIGNN predictions correlate with DFT vacancies (MAE 1.51 eV) and improve with a global scissor-shift to MAE 1.0 eV. Subset performance: Elements MAE 1.53 -> 1.2 eV (after shift), Oxides 2.3 -> 1.4 eV, 2D monolayers 1.9 -> 1.2 eV. Authors note better transfer for oxides and 2D semiconducting/insulating systems versus elemental/metals due to local message passing and bonding differences. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Authors varied the amount of bulk pretraining data used (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, 100% of energy-per-atom training set) and reported corresponding vacancy-prediction MAEs: 1.20 eV, 1.22 eV, 1.11 eV, 1.05 eV, and 1.00 eV respectively, showing improved defect prediction with larger bulk pretraining sets (evidence that more diverse perfect-structure training improves defect transfer). |
| evaluation_protocol | Pretrained ALIGNN model (trained on bulk JARVIS-DFT) used without defect fine-tuning. Test set: independently computed DFT vacancy dataset of 508 entries. ALIGNN predicted energies for both defect and perfect structures; vacancy formation energies calculated via Eq. 2 using chemical potentials from JARVIS. No cross-validation on defect data (no defect-training). Comparison metrics reported as MAE versus DFT. Defect structures passed to ALIGNN were generated by deleting an atom at a unique Wyckoff position without relaxing atomic positions (while DFT defect energies were computed with relaxation). |
| baselines_and_ablations | Comparisons: (1) Original ALIGNN predictions vs DFT, (2) ALIGNN + scissor-shift heuristic (+1.3 eV) to reduce systematic underestimation, (3) literature ML models trained on defect-specific datasets (reported MAEs 0.40 eV and 0.67 eV) mentioned as specialized baselines. Ablation: effect of pretraining dataset size on defect MAE (20–100% experiments). No ablation explicitly comparing defect-centered vs full-supercell encodings or inclusion/exclusion of angle features. |
| performance_metrics | Vacancy formation energy MAE (vs DFT): overall original ALIGNN MAE = 1.51 eV; with global scissor-shift (add 1.3 eV) MAE = 1.00 eV. Subsets (original -> scissor-shift MAE): Elements 1.53 -> 1.2 eV; Oxides 2.30 -> 1.4 eV; 2D monolayers 1.90 -> 1.2 eV. Pretrained ALIGNN energy-per-atom model (reported from ref.) MAE = 0.037 eV for energy-per-atom prediction on perfect structures. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | None — the paper does not attempt to predict phonon scattering rates or lattice thermal conductivity degradation, nor to connect ML defect energetics to phonon transport models. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Authors suggest ALIGNN captures a transferable functional form for energies via local message passing and angle information; message-passing locality may favor insulating/less-bonded systems (oxides, 2D) over metallic systems with delocalized electrons and many bonds. They argue increasing diversity/size of perfect-structure pretraining data should improve defect transferability. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Explicit limitations: only charge-neutral vacancies considered; finite supercell size effects; ALIGNN tends to systematically underestimate vacancy formation energies (necessitating a scissor-shift); poorer accuracy for elemental solids/alloys (metallic systems) relative to oxides/2D; defect structures used unrelaxed for ALIGNN prediction whereas DFT defect energies are relaxed (mismatch); no treatment of charged defects, defect complexes, or long-range electrostatics/background-charge corrections; relatively small DFT defect dataset (508) limits evaluation. |
| recommended_best_practices | Authors recommend leveraging pretrained total-energy models trained on large, diverse perfect-structure datasets to rapidly screen defect energetics, increasing the diversity/size of perfect-structure training sets to improve transfer, and being aware of limitations: explicitly handle/compute charged defects separately, consider supercell-size effects, and validate via DFT for high-value candidates; a simple heuristic correction (global scissor-shift) may reduce systematic bias. |

| --- | --- |
| name_short | ALIGNN-representation |
| name_full | Atomistic Line Graph representation (ALIGNN) featurization |
| brief_description | The ALIGNN featurization constructs an atomistic graph with atomic-property node features and distance-based edge features, augmented by a line-graph that encodes bond-angle information, enabling message passing that incorporates both radial and angular structural information. |
| citation_title | A Deep-learning Model for Fast Prediction of Vacancy Formation in Diverse Materials |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Applied across a broad set of crystalline materials in this paper (bulk solids and 2D), and pretrained on 55,723 JARVIS-DFT bulk entries. |
| defect_types | Used in this work to represent vacancy-containing supercells (single neutral vacancies); ALIGNN itself is a general crystal representation not limited to vacancies. |
| charge_state_handling | No explicit charge-aware features in the representation described; charged-defect handling was not performed in this study. |
| target_properties | Originally used to predict total energy / energy per atom; in this paper used to produce vacancy formation energies via energy differences. |
| representation_strategy_name | Atomistic line-graph featurization (distance + angle features) with atomic-property node embeddings |
| representation_strategy_description | Nodes = atoms with continuous atomic-property features (9 properties). Edges = bond/distances encoded with radial basis functions up to 8 Å and limited to 12 nearest neighbors. A line graph is constructed where bond-distances become nodes and bond-angles serve as line-graph edges; message passing updates both node and edge/line-graph features. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Full-structure encoding (entire supercell) rather than extracting a strictly local, defect-centered subgraph. Vacancy formation energy uses predicted energies for both defective and pristine full cells as the reference. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Key settings: radial basis expansion of interatomic distances, cutoff 8 Å, 12-NN neighbor list; atomic species encoded via 9 continuous atomic-property features (no one-hot), angles included through line graph; invariances: uses distance and angle features so representation is invariant to translation/rotation via scalar geometric descriptors (no explicit equivariant vector/tensor features reported). |
| graph_model_architecture | ALIGNN architecture (atomistic graph + line graph) with edge-gated graph convolution and propagation functions; implemented in PyTorch + DGL. The model uses both node and edge updates and incorporates angle information via the line graph. |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | ALIGNN model used here was pretrained for energy-per-atom prediction on JARVIS-DFT; the same pretrained representation/weights were used directly for defect energy inference. |
| data_regime_and_dataset | ALIGNN pretrained on 55,723 JARVIS-DFT bulk entries (OptB88vdW energies). In this work the representation is evaluated on a defect DFT set of 508 neutral vacancies. |
| transferability_evidence | ALIGNN representation/weights trained on perfect crystals transferred to predicting defect energetics (vacancies) with moderate accuracy (MAE 1.51 eV before correction), showing representation-level transfer from pristine to defective structures. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Increasing the amount of bulk data used to train the ALIGNN energy model improves downstream vacancy-prediction MAE (reported for 20–100% of bulk training data); no few-shot defect fine-tuning experiments reported. |
| evaluation_protocol | Pretrained ALIGNN energy model trained on bulk energies, then applied unchanged to defective and pristine supercell graphs to compute formation energies; testing performed against an independent DFT vacancy dataset of 508 entries. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Reported ablation-like experiment: effect of varying the fraction of bulk training data on vacancy prediction MAE. No direct ablations isolating the contribution of angle features, RBF cutoff, or node-feature sets reported in this paper. |
| performance_metrics | Indirect performance reported through vacancy-formation MAE when using the pretrained ALIGNN energy predictions (overall MAE 1.51 eV; energy-per-atom ALIGNN reported elsewhere MAE 0.037 eV). |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | None — no explicit use of ALIGNN representation for phonon-scattering or thermal-transport predictions in this work. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Authors argue that including bond-angle information via the line graph and atomic-property features helps capture local energetic contributions; locality of message passing favors systems with more localized bonding (insulators/oxides/2D) over delocalized metallic systems. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Representation lacks explicit charge-aware descriptors and long-range electrostatics treatment; performance degraded on metallic/delocalized systems; no tests on charged defects or defect complexes; prediction used unrelaxed defective geometries which can mismatch relaxed DFT energetics. |
| recommended_best_practices | Use large, diverse bulk datasets for ALIGNN pretraining if the goal is transfer to defect energetics; include angular information and atomic-property features; validate predictions for metals and charged defects separately as the representation lacks explicit long-range/charge handling. |
