metadata.title: Overcoming systematic softening in universal machine learning interatomic potentials by fine-tuning

tldr.text: This study highlights a consistent potential energy surface (PES) softening effect in three uMLIPs and finds that the PES softening behavior originates from a systematic underprediction error of the PES curvature, which derives from the biased sampling of near-equilibrium atomic arrangements in uMLIP pre-training datasets.

metadata.abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have introduced a new paradigm for atomic simulations. Recent advancements have seen the emergence of universal MLIPs (uMLIPs) that are pre-trained on diverse materials datasets, providing opportunities for both ready-to-use universal force fields and robust foundations for downstream machine learning refinements. However, their performance in extrapolating to out-of-distribution complex atomic environments remains unclear. In this study, we highlight a consistent potential energy surface (PES) softening effect in three uMLIPs: M3GNet, CHGNet, and MACE-MP-0, which is characterized by energy and force under-prediction in a series of atomic-modeling benchmarks including surfaces, defects, solid-solution energetics, phonon vibration modes, ion migration barriers, and general high-energy states. We find that the PES softening behavior originates from a systematic underprediction error of the PES curvature, which derives from the biased sampling of near-equilibrium atomic arrangements in uMLIP pre-training datasets. We demonstrate that the PES softening issue can be effectively rectified by fine-tuning with a single additional data point. Our findings suggest that a considerable fraction of uMLIP errors are highly systematic, and can therefore be efficiently corrected. This result rationalizes the data-efficient fine-tuning performance boost commonly observed with foundational MLIPs. We argue for the importance of a comprehensive materials dataset with improved PES sampling for next-generation foundational MLIPs.

content.title: Atom-centered local energy contributions (E = sum_i E_i)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Atom-centered energy partitioning |
| name_full | Atom-centered local energy contributions (E = sum_i E_i) |
| brief_description | Standard MLIP featurization where total energy is modeled as a sum of learnable per-atom contributions that depend on the positions and species of neighbors; used as the base representation in the tested uMLIPs. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Wide range of crystalline materials studied in the paper: 29 elements and binaries for surfaces (147 slabs), 32 chemical systems for point defects (~129–134 defects), Ca_xMg_{2-x}O_2 solid-solution (many orderings), 229 phonon materials from PhononDB, ~470 Mg-ion migration paths across 110 structures, 1000 WBM compounds for OOD sampling. Multiple hosts used (metals, oxides, halides, sulfides, Li-containing compounds, etc.). |
| defect_types | Point defects benchmarked include vacancies, interstitials, and antisites (substitutional); defect complexes are not reported as included. |
| charge_state_handling | Not explicitly represented for charged point defects in the defect benchmarks; defect energies referenced to elemental chemical potentials; overall approach in benchmarks appears neutral/no explicit charged-defect pipeline. |
| target_properties | Defect formation/point defect energies, relaxed defect structure energies (referenced to bulk), migration barriers (ion migration paths), surface energies, phonon frequencies (vibrational modes) — all obtained via MLIP energy/force predictions. |
| representation_strategy_name | Atom-centered local descriptor / energy partitioning |
| representation_strategy_description | Each atomic contribution E_i is a learnable function of the local neighborhood (positions and chemical identities of neighbors). The MLIP sums atomic contributions to predict total energy; forces derived by analytic differentiation. Descriptor implementation is via the underlying model (graph/GNN or other) but conceptually atom-centered. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Full supercell / atom-local representation: models operate on the full atomic configuration (supercell) and compute per-atom contributions; no specialized defect-centered subgraph or delta-to-pristine encoding is described for the defect benchmarks. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Paper states importance of informative local descriptors with proper translational/rotational symmetries; mentions use of graph representations, high-order interactions, preservation of SE(3)/E(3)-equivariance (tensor products based on spherical harmonics), Fourier basis, and Cartesian atomic density expansions in general MLIP literature. Specific neighbor cutoff values for defect calculations are not reported in the main text (ionic relaxations converged to 0.05 eV/Å). |
| graph_model_architecture | Not specific to this entry (see separate GNN entry), but atom-centered partitioning is implemented by the used uMLIPs (M3GNet, CHGNet, MACE) which are graph or equivariant-graph based. |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | All three uMLIPs used are pretrained foundation potentials (M3GNet / CHGNet / MACE) trained on Materials Project-derived datasets; the atom-centered energy partitioning is the basis for these pretrained potentials which are then fine-tuned. |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Pretraining datasets: MPF (Materials Project formation?) 188.3k structures for M3GNet; MPtrj 1.58M structures for CHGNet and MACE (Table I). Defect benchmarks: 129–134 point defects across 32 systems; DFT labels used for defect, surface, phonon, and migration benchmarks. High-energy OOD samples: 1000 WBM compounds with 10 high-temperature MD samples each. |
| transferability_evidence | Extensive OOD testing: uMLIPs pretrained on near-equilibrium Materials Project trajectories systematically underpredict energies/forces for OOD states (surfaces, defects, migration barriers, phonons); >90% of 1000 WBM compounds show PES softening (softening scale <1). Evidence indicates limited transfer to high-energy/low-symmetry defect environments without fine-tuning. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Fine-tuning pretrained uMLIP (CHGNet) with a single high-energy DFT label via a scalar linear correction greatly reduces systematic error (e.g., CHGNet force MAE improved from 0.190 eV/Å to 0.166 eV/Å with 1 configuration). Full parameter fine-tuning with 10 DFT structures reduced force MAE to 0.125 eV/Å. The paper argues that pretrained atom-centered models provide data-efficient starting points because many errors are systematic. |
| evaluation_protocol | Benchmarks use DFT reference calculations; for high-energy sampling 20 ps, 1000 K MD with CHGNet produced samples (NVT). For fine-tuning CHGNet: train/val 9:1, test set of 100 DFT structures reserved; losses include energy/force/stress with 0.1-100-0.1 weighting. For defect and surface relaxations, ionic relaxations converged to 0.05 eV/Å. OOD evaluation explicitly uses compounds not in pretraining datasets (WBM substitutions). |
| baselines_and_ablations | Comparisons across three uMLIPs of differing architectures/sizes (M3GNet, CHGNet, MACE) and model-size variants (CHGNet-matgl and M3GNet-matgl in supplement). Ablation-style experiment: freezing all weights and training only a scalar multiplicative energy layer (linear correction) vs full fine-tuning; the scalar correction with one label recovers much systematic error. |
| performance_metrics | Representative numbers reported: surface energies MAE (MACE) = 0.032 eV/Å; ion migration barrier MAEs: MACE = 0.30 eV, CHGNet = 0.39 eV, M3GNet = 0.49 eV; force MAEs (high-energy MD sampling) pre-trained M3GNet/CHGNet/MACE = 0.220 / 0.190 / 0.176 eV/Å and linear-corrected cMAEs = 0.184 / 0.162 / 0.155 eV/Å. CHGNet fine-tune: 1-structure scalar correction MAE = 0.166 eV/Å (from 0.190), full fine-tune with 10 structures MAE = 0.125 eV/Å. >90% of 229 phonon materials show reduced max frequency relative to DFT (softening). |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | MLIPs are used to compute harmonic phonons (finite displacement) and show systematic reduction of vibrational frequencies (phonon softening) compared to DFT across many materials; this implies softened force constants which would affect phonon scattering and lattice thermal conductivity, but the paper does not directly predict phonon scattering rates or lattice thermal conductivity degradation or perform BTE/relaxation-time calculations with MLIPs. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Authors attribute the systematic underprediction (PES softening) to biased pretraining data that sample predominantly near-equilibrium ionic relaxation trajectories, providing poor coverage of high-energy curvature/force gradients; larger model capacity reduces softening somewhat; the systematic nature of errors is why a simple global scalar correction is effective and why fine-tuning is data-efficient. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Universal softening (energy/force underprediction) for OOD states including surfaces, undercoordinated defect sites, migration transition states, and phonons; poor extrapolation to high-energy curvature regions; lack of explicit handling for charged defects/charge states in defect benchmarks; non-analytic phonon corrections unavailable because MLIPs lack electronic Born charges; dataset bias towards near-equilibrium configurations limits generalization. |
| recommended_best_practices | Include a small number of high-energy/out-of-distribution DFT samples in fine-tuning to correct systematic softening (even a single force label can help via a scalar correction); construct pretraining datasets with broader PES sampling (include high-energy states, strained configurations); consider larger model capacity or enhanced sampling strategies to reduce softening; use hybrid MLIP-DFT workflows for properties requiring electronic quantities (e.g., Born charges for NAC). |

content.title: Graph-based representations with SE(3)/E(3)-equivariance (equivariant message-passing networks)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Graph / equivariant GNN featurization |
| name_full | Graph-based representations with SE(3)/E(3)-equivariance (equivariant message-passing networks) |
| brief_description | Use of graph representations and E(3)/SE(3)-equivariant message-passing or high-order interaction blocks (spherical harmonics/tensor products, Fourier basis) to encode atomic neighborhoods and preserve rotational/translational symmetries; underlying architecture for the uMLIPs tested (M3GNet, CHGNet, MACE). |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Same broad set as above (surfaces, defects across dozens of chemistries, phonons, migration paths). |
| defect_types | Vacancies, interstitials, antisites (as used in defect benchmarks); no explicit defect-complex graph-specific treatment reported. |
| charge_state_handling | Equivariance/graph encoding itself does not provide charged-defect handling; charge-aware variants exist (CHGNet includes charge information) but the defect benchmarks here do not explicitly model charged defect states. |
| target_properties | Energetics, forces (used to compute relaxed defect energies, migration barriers, phonons), phonon spectra (via forces), and derived material properties. |
| representation_strategy_name | Graph / E(3)/SE(3)-equivariant message-passing networks |
| representation_strategy_description | Crystals represented as graphs (atoms as nodes, bonds/neighborhood as edges) with message passing that respects rotational and translational symmetries; higher-order interactions captured via equivariant tensor products (spherical harmonics) or other basis (Fourier, atomic density expansion). Edge features and multi-body interactions encode local geometry and species. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Full-structure graph applied to defective supercells; no dedicated defect-centered subgraph or delta-to-pristine encoding described in experiments — the entire supercell graph is fed to the uMLIP. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Paper references SE(3)/E(3)-equivariance with tensor products based on spherical harmonics, Fourier basis, Cartesian atomic density expansion; species information included (chemical identity) and in CHGNet additional charge information can be included; exact neighbor cutoffs and angular/radial basis details are model-dependent and not enumerated in the main text. |
| graph_model_architecture | Specific uMLIPs used: M3GNet (graph deep learning interatomic potential), CHGNet (charge-informed graph NN), MACE (equivariant architecture). The paper notes MACE is larger (~4.69M params) and E(3)-equivariant approaches and tensor-product based equivariant blocks are used in modern MLIPs. Edge features and interaction blocks are part of these models but exact block counts/hyperparams not listed. |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | All models are pretrained graph/equivariant GNNs on Materials Project-derived datasets (MPF, MPtrj); the pretrained graph weights act as foundation models for downstream fine-tuning on defect/surface/phonon tasks. |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Pretraining: MPF (188.3k) for M3GNet, MPtrj (1.58M) for CHGNet and MACE. Downstream datasets: DFT-relaxed defective supercells (129–134 defects), 147 surfaces, 229 phonon materials, 470 migration pathways. OOD WBM sampling: 1000 compounds × 10 samples each. |
| transferability_evidence | OOD benchmarks show systematic underprediction across graph/equivariant architectures; MACE (largest equivariant model) performs better and shows less softening, suggesting better transfer with larger equivariant models but still exhibits systematic errors in many OOD scenarios. Softening scale distributions reported for 1000 WBM compounds show <1 for >90% of cases across models. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Pretrained graph/equivariant models fine-tuned with very small datasets (1 label via scalar correction; 10 structures for full fine-tune) show substantial error reduction, demonstrating data-efficiency of foundation graph models relative to training from scratch (supplementary comparisons). |
| evaluation_protocol | Pretrained graph models tested on DFT reference data across multiple OOD tasks; for fine-tuning CHGNet used energy/force/stress MSE loss weights 0.1/100/0.1, Adam optimizer, lr schedule and early stopping on validation force MAE; held-out test sets of DFT MD structures used. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Direct comparisons between three different graph/equivariant models (M3GNet, CHGNet, MACE), and model-size variants (CHGNet-matgl, M3GNet-matgl) show performance and softening differences; ablation of only training a scalar linear layer vs full fine-tuning quantifies how much of the error is systematic and correctable with minimal change. |
| performance_metrics | See atom-centered entry for numbers. Equivariant graph model (MACE) had best overall metrics: migration barrier MAE 0.30 eV; force MAE 0.176 eV/Å pre-fine-tune. CHGNet (charge-informed graph) and M3GNet larger/smaller differences reported. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | Graph/equivariant GNNs used to produce forces for phonon finite-displacement calculations; predicted phonon bands systematically softened (lower frequencies) relative to DFT. No direct thermal-conductivity (kappa) or scattering-rate calculations performed using the ML-derived force constants in this work. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Equivariance and expressive graph architectures improve ability to capture PES curvature; larger equivariant models reduce softening, indicating architecture and capacity matter; nonetheless, dataset sampling matters greatly for extrapolating to defect/high-energy regions. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Even equivariant graph models trained on near-equilibrium data underpredict forces/curvature for defect and high-energy configurations; lack of explicit treatment for long-range electrostatics and electronic-response in many graph models limits ability to model charged defects and non-analytic phonon corrections. |
| recommended_best_practices | Use pretrained equivariant graph models as foundations and include targeted high-energy/defect-like samples for fine-tuning; consider increasing model capacity and/or dataset PES diversity; for properties needing electronic response (Born charges, NAC) use hybrid MLIP-DFT corrections. |

content.title: Charge-informed graph neural network embedding (CHGNet)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Charge-aware embedding (CHGNet) |
| name_full | Charge-informed graph neural network embedding (CHGNet) |
| brief_description | CHGNet is a pretrained universal MLIP that explicitly incorporates charge information into the atomistic representation to improve prediction accuracy for charged/ionic systems; used in this paper as one of three uMLIPs benchmarked. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Benchmarks include oxides, halides, sulfides, metallic compounds, Li-containing compounds and others; CHGNet was evaluated on the same defect/surface/phonon/migration datasets as the other uMLIPs. |
| defect_types | Point defects benchmarked are vacancies, interstitials, antisites (neutral reference used); no explicit charged-defect examples or charge-transition level predictions reported in the benchmarks. |
| charge_state_handling | CHGNet includes charge as part of its representation (paper states incorporation of chemical information such as charge can enhance MLIPs). However, in the defect benchmarks this study did not perform charged-defect formation energy calculations with explicit electron chemical potential/Fermi-level features or background charge corrections; the defect energies were referenced to elemental chemical potentials (neutral references). |
| target_properties | Defect formation energies (neutral references), surface energies, migration barriers, phonon frequencies and forces. |
| representation_strategy_name | Charge-aware graph embedding (CHGNet) |
| representation_strategy_description | Graph-based representation that includes additional chemical information related to charge (charge-informed features/embeddings) alongside atomic coordinates and species; used within the CHGNet pretrained model to produce energies and forces. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Full-supercell graph encoding; no specialized defect-centered subgraph/difference features employed for defect benchmarks reported here. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Species and charge-related information are embedded in node/graph features; model preserves necessary symmetries via the underlying graph/equivariant architecture. Specific cutoffs and basis choices are model-internal and not enumerated in main text. |
| graph_model_architecture | CHGNet (v0.3.0) — a charge-informed graph neural network; model size ~412.5K parameters per Table I. Underlying architecture is graph-based and charge-aware. |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | CHGNet is used as a pretrained foundation potential (pretrained on MPtrj dataset, 1.58M structures) and evaluated out-of-the-box on OOD tasks; fine-tuned in this work (scalar correction and small-data fine-tuning) to mitigate PES softening. |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Pretraining on MPtrj (1.58M structures). Defect/surface/migration/phonon benchmark datasets described above. Fine-tuning experiments used Li2B3PO8 DFT ab-initio MD (small number of structures: 1 for scalar correction, 10 for small-data full fine-tune). |
| transferability_evidence | CHGNet shows the same systematic PES softening as other uMLIPs on OOD tasks but performs closer to DFT than M3GNet in some energy tasks; fine-tuning with very small data (1–10 structures) substantially improves force MAE, demonstrating transferability via fine-tuning. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Scalar linear correction with one DFT configuration improved CHGNet force MAE from 0.190 to 0.166 eV/Å; full fine-tune with 10 structures reduced MAE to 0.125 eV/Å. These show high data efficiency when fine-tuning a pretrained, charge-aware model. |
| evaluation_protocol | CHGNet pretrained weights frozen except scalar layer for the one-label experiment; full fine-tune optimized all parameters with a small dataset (energy/force/stress loss weighting 0.1/100/0.1). Validation-based checkpointing used. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Compared against M3GNet and MACE (both pretrained) and model-size variants in supplement; ablation by training only scalar multiplicative layer vs full fine-tuning quantified systematic error correction. |
| performance_metrics | CHGNet migration barrier MAE = 0.39 eV; pre-trained CHGNet force MAE (OOD high-energy sampling) = 0.190 eV/Å; cMAE after linear correction = 0.162 eV/Å; scalar-finetune MAE = 0.166 eV/Å; full fine-tune (10 structures) MAE = 0.125 eV/Å. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | CHGNet predicted phonon spectra show systematic frequency reduction similar to other uMLIPs; no direct thermal conductivity or phonon scattering rate predictions presented. The paper notes non-analytic corrections (Born charges) are unavailable from MLIPs without electronic info, limiting phonon accuracy for polar materials. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Charge-informed embeddings help capture ionic/charge effects in materials, but pretraining data bias still yields PES softening in defect/high-energy regions; fine-tuning can correct systematic scaling errors even in charge-aware models. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | CHGNet, despite charge-aware features, still underpredicts energies/forces in OOD defect/high-energy scenarios; the present work does not demonstrate explicit charged-defect formation energies or charge-state dependent properties with CHGNet; MLIPs lack electronic response variables (e.g., Born charges) necessary for some phonon corrections. |
| recommended_best_practices | When applying charge-aware MLIPs to defect problems, include explicit high-energy/defect-state training samples and consider hybrid DFT steps for electronic-response properties; use small-data fine-tuning for rapid correction of systematic errors. |

content.title: Pretrained universal MLIPs (foundation potentials) and downstream fine-tuning strategies

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Pretrained foundation potentials + fine-tuning |
| name_full | Pretrained universal MLIPs (foundation potentials) and downstream fine-tuning strategies |
| brief_description | Use of large, pretrained uMLIPs (M3GNet, CHGNet, MACE) trained on Materials Project-derived datasets as foundation models that can be fine-tuned with small amounts of task-specific DFT data to correct systematic PES softening and improve defect-related predictions. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Same broad crystalline materials used in the benchmarks; fine-tuning experiments performed on Li2B3PO8 (ab-initio MD) as an example and applied to OOD WBM compounds evaluation. |
| defect_types | Benchmarks cover point defects (vacancy/interstitial/antisite) and migration transition states; fine-tuning primarily targeted high-energy OOD atomic configurations rather than explicit defect charge-state labels. |
| charge_state_handling | Fine-tuning procedure described does not incorporate explicit electron chemical potential or charged-defect labels; scalar correction fine-tunes energy scale only and full fine-tuning uses standard energy/force/stress DFT labels (presumably neutral supercells). |
| target_properties | Improved energy/force predictions used to calculate defect formation energies (neutral references), migration barriers, surface energies, and phonon frequencies; the fine-tuned potentials reduce MAEs for these downstream tasks. |
| representation_strategy_name | Foundation-potential pretraining with small-data fine-tuning (including scalar linear correction) |
| representation_strategy_description | Models are pretrained on large datasets of near-equilibrium ionic relaxation trajectories (Materials Project/MPtrj). Downstream, either (a) a single scalar multiplicative energy layer is trained (all other weights frozen) using one high-energy force label, or (b) full model fine-tuning with small DFT datasets (e.g., 10 structures) is performed to correct systematic errors. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Fine-tuning operates on full-structure labels (energies/forces) from defective or high-energy configurations; no specialized defect-centered delta features are described as part of the fine-tuning. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Pretraining encodes local environments via the chosen uMLIP architecture (graph/equivariant). Fine-tuning updates model parameters to better represent high-energy curvature; scalar correction multiplies predicted energies globally (equivalent to scaling all forces). |
| graph_model_architecture | Applied to pretrained M3GNet (graph), CHGNet (charge-aware graph), and MACE (equivariant); scalar correction is model-agnostic and implemented as an extra scalar linear layer on top of the energy output. |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | Explicit use of pretrained foundation potentials: M3GNet (MPF, 188.3k), CHGNet (MPtrj, 1.58M), MACE (MPtrj, 1.58M). The pretrained weights serve as the starting point for fine-tuning experiments. |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Pretraining: large datasets described above. Fine-tuning datasets: extremely small examples shown — single high-energy configuration (1 force label) and 10-structure small datasets from DFT ab-initio MD (Li2B3PO8). OOD evaluation: 1000 WBM compounds sampled at 1000 K (10 states each). |
| transferability_evidence | Fine-tuning foundation models with minimal data substantially improves OOD force predictions across sampled materials; the scalar correction brought the CHGNet softening scale closer to 1 (from 0.859 to 0.965) and reduced MAE. This supports transferability via small-data fine-tuning rather than zero-shot transfer. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Numeric examples: single-label scalar fine-tune reduced CHGNet MAE from 0.190 to 0.166 eV/Å; ten-structure full fine-tune reduced MAE to 0.125 eV/Å. Authors argue a large fraction of pretrained errors are systematic and thus correctable with few labels. |
| evaluation_protocol | Scalar correction: freeze all pretrained weights, add scalar linear multipler initialized to 1, train on a single high-energy force label. Full fine-tune: optimize all parameters on small DFT datasets with energy/force/stress loss weighting and validation-based checkpointing. Test sets withheld (e.g., 100 structures reserved). |
| baselines_and_ablations | Baseline is pretrained model without fine-tuning. Ablation: scalar-only fine-tune (1 parameter) vs full fine-tune (all parameters) demonstrates that most systematic scaling error can be removed by a single scalar, but further MAE reductions come from full fine-tuning with more labels. Comparisons to training from scratch (supplement) show pretrained fine-tuning is more data-efficient. |
| performance_metrics | See entries above: CHGNet example numbers (0.190 → 0.166 eV/Å with scalar correction; →0.125 eV/Å with 10-structure full fine-tune); cMAE reductions for all three uMLIPs: M3GNet/CHGNet/MACE cMAEs 0.184 / 0.162 / 0.155 eV/Å (from 0.220 / 0.190 / 0.176). |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | Fine-tuning corrects force magnitudes and PES curvature, yielding phonon frequencies closer to DFT and thus could improve MLIP-derived phonon properties; however, the paper does not perform direct lattice thermal conductivity calculations or phonon-scattering-rate predictions post fine-tuning. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Because pretrained uMLIPs are biased toward near-equilibrium configurations, a large fraction of their errors are systematic (global curvature/scale); therefore small-data fine-tuning can efficiently correct these systematic components (hence foundation models are data-efficient). |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Scalar correction is a global remedy and may not fix non-linear or chemistry-specific errors; fine-tuning requires at least targeted DFT labels from the relevant OOD regions; foundation models still limited by pretraining dataset bias and absence of electronic response descriptors for charged-defect/phonon NAC corrections. |
| recommended_best_practices | For defect/high-energy applications start from a pretrained uMLIP and include a few targeted high-energy/defect DFT samples for fine-tuning (even a single force label can significantly reduce systematic softening); prefer small full-parameter fine-tuning when more labels are available; construct pretraining datasets with better PES coverage for next-generation foundation models. |

content.title: Single-parameter scalar energy scaling (linear correction) for MLIP fine-tuning

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Global scalar linear correction |
| name_full | Single-parameter scalar energy scaling (linear correction) for MLIP fine-tuning |
| brief_description | A minimal fine-tuning strategy adding a single scalar multiplicative layer on the MLIP energy output (E_corr = c * MLIP) to correct systematic underprediction of PES curvature and forces; can be trained with a single force label to rotate force parity distribution back toward unity slope. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Demonstrated on high-energy OOD MD samples of Li2B3PO8 and statistically evaluated over 1000 WBM compounds; applied to uMLIPs (CHGNet, M3GNet, MACE) in benchmarks. |
| defect_types | Used to correct systematic force/energy errors relevant for defects, surfaces and migration barriers generally; not a defect-specific featurization but a fine-tuning trick applicable to defect calculations. |
| charge_state_handling | Does not introduce charge awareness; purely a scalar correction to predicted energies/forces irrespective of charge state. |
| target_properties | Improves force predictions (MAE), which in turn improves derived properties such as migration barrier height, phonon frequencies, and defect/surface energies indirectly by correcting PES curvature scale. |
| representation_strategy_name | Scalar multiplicative energy correction (single-parameter fine-tune) |
| representation_strategy_description | Add a scalar linear layer multiplicative factor c to the MLIP predicted energy: E_corr = c * MLIP(...). Since forces are gradients, f_corr = c * f_MLIP. Fit c by minimizing MSE on a small set (even a single force component suffices) to counteract systematic underprediction (softening). |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Applies globally to full-supercell MLIP predictions; does not require defect-centered descriptors or pristine references. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | No change to local descriptors; the scalar corrects output energy scale globally across all local-environment encodings. |
| graph_model_architecture | Model-agnostic; implemented on top of CHGNet in experiments (all other parameters frozen during scalar training). |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | Designed specifically as a low-cost fine-tuning step for pretrained foundation MLIPs to correct systematic scale errors with minimal data/parameter updates. |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Demonstrated with 1 DFT high-energy configuration (single force component) and evaluated across 1000 WBM compounds; also compared to 10-structure full fine-tune. |
| transferability_evidence | Scalar correction trained on one configuration from Li2B3PO8 shifted CHGNet softening scale from 0.859 → 0.965 and reduced force MAE (0.190 → 0.166 eV/Å) on withheld test OOD states from the same material; distributionally across WBM compounds cMAE indicates meaningful lower-bound error reduction potential. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | One-parameter correction trained on a single force label yields measurable MAE reduction (example above). Authors present cMAE distributions showing ~15% typical error reduction achievable with such a linear correction. |
| evaluation_protocol | Scalar layer initialized at 1.0; all other model parameters frozen; trained on one DFT configuration (or last-epoch for 1-structure case) and evaluated on withheld high-energy OOD samples. Larger fine-tuning (10 structures) used full-parameter optimization for comparison. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Baseline: pretrained model without correction. Ablation: single-parameter correction vs full fine-tune. Full fine-tune yields further MAE decreases beyond scalar correction (e.g., CHGNet: scalar MAE 0.166 eV/Å; full fine-tune with 10 structures MAE 0.125 eV/Å). |
| performance_metrics | Example numeric results: CHGNet pre-trained force MAE 0.190 eV/Å → scalar-corrected MAE 0.166 eV/Å (softening scale from 0.859 to 0.965). cMAE reductions across 1000 WBM compounds ~15% typical improvement reported. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | Because scalar correction scales forces, it directly affects phonon force-constant magnitudes and thus phonon frequencies; scalar correction moves phonon spectra closer to DFT by restoring PES curvature scale, but paper does not compute thermal conductivity consequences explicitly. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | A large fraction of pretraining error is systematic multiplicative bias in PES curvature (softening); a global scalar corrects this dominant mode of error efficiently, explaining data-efficient fine-tuning benefits of foundation models. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Scalar correction only remedies global multiplicative bias and cannot correct spatially or chemically local systematic errors or non-linear discrepancies; if errors vary strongly by chemistry, local environment, or defect type, scalar may not suffice; must still supply at least one relevant high-energy label from the OOD regime of interest. |
| recommended_best_practices | Use scalar multiplicative correction as a first, very low-cost fine-tuning step when applying pretrained MLIPs to defect/high-energy tasks; follow with small full-parameter fine-tuning if residual errors remain; choose training label(s) representative of the OOD regimes (defect, migration TS, strained states). |

metadata.title: Machine learning approaches to point defects in non-metallic materials: a review of methods

tldr.text: This work identifies charged-defect formation energies as a central frontier, where Fermi-level alignment, finite-size corrections, and long-range electrostatics must be handled carefully and consistently to enable meaningful comparisons and transferable predictions across different materials.

metadata.abstract: We review recent machine learning (ML) approaches for point defects in non-metallic materials, with an emphasis on defect formation energies. Existing studies largely fall into two categories: direct ML models that predict defect energies from local structural representations, and ML potentials that approximate the defect-containing potential energy surface. We summarize key achievements as well as persistent bottlenecks, emphasizing that dataset quality often dominates practical model performance. We further identify charged-defect formation energies as a central frontier, where Fermi-level alignment, finite-size corrections, and long-range electrostatics must be handled carefully and consistently to enable meaningful comparisons and transferable predictions across different materials.

content.title: Handcrafted physical descriptors

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Physical descriptors (PD) |
| name_full | Handcrafted physical descriptors |
| brief_description | Tabulated, expert-designed scalar features built from elemental (electronegativity, ionic radii), structural (coordination number, Bader volume), and host properties (band gap, dielectric constant) used as inputs to regressors for defect energetics. |
| citation_title |  |
| mention_or_use | mention |
| material_systems | Applied across many chemistries in reviewed works (oxides, halide perovskites, zincblende semiconductors, CdX, HfO2, BaTiO3, LaMnO3, etc.); both single-host studies and multi-host datasets (hundreds–~1000s of compositions) use PD. |
| defect_types | Vacancies (especially oxygen vacancies), substitutional dopants, antisites, some interstitials (if site list is predefined); defect complexes generally not represented explicitly with PD. |
| charge_state_handling | Often only neutral defects; when transition levels or charged defects are targeted PD models may include explicit charge-state label or derived features (e.g., VBM position) but charged-defect electrostatic alignment/finite-size corrections are typically handled separately in the data rather than encoded directly in PD. |
| target_properties | Defect formation energies (FE) and charge transition levels (TL, sometimes as a classification deep vs shallow); rarely phonons or thermal transport directly. |
| representation_strategy_name | Handcrafted physical descriptor set |
| representation_strategy_description | Concatenate scalar features capturing chemistry (atomic properties), local geometry (coordination numbers, local volumes), and host macroscopic properties (band gap, dielectric constant); used as fixed-length vectors into regressors (RFR, KRR, GBR, NN). |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Implicitly defect-centered in that descriptors are computed for the site or local neighborhood, but typically do not encode a pristine-vs-defective delta; many works use only pristine host/site features to predict formation energy of a defect at that site. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Feature sets vary by study; include coordination numbers, Bader volumes, oxide formation energy, band gap, dielectric constants, ionic radii, electronegativity differences; no unified cutoff rule reported (handcrafted neighborhoods or site-specific values used). |
| graph_model_architecture |  |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings |  |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Used across small single-material datasets (1–3 compositions) up to large multi-material datasets (e.g., metal-oxide oxygen-vacancy datasets with hundreds to ~1000 compositions cited in the review: Wan 2021 ~1750 oxides; Kumagai 2021 ~937 oxides; Baldassarri 2023 1157 oxides; Park 2024 ~1000 oxides). Many PD studies trained on DFT (primarily GGA or GGA+U) computed labels. |
| transferability_evidence | Review notes a generality–accuracy trade-off: PD models can be interpretable but may struggle to generalize across diverse structure-types; no standardized large-scale cross-chemistry transfer benchmarks reported in the review, though PDs have been used for wide oxide datasets with qualitative success. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Kernel and tree-based regressors on PD often used for data-efficient learning; review states PD models enable physical interpretability (feature importances) and have been successful on mid-sized datasets, but quantitative learning-curve results are not reported in the review. |
| evaluation_protocol | Varies by study; review emphasizes need for composition- or host-split evaluation for transferability but many earlier works used random splits; explicit protocols vary and are not standardized across PD studies summarized. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Several works compared PD baselines with graph-based models; review reports that graph representations often outperform PD in predictive accuracy but PD remains useful for interpretability. No single ablation meta-analysis with numeric outcomes is provided in the review. |
| performance_metrics | The review summarizes many studies but does not aggregate a single numeric metric for PD approaches; specific per-paper MAE/RMSE values are not reported in the review text. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | PD-based direct models are generally not used to predict phonon scattering or lattice thermal conductivity; review indicates PD approaches lack atomic-structure outputs required for phonon calculations. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | PDs are useful because they encode known physical drivers (oxidation enthalpy, band gap, coordination) and allow interpretable feature importance analysis to extract governing factors for defect energetics. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Poor handling of unusual relaxations (split vacancies, DX centers), inability to produce atomic structures for downstream phonon/kinetic analysis, limited capture of long-range electrostatics and charge-state dependent effects unless these are added as separate features or handled in pre-processing. |
| recommended_best_practices | Use PDs for interpretable baselines and small-to-mid sized datasets; carefully curate datasets to remove PHS/shallow defects and migration-relaxed examples; include host properties (VBM/CBM, dielectric) when predicting charged/transition-level quantities. |

content.title: Crystal-graph / graph neural network representations (CGCNN, MEGNet, ALIGNN, other GNNs)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Crystal-graph representations (CGR) |
| name_full | Crystal-graph / graph neural network representations (CGCNN, MEGNet, ALIGNN, other GNNs) |
| brief_description | Graph-based featurizations that represent crystals as atom nodes and edges (bond or neighbor relations), learned by message-passing neural networks (e.g., CGCNN, MEGNet, ALIGNN) and widely used to predict defect formation energies and transition levels from local or global graph encodings. |
| citation_title |  |
| mention_or_use | mention |
| material_systems | Applied to large multi-material datasets including metal oxides (~hundreds to ~1000s), zincblende semiconductors (34), perovskites (~233–1100), halide perovskites (38), and many single-material studies cited. |
| defect_types | Vacancies (oxygen vacancies predominant), substitutional dopants, antisites, some interstitials when sites are predefined; most CGR studies target single-point defects rather than complexes. |
| charge_state_handling | Typically include explicit charge-state label q as an input in direct ML regression when charged defects are modeled; however, many CGR studies focus on neutral defects because charged-defect DFT labels require special alignment and correction. |
| target_properties | Defect formation energies and sometimes transition levels; direct graph models do not produce relaxed atomic geometries but can predict site-resolved energetics rapidly. |
| representation_strategy_name | Defect/host crystal graph |
| representation_strategy_description | Build a graph from the host/pristine crystal (or a local subgraph around a site) with nodes = atoms (element identity, optional learned embeddings) and edges = neighbor relations (distance, bond features); feed into GNNs (CGCNN/MEGNet/ALIGNN) to regress defect energetics; some studies combine graph features with site index i and charge q. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Often defect-centered in the sense that the graph input is the pristine host crystal plus a marker for the defect site index i; some models encode local subgraphs rather than full supercells. The review highlights f(X,i,q) formulation (pristine X, site i, charge q) for direct ML. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Graphs typically use radial cutoffs (implicit in neighbor lists used by CGCNN/MEGNet/ALIGNN), include species one-hot/learned embeddings, and edge features such as pair distances/angle-derived line-graph features (ALIGNN). Specific cutoff distances depend on implementation but are not standardized in the review. |
| graph_model_architecture | CGCNN, MEGNet, ALIGNN and general GNNs; ALIGNN uses atomistic line-graph to capture angles; MEGNet/CGCNN use message passing; implementations vary with number of interaction blocks and learned node/edge embeddings, as cited in Table 2/3. |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | Some studies leverage pretrained models or shared representations (the review cites M3GNet/CHGNet architectures in the MLP context but does not report a standardized pretrained graph embedding transfer for direct-defect CGR models). |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Used with datasets from tens to thousands of compositions; examples in Table 2 include large oxide datasets (e.g., Kiyohara 2025: 932 oxides), perovskite and zincblende compilations, typically DFT-computed labels (PBE or PBE+U, some HSE/SCAN). |
| transferability_evidence | Review states CGR/GNNs often achieve higher predictive accuracy than PD and are used for cross-material prediction, but also emphasizes generality–accuracy trade-offs; explicit cross-host holdout experiments are described in individual cited works but the review does not collate numeric cross-material transfer scores. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | GNNs often outperform PD with moderate-to-large datasets but may require more data than kernel methods for best performance; review notes increasing adoption as datasets grow but does not provide quantitative learning curves. |
| evaluation_protocol | Varies across studies; the review recommends consistent Fermi-level alignment and careful dataset curation (exclude PHS and migration cases) to avoid leakage and improve transferability; many prior works used random splits whereas broader-transfer evaluations require holdout-by-composition. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Many entries in Table 2 compare CGR models to PD baselines (RFR, KRR) and show improved accuracy; specific ablation results are reported in cited papers but not summarized numerically in the review. |
| performance_metrics | The review does not present a unified numeric MAE/RMSE for CGR models; it reports that CGR-based models are increasingly replacing PDs due to better predictive accuracy in multiple cited studies. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | Direct CGR models predict energetics only and do not directly deliver forces/phonons; review notes that MLPs (rather than CGR direct models) are required to compute phonon scattering or lattice thermal conductivity degradation. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | CGRs automatically learn local chemical environments and capture coordination and bonding patterns without handcrafted features; ALIGNN's line-graph captures angular information which helps distinguish local geometries relevant to defect energetics. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Direct CGR models assume typical substitutional/vacancy geometries and fail if defects undergo large relaxations or migration to other lattice sites unless such cases are included or detected; charged-defect electrostatics and long-range screening are not inherently encoded and require special data alignment. |
| recommended_best_practices | Curate datasets to exclude PHS and migration-relaxed examples, include explicit defect-site and charge labels, align Fermi levels across materials (see oxygen-core potential alignment), and prefer holdout-by-composition tests when evaluating transferability. |

content.title: Direct defect-formation-energy ML mapping f(X, site i, charge q)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Direct ML (f(X,i,q)) |
| name_full | Direct defect-formation-energy ML mapping f(X, site i, charge q) |
| brief_description | A modeling strategy that directly regress the defect formation energy from the pristine crystalline structure X, the defect site index i, and the defect charge q using local descriptors or graph representations, without predicting relaxed defective geometry. |
| citation_title |  |
| mention_or_use | mention |
| material_systems | Used for single-material and multi-material settings across oxides, perovskites, zincblende semiconductors, halide perovskites, and others as summarized in Table 2. |
| defect_types | Primarily vacancies and substitutional dopants; interstitials only when interstitial sites are predefined; defect complexes generally not handled. |
| charge_state_handling | Charge q is supplied as an explicit input label in the mapping; transition levels can be predicted by combining formation energies at different q, but accurate training labels require consistent Fermi-level alignment and finite-size corrections. |
| target_properties | Formation energies and charge transition levels (TLs); classification of deep vs shallow levels in some works. |
| representation_strategy_name | Defect-centered regression using local descriptors or graph encodings |
| representation_strategy_description | Input is pristine host structure plus the index of the site to be removed or substituted and an explicit charge label; models learn a mapping from the local neighborhood (handcrafted or graph-encoded) to the formation energy without requiring a relaxed defective structure as input. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Explicitly defect-centered: model conditions on the site index i and usually encodes only local environment around that site (sometimes with global host context). Pristine reference X is used rather than the defective relaxed coordinates. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Either handcrafted feature vectors describing the site neighborhood or graph subgraphs centered on the site; cutoffs and specific features vary by implementation and dataset. |
| graph_model_architecture | When graph-based, CGCNN/MEGNet/ALIGNN variants are used with a defect-site token or mask indicating the target node; architectures vary across studies. |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings |  |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Applied to datasets ranging from small (single material) to large (hundreds–~1000 compositions). The review highlights oxygen-vacancy datasets (authors' oxygen-vacancy DB: ~5000 datapoints across 927 oxides referenced) as a central multi-host dataset used for direct ML. |
| transferability_evidence | Review emphasizes need for standardized Fermi-level alignment and dataset curation for transferability; direct ML models can generalize across hosts if training data are standardized (authors propose oxygen core potential alignment), but numeric cross-host transfer results are left to original studies. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Direct ML models are computationally cheap at inference; data efficiency depends on representation (PD vs CGR), with CGR typically requiring more data; review does not provide learning-curve numbers. |
| evaluation_protocol | The review recommends excluding perturbed-host shallow defects and migration-relaxed cases and aligning Fermi levels to create consistent labels; many earlier studies used random splits but transfer evaluations require host-wise splits. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Direct ML has been compared against MLP approaches (which provide forces and phonons) and PD baselines; direct ML is faster but cannot produce relaxed defective geometries. |
| performance_metrics | No uniform numeric metrics reported in the review for direct ML; individual cited papers report MAE values but these are not aggregated here. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | Direct ML cannot provide forces/phonons and thus cannot directly predict phonon scattering or lattice thermal conductivity degradation; MLP workflows are recommended for those tasks. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Direct ML works when defects do not undergo atypical relaxations; authors claim that aligning Fermi levels and excluding PHS improves predictive performance and transferability. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Fails for defects that relax/migrate to different lattice sites, split-vacancies, DX-centers, and perturbed-host shallow states; does not give atomic structure for downstream phonon or kinetic calculations. |
| recommended_best_practices | Use atom mapping to detect migration-relaxed cases, exclude PHS/shallow defects from training, align Fermi levels across datasets (oxygen core potential approach), and include charge label q explicitly if charged defects are targeted. |

content.title: Atom pairing / atom mapping technique for defect dataset curation

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Atom mapping / pairing |
| name_full | Atom pairing / atom mapping technique for defect dataset curation |
| brief_description | A procedure to establish one-to-one correspondence between atoms in pristine and (relaxed) defective supercells to detect defect migration, unusual relaxations and to identify whether the intended defect configuration was preserved. |
| citation_title |  |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Used in authors' prior oxygen-vacancy dataset and discussed across oxide datasets; applicable to any supercell-based defect calculation. |
| defect_types | Used to detect migrations for vacancies, substitutions and interstitial relaxations; applicable to identifying split vacancies and DX-type centers. |
| charge_state_handling | Independent of charge handling; used as a structural curation tool prior to ML training for neutral and charged cases. |
| target_properties | Not a predictive model; used to curate reliable training labels for formation energies and to flag cases where atomic identity/mapping invalidates the intended defect label. |
| representation_strategy_name | Atom-pairing based structural correspondence |
| representation_strategy_description | Find one-to-one atom correspondences between pristine and relaxed defect supercells (or between initial and relaxed defect structures) to identify whether the defect migrated or caused large neighbor rearrangements; paired atoms are flagged and outlier relaxations excluded from training. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Uses both pristine reference and defective relaxed structure to evaluate whether the defect stayed localized at the intended site. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Implementation inspects atomic indices and positions; no fixed radius cutoff described, but practical implementation uses supercell atom identity and mapping heuristics as shown in Fig. 3. |
| graph_model_architecture |  |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings |  |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Used in the authors' oxygen-vacancy database (ref. cited as Ref. 51) and recommended as a curation step for multi-material datasets. |
| transferability_evidence | Atom mapping improves dataset quality and thus model transferability by removing mislabeled examples (migration and split-type relaxations) that would otherwise degrade generalization. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Improves effective training signal by removing noisy labels; quantitative learning-curve effects not provided in the review. |
| evaluation_protocol | Used as a preprocessing/curation step prior to ML model training and evaluation; recommended to avoid label leakage from migration-relaxed cases. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Authors show that excluding problematic relaxations identified by atom mapping improves oxygen-vacancy prediction accuracy (qualitative claim in review; numbers in original Ref. 51). |
| performance_metrics | No numeric metrics provided in the review; claim of improved prediction accuracy after curation is reported qualitatively and illustrated in cited figures. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | Primarily a dataset curation tool; indirect benefit to phonon/thermal studies because reliable geometries/labels improve downstream MLP training for phonon calculations. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Essential to avoid mislabeled data where the target defect no longer corresponds to the assumed site due to large relaxations or migrations; increases label fidelity. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Requires consistent atom indexing and careful handling of symmetric equivalences; may flag borderline relaxations that are physically relevant configurations rather than errors. |
| recommended_best_practices | Apply atom mapping to identify and remove migration-relaxed or split-type vacancy examples from ML training datasets; combine with visual inspection for edge cases. |

content.title: Perturbed-host-state (PHS) exclusion and oxygen-core-potential Fermi-level alignment

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | PHS exclusion + Fermi alignment |
| name_full | Perturbed-host-state (PHS) exclusion and oxygen-core-potential Fermi-level alignment |
| brief_description | Dataset standardization procedures: (1) remove defects whose excess carriers form delocalized perturbed-host (shallow/hydrogenic) states (unsuitable as DFT ML labels), and (2) align Fermi levels across calculations using oxygen core potentials and an overlap-maximization procedure to make charged-defect labels consistent across hosts. |
| citation_title |  |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Applied to large oxide oxygen-vacancy datasets (authors' oxide datasets, Kiyohara 2025, Kumagai 2021 etc.); principally discussed for oxides where oxygen core potentials are a common reference. |
| defect_types | Mainly oxygen vacancies and other defects in oxides; applicable whenever PHS/shallow states or electrostatic reference variability across materials are a concern. |
| charge_state_handling | Charge states remain explicit, but Fermi-level alignment standardizes the vertical offset for comparing formation energies of different q across materials; PHS defects (unable to be described by finite supercells) are excluded from training. |
| target_properties | Formation energies and transition levels for localized (non-PHS) defects across multiple hosts. |
| representation_strategy_name | Label standardization via PHS filtering and oxygen-core-potential alignment |
| representation_strategy_description | Identify and remove defects whose excess carriers form delocalized PHS (shallow) states; align the electrostatic references across different materials using a common core-potential (oxygen core), then choose a constant Fermi-level offset to maximize overlap between formation-energy distributions for different charge states, producing consistent training targets. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | This is a preprocessing/label-standardization strategy that uses pristine host core potentials as a common reference for aligning formation-energy labels; models themselves remain defect-centered. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | N/A (label preprocessing step rather than descriptor design). |
| graph_model_architecture |  |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings |  |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Developed/applied on large oxide vacancy datasets (authors' dataset: ~5000 datapoints over 927 oxides referenced; Kiyohara 2025: 932 oxides; Kumagai 2021: 937 oxides). |
| transferability_evidence | Authors report that aligning Fermi levels via oxygen core potentials and excluding PHS improves overlap of formation-energy distributions across charge states and generally improves ML training dynamics and transferability; qualitative improvements are shown in distribution plots in the review (Figs. 4(d),(e)). |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Standardizing targets improves training stability and weight updates, indirectly increasing data efficiency; no explicit numeric few-shot curves provided. |
| evaluation_protocol | Authors recommend removal of PHS and consistent Fermi alignment before training cross-material models; specific optimization chosen to minimize mean differences between charge-state distributions. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Review contrasts models trained with and without PHS exclusion/Fermi alignment and reports improved predictions when these steps are applied (qualitative description; detailed numbers in original referenced study). |
| performance_metrics | Qualitative reduction in inter-charge-state distribution differences illustrated; exact MAE improvements not reproduced numerically in the review. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | Indirect: by ensuring charged-defect formation energies are consistent across datasets, subsequent MLP or defect-MD workflows that couple to phonon calculations have a more reliable energetic baseline; no direct phonon predictions from this procedure. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | PHS labels are unreliable for ML because supercells cannot capture long-range hydrogenic states; oxygen-core alignment removes spurious electrostatic offsets between calculations and yields more physically consistent labels across materials. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Oxygen-core alignment is material-class-specific (oxides); generalizing to non-oxide chemistries requires a different core reference or procedure. The approach does not remove finite-size electrostatic errors entirely and must be used together with finite-size corrections (FNV or extended schemes). |
| recommended_best_practices | Before training cross-material charged-defect models, exclude PHS/shallow defects, apply finite-size corrections, and align electrostatic references (e.g., oxygen core potential for oxides) to standardize labels. |

content.title: Freysoldt–Neugebauer–Van de Walle (FNV) finite-size correction and extended scheme

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | FNV + extended finite-size corrections |
| name_full | Freysoldt–Neugebauer–Van de Walle (FNV) finite-size correction and extended scheme |
| brief_description | Standard electrostatic finite-size correction for charged-defect supercell DFT calculations (FNV), with an extended scheme developed by the authors to broaden applicability across defect types and materials; implementations available in pydefect and pycdt. |
| citation_title |  |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Applies broadly to periodic supercell charged-defect DFT calculations across ionic and covalent materials; review emphasizes use for localized charged defects in non-metallic systems. |
| defect_types | Charged vacancies, substitutional charged defects, and other localized charged defects that can be treated within supercells. |
| charge_state_handling | Provides the finite-size correction E_corr[D^q] used to produce consistent formation-energy labels for charged defects; essential preprocessing for any ML training on charged-defect energies. |
| target_properties | Corrected charged-defect formation energies and transition levels. |
| representation_strategy_name | Finite-size electrostatic correction preprocessing (FNV and extended) |
| representation_strategy_description | Compute and subtract a physically motivated correction term E_corr[D^q] based on electrostatic model potentials and dielectric screening (FNV method); authors present an extended scheme that handles a wider variety of defect types and materials and is implemented in common defect workflow packages. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Label correction applied to defective supercell energies; does not change descriptor representation but is required to make labels physically meaningful and comparable across supercells and materials. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | N/A (preprocessing of DFT total energies). |
| graph_model_architecture |  |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings |  |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Used as standard post-processing for charged-defect datasets prior to ML training; authors' own oxide datasets apply this correction. |
| transferability_evidence | Finite-size corrections are necessary to compare charged-defect formation energies across different supercell sizes and materials; review argues that without them ML models cannot be meaningfully transferred across supercell geometries or different materials. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | By producing physically consistent labels, finite-size corrections improve the signal-to-noise in training data; no explicit numerical data-efficiency curves presented. |
| evaluation_protocol | Apply FNV (or extended) correction to all charged-defect energies before inclusion in training/testing; the review recommends this as standard practice for charged-defect ML. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Not reported as ablation studies in the review, but authors emphasize necessity; excluding corrections leads to inconsistent labels between charge states and materials. |
| performance_metrics | No numeric metrics in the review quantifying improvement due to FNV extensions, but the approach is presented as required for accurate charged-defect ML. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | Finite-size corrections affect formation energies and transition levels; indirect benefit for MLPs and MD-based phonon scattering studies by providing correct charge-state energetics when charged defects are included. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Correcting supercell electrostatic artifacts is essential to isolate intrinsic defect energetics and enable cross-material comparisons and ML generalization. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Corrections apply only to localized defects that fit within the supercell; they are not applicable to PHS/shallow states or defect states that delocalize beyond the cell size. For 2D and slab models, specialized corrections are required. |
| recommended_best_practices | Always apply FNV or improved finite-size corrections (and document them) when creating ML training labels for charged defects; combine with Fermi-level alignment and PHS exclusion for cross-material ML. |

content.title: Machine-learning potentials with explicit long-range Coulomb interactions (short-range MLP + Ewald)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | MLPs + LR Coulomb |
| name_full | Machine-learning potentials with explicit long-range Coulomb interactions (short-range MLP + Ewald) |
| brief_description | ML potentials that couple a learned short-range atomic-energy model to an explicit long-range electrostatic term (e.g., Ewald-summed Coulomb interactions) to better capture ionic screening and transferability in charged/ionic systems and defects. |
| citation_title |  |
| mention_or_use | mention |
| material_systems | Applied to ionic solids and defect-containing ionic materials (examples in MLP literature include Li-conductors, perovskites, oxides). |
| defect_types | Point defects in ionic materials where long-range Coulomb interactions matter (charged vacancies, dopants that change local charge distributions); MLPs can handle neutral defects by energy/force predictions and some approaches have been extended to charged cases. |
| charge_state_handling | Long-range Coulomb term helps model electrostatics but ML training still requires handling of charged-supercell reference ambiguity; LR Coulomb inclusion improves description of dielectric screening, partial charges, and polarization. |
| target_properties | Energies, forces, phonons, diffusion coefficients, and phonon scattering by defects; enables lattice dynamics and thermal-transport calculations with defects. |
| representation_strategy_name | Short-range learned local model + explicit LR Coulomb interactions (Ewald/physical electrostatics) |
| representation_strategy_description | Decompose total energy into a learned short-range contribution (local cutoff-based) plus an explicit long-range electrostatic model (Ewald sum with model charges or learned charge predictors), sometimes augmented by learned polarization/Born-effective-charge outputs. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | MLP energy is global sum of local contributions plus LR electrostatics; defect is handled through local environments and global LR term rather than a defect-centered delta encoding. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Short-range models use local neighbor lists with cutoffs; species included via embeddings; polarization/Born-charge predictors may be learned concurrently. |
| graph_model_architecture | MLP families include kernel-based GAP, neural-network potentials, message-passing MLPs (CHGNet, M3GNet) that can be coupled to LR terms; review cites explicit LR frameworks in literature (refs. 115–119) but specifics vary per study. |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings |  |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Used in MLP training sets for ionic materials; Table 3 marks several works that included LR Coulomb interactions (Miwa 2018, Deng 2019 eSNAP, Qi 2021 MTP etc.). Datasets are DFT-derived energies/forces from AIMD and static calculations. |
| transferability_evidence | Review states including LR Coulomb terms enhances transferability and accuracy for ionic systems; authors argue such explicit electrostatic modeling is important for charged-defect descriptions and dielectric screening across materials. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Explicit physics (LR Coulomb) reduces the burden on ML to learn long-range interactions, likely improving data efficiency; review references this as a qualitative advantage but does not provide numeric evidence. |
| evaluation_protocol | MLPs are trained on DFT energies/forces from pristine and defective cells (sometimes using active-learning pipelines). For charged defects additional care regarding energy reference is needed; some studies preserved charge neutrality via dopants or compensating backgrounds. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Review contrasts MLPs that include LR Coulomb to those that do not, stating improved performance for ionic materials; numerical ablations are provided in original cited papers rather than in the review. |
| performance_metrics | Specific metrics (MAE in energies/forces, phonon properties) are reported in original works; the review does not reproduce consolidated numerical performance for LR-enabled MLPs. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | MLPs with LR Coulomb enable force predictions necessary for phonon calculations and hence allow phonon-scattering computations and lattice thermal conductivity (kappa) predictions/degradation due to defects; review explicitly notes MLPs permit phonon and long-time MD simulations to study defect-driven thermal transport. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Including explicit LR Coulomb interactions and learned polarization/Born effective charges yields more physically consistent descriptions of ionic screening and charge localization near defects, improving transferability. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Even with LR terms, charged-defect total-energy reference ambiguity remains for charged supercells; treating single charged defects in periodic MLP training remains challenging without consistent reference schemes or multiple-defect neutralization strategies. |
| recommended_best_practices | For ionic defect studies use MLPs that include explicit LR Coulomb interactions or learned polarization outputs; carefully design training data and handle charge-reference issues when including charged defects. |

| name_full | Descriptor-based machine-learning potentials (Behler–Parrinello symmetry functions, GAP, MTP, SNAP/eSNAP) |
| brief_description | ML potentials built on fixed local environment descriptors (symmetry functions, bispectrum/SNAP, spectral neighbor features) combined with kernel or neural-network regressors, used to model energies/forces for defective and pristine structures. |
| citation_title |  |
| mention_or_use | mention |
| material_systems | Used across semiconductors (Si, GaN), ionic conductors (Li, Na conductors), thermoelectrics (Bi2Te3, Sb2Te3), and oxides in many cited MLP defect studies (Table 3). |
| defect_types | Vacancies, interstitials, substitutional dopants, polarons in some studies; used for diffusion, phonon, and formation-energy calculations of defects. |
| charge_state_handling | Most descriptor-based MLPs are trained for charge-neutral simulations; some studies simulate charged behavior using compensated dopants or background charge in DFT reference data but energy-reference ambiguity remains an issue. |
| target_properties | Energies, forces, diffusion coefficients, phonon properties, phonon scattering, formation energies (when neutral), activation barriers. |
| representation_strategy_name | Local atomic environment descriptors (symmetry functions, bispectrum, spectral neighbor features) |
| representation_strategy_description | Compute fixed numerical descriptors per-atom based on radial and angular neighbor distributions within a cutoff (Behler symmetry functions, SNAP bispectrum, eSNAP spectral features), and use kernel or NN regression to predict atomic contributions to energy and derive forces. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Atom-centered (local), energy assembled by summation of per-atom contributions; defect information arises from altered local environments rather than an explicit defect-centered graph or delta-feature. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Descriptors include radial/ angular basis (symmetry functions), bispectrum components (SNAP), spectral neighbor analysis (eSNAP); cutoff radii are set per model (not specified generically in review); chemical species enter via one-hot or weighted channels in descriptors. |
| graph_model_architecture | Not a graph model; kernel methods (GAP), local NN potentials (Behler–Parrinello), MTP are examples. |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings |  |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Training data are DFT energies/forces from AIMD and static defect calculations; many studies used active-learning to sample configurations (DP-GEN style) and datasets range from small to sizable depending on system complexity (see Table 3 entries). |
| transferability_evidence | Descriptor-based MLPs (especially kernel methods like GAP) are cited as data-efficient and can generalize well within similar chemical environments; however transfer across chemistries and to charged defects is limited without explicit physics. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Kernel approaches often show strong data efficiency; review explicitly notes GAP and related kernel methods often provide high accuracy with good sample efficiency. |
| evaluation_protocol | Train on DFT energies+forces; validate on held-out configurations or MD trajectories; care needed to include defective configurations and relaxations in training set for defect transferability. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Descriptor-based MLPs are compared to message-passing and equivariant MLPs; review indicates recent equivariant MPNNs often improve over descriptor-based methods when data are abundant. |
| performance_metrics | Specific MAE/RMSE values reported in the individual MLP studies referenced in Table 3 (not reproduced numerically in the review). |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | Descriptor-based MLPs have been used to compute phonons and thermal transport with defects; several cited works used GAP/Behler or eSNAP to compute phonon properties and defect scattering. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Fixed descriptors inject prior physical knowledge and can be very data-efficient for energies/forces in similar chemical environments; they are, however, limited by descriptor completeness and locality assumptions. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Locality assumption may miss long-range electrostatics unless explicitly added; descriptor completeness may limit accuracy for complex defect distortions or charge localization phenomena. |
| recommended_best_practices | Include representative defective configurations in training (including relaxations), consider adding explicit LR electrostatic terms or learned charges for ionic systems, and use active learning to sample rare defect-induced distortions. |
