metadata.title: A foundation model for atomistic materials chemistry.
metadata.abstract: Atomistic simulations of matter, especially those that leverage first-principles (ab initio) electronic structure theory, provide a microscopic view of the world, underpinning much of our understanding of chemistry and materials science. Over the last decade or so, machine-learned force fields have transformed atomistic modeling by enabling simulations of ab initio quality over unprecedented time and length scales. However, early machine-learning (ML) force fields have largely been limited by (i) the substantial computational and human effort required to develop and validate potentials for each particular system of interest and (ii) a general lack of transferability from one chemical system to the next. Here, we show that it is possible to create a general-purpose atomistic ML model, trained on a public dataset of moderate size, that is capable of running stable molecular dynamics for a wide range of molecules and materials. We demonstrate the power of the MACE-MP-0 model-and its qualitative and at times quantitative accuracy-on a diverse set of problems in the physical sciences, including properties of solids, liquids, gases, chemical reactions, interfaces, and even the dynamics of a small protein. The model can be applied out of the box as a starting or "foundation" model for any atomistic system of interest and, when desired, can be fine-tuned on just a handful of application-specific data points to reach ab initio accuracy. Establishing that a stable force-field model can cover almost all materials changes atomistic modeling in a fundamental way: experienced users obtain reliable results much faster, and beginners face a lower barrier to entry. Foundation models thus represent a step toward democratizing the revolution in atomic-scale modeling that has been brought about by ML force fields.

content.title: MACE high-body-order equivariant atom-centered features

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | MACE atomic-environment representation |
| name_full | MACE high-body-order equivariant atom-centered features |
| brief_description | Atom-centered, equivariant high-body-order features produced by the MACE message-passing architecture (4-body messages, spherical expansion up to l_max=3) used as the primary featurization for predicting energies, forces and derived properties across crystals, molecules and defects; features are element-aware and constructed from local neighbour geometry within a radial cutoff. |
| citation_title | Mace: Higher order equivariant message passing neural networks for fast and accurate force fields |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Many hosts across the paper: inorganic crystals (Materials Project coverage), BCC metals (point and extended defects), Si (Si interstitials), metal oxides (CeO2), MOFs (Mg-MOF-74), water and aqueous interfaces, catalytic surfaces (Pt(111), Cu, In2O3), alloys and more — i.e. multiple hosts and chemistries. |
| defect_types | Point defects and extended defects are reported in applications (Si interstitials, proton defects H3O+/OH- in water, point and extended defects in BCC metals, activation energies for point defect and dislocation motion); explicit mention of defect complexes is not given in detail in main text but extended/complex defects (dislocations) are considered in SI. |
| charge_state_handling | No explicit charge-state encoding: the representation is structural (atomic positions and species) only. Charged species (e.g., hydronium, hydroxide, dissolved ions) appear in simulations implicitly via atomic identities and positions, but there is no explicit electron chemical potential, background-charge correction, nor explicit electrostatic/charge labels incorporated into the learned representation; model also lacks explicit long-range electrostatics beyond the ~12 Å receptive field. |
| target_properties | Total energies, forces and stresses (used to obtain: defect formation and migration activation energies and NEB profiles, reaction barriers, phonon dispersions), examples include activation energies for point-defect/dislocation motion, NEB energy profiles for catalytic pathways, phonon dispersions (in SI); direct prediction of phonon scattering rates or lattice thermal-conductivity degradation is not reported in the main text. |
| representation_strategy_name | Atom-centered equivariant high-body-order descriptor (MACE features) |
| representation_strategy_description | Each atom has an element embedding; local geometric information up to a radial cutoff is expanded in a spherical basis and combined into 4-body equivariant messages via tensor products; messages are passed through two MACE layers to produce per-atom energy contributions. Short-range ZBL repulsion and Agnesi distance transform are used to stabilize close approaches; a learnable density-normalisation scales the atomic basis. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Atom-centered (local) representation — not a defect-centered subgraph or explicit delta-to-pristine encoding; defect-related tasks are handled by feeding defective supercells through the same atom-centered MACE representation (the paper uses the internal features to compare local environments between training and defect NEB images). |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Radial cutoff (effective receptive field) ≈ 6 Å (two-message-passes → ≈12 Å global receptive field), radial expansion: 10 Bessel functions × polynomial cutoff, spherical expansion up to l_max = 3; 4-body messages (correlation order 3) per layer; tensor-decomposed 128-channel representation; element identity encoded via learned element embeddings; equivariant (E(3)) features implemented with e3nn. |
| graph_model_architecture | MACE (equivariant message-passing graph tensor network) with two message-passing layers, high body-order (4-body) equivariant messages, mild nonlinearity (nonlinearities in radial basis and final readout), tensor-decomposition parameterisation; L=1 ('medium') model used in this paper. |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | Yes — the MACE-MP-0 foundation model (pretrained on the MPtrj dataset) provides the internal atomic/environment embeddings used out-of-the-box and then fine-tuned for downstream tasks; internal high-dimensional MACE features are projected (UMAP) to assess similarity between training and out-of-domain environments (e.g., NEB images). |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Pretrained on MPtrj (Materials Project trajectories) containing ≈1.5M configurations (approx. 150k unique MP structures, mostly small periodic unit cells, ~90% under 70 atoms), DFT (PBE) labels; defect-specific training data are not enumerated — downstream defect/catalysis tasks are handled by fine-tuning on small application-specific datasets (typical fine-tuning size ≈100 configurations; NEB fine-tuning examples used as few as 5 single-point DFT labels per profile). |
| transferability_evidence | Strong out-of-domain performance reported: MOF energy prediction on QMOF (13,912 structures) MAE = 0.040 eV/atom despite no QMOF training; catalysis NEB paths on In2O3 and Cu show qualitatively correct barriers out-of-the-box and excellent quantitative agreement after few-shot fine-tuning (5 DFT points); UMAP projections of MACE features show overlap between training atomic environments and NEB defect environments indicating shared representation; general stable MD for many chemistries including charged species in liquids reported. Reported baseline/model-level metrics: pretrained medium model energy MAE ≈ 18 meV/atom and force MAE ≈ 39 meV/Å; after fine-tuning energy MAE down to ≈13 meV/atom on some tasks. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Fine-tuning evidence: NEB/catalysis examples achieved near-DFT quantitative agreement after fine-tuning with as few as 5 single-point DFT calculations per energy profile; typical fine-tuning for applications used ≈100 configurations and multi-head replay to avoid catastrophic forgetting; comparisons in Fig.4 show fine-tuned foundation model substantially outperforms models trained from scratch on the same small datasets. |
| evaluation_protocol | Fine-tuning protocol: multi-head replay fine-tuning (replays a subset of foundation training data during FT). For downstream tasks the paper reports small-sample fine-tuning (≈100 configs) and occasional 5-point NEB fine-tunes; explicit train/validation/test split strategies for defect-specific datasets are not detailed in the main text (many defect/phonon/NEB results and detailed protocols referred to SI/appendices). |
| baselines_and_ablations | Main comparisons: pretrained MACE-MP-0 vs the same model after fine-tuning (multi-head replay FT) vs a model trained from scratch only on the small fine-tuning dataset (the FT model consistently wins). The paper also compares to DFT references (PBE-D3) and custom ML potentials in application cases; ablation of long-range interactions and spin/electrostatics is discussed as limitations but not ablated experimentally in the main text. |
| performance_metrics | Reported numbers relevant to defect/transfer tasks include: pretrained medium model energy MAE ≈ 18 meV/atom and force MAE ≈ 39 meV/Å; MOF (QMOF) PBE energy MAE = 0.040 eV/atom; ice-polymorph relative lattice energies MAE ≈ 5 meV; phonon and defect benchmarks reported in SI (numbers not all reproduced in main text). NEB/catalysis FT agreement described qualitatively as 'excellent' after 5-point fine-tunes, but full numeric tables are in SI. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | Paper reports the model can predict phonon dispersions (benchmarked in SI) and therefore can supply the harmonic phonon spectrum needed for phonon transport calculations; however, no direct workflow or reported results for ML prediction of phonon scattering rates or explicit lattice thermal conductivity degradation due to point defects is presented in the main text — the paper does not report direct ML predictions of scattering rates or kappa degradation nor coupling to BTE/relaxation-time-approximation in the main body (phonon results are limited to dispersions and related benchmarks in SI). |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Authors argue the high body-order equivariant features capture many-body local geometry and chemistry necessary for transferability, and that the foundation model's internal features enable identification of similar local environments across domains (UMAP example) explaining out-of-domain performance; fine-tuning with a handful of data points corrects local energetic offsets efficiently, supporting the foundation + few-shot paradigm. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Reported limitations relevant to defects: absence of explicit long-range electrostatics and spin degrees of freedom (limits accuracy for charged defects, dilute ionic screening, interfaces); inconsistencies in training data due to sporadic Hubbard U application in Materials Project (affects systems with certain transition metals and O/F, creating discontinuities); model inherits PBE functional limitations (no dispersion unless additive D3 applied), and short radial cutoff may hamper description of long-range fields produced by charged defects. Also, while MD stability is good, quantitative accuracy for intermolecular interactions and some catalytic states remains limited without FT. |
| recommended_best_practices | Use the foundation MACE-MP-0 model out-of-the-box for exploration and then fine-tune with a small, application-specific DFT dataset (≈5–100 configurations) using multi-head replay FT to avoid catastrophic forgetting; apply additive DFT-D3 corrections when dispersion matters; for charged-defect problems or long-range electrostatic effects, augment the model/representation to include explicit electrostatics or use larger receptive fields / targeted FT data; ensure consistent electronic-structure settings in training/FT to avoid Hubbard-U related inconsistencies. |

content.title: Multi-head replay fine-tuning (foundation model adaptation protocol)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Multi-head replay fine-tuning |
| name_full | Multi-head replay fine-tuning (foundation model adaptation protocol) |
| brief_description | A fine-tuning protocol used to adapt the MACE-MP-0 foundation potential to downstream tasks (including NEB/catalysis and defect-related calculations) by training on a small new dataset while replaying a subset of the foundation training data to avoid catastrophic forgetting. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Applied across multiple downstream examples in the paper: catalytic NEB paths (Cu and In2O3), MOF adsorption dynamics, and other application-specific examples including defect-related NEBs and point-defect activation energies in SI. |
| defect_types | Used to improve predictions on tasks that include reaction paths and defect migration barriers (NEB images, point-defect/dislocation motion), but the protocol itself is general-purpose (not defect-specific). |
| charge_state_handling | Protocol does not add explicit charge-state features; it fine-tunes the same structure-only MACE representation. Handling of charged defects remains governed by the underlying representation (i.e., no explicit charge labels added by FT unless user supplies charged configurations during FT). |
| target_properties | Used to lower force and energy errors for application-specific targets: NEB energy profiles (reaction and migration barriers), forces, and energies; thereby improving predicted activation energies and reaction energetics relevant to defects and catalysis. |
| representation_strategy_name | Foundation-model fine-tuning with replay (multi-head replay FT) |
| representation_strategy_description | During FT the loss includes both the new small application dataset and a replayed subset of the original foundation training data; separate model head(s) may be used to preserve foundation capabilities while adapting to new tasks. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | No change to centering: fine-tuning still operates on full supercells/atom-centered inputs; practitioners can supply defective supercells during FT to adapt locally to defect environments. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Does not change descriptor hyperparameters (radial cutoff, spherical expansion, message order); it updates model weights starting from pretrained MACE parameters and uses a replay subset to stabilize representations. |
| graph_model_architecture | Applied to the MACE graph-tensor-network architecture (two MACE layers, equivariant messages). |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | Relies on pretrained MACE-MP-0 weights as initialization; FT modifies these weights while replaying foundation data. |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Typical FT regimes shown: ≈100 configurations for many applications; for NEB reaction profiles FT with as few as 5 single-point DFT calculations per profile was sufficient to reach near-DFT agreement in examples presented. |
| transferability_evidence | FT demonstrably improves out-of-domain predictions: NEB reaction profiles for CO oxidation on Cu and CO2→methanol step on In2O3 achieve excellent agreement with DFT after small-number FT (5 points) where pretrained model alone was only qualitatively correct; FT models retain foundation robustness due to replay. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Strong few-shot evidence: 5 single-point DFT labels per NEB profile produced excellent quantitative agreement with DFT for several reaction barriers; FT with ≈100 configs substantially reduces force errors across several applications compared to pretrained-only and to models trained from scratch on the small dataset. |
| evaluation_protocol | Multi-head replay FT: the loss includes the small FT dataset and a subset of the original training data; specific training hyperparameters and replay subset sizes are given in SI/appendices but main-text examples report FT epochs ≈50 for some energy-weighted FT runs. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Comparison shown between pretrained model, fine-tuned model (multi-head replay) and a model trained from scratch only on the small FT dataset — fine-tuned model consistently outperforms 'from-scratch' baseline and improves over pretrained-only for quantitative accuracy. |
| performance_metrics | Qualitative statements and selected numbers: fine-tuning reduces force RMS errors significantly across several tasks (Fig.4). Example: several NEB profiles reach 'excellent agreement' with DFT after FT with only a few points (numeric NEB errors are provided in SI but not all reproduced in main text). |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | FT can be used to improve phonon predictions when FT data includes phonon-related configurations (the paper fine-tunes to r2SCAN for XC upgrade in SI); no explicit example of FT targeted to defect-induced phonon scattering or thermal conductivity was reported in main text. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Authors argue that starting from a foundation potential and fine-tuning with a handful of application-relevant configurations is an efficient workflow: the foundation captures broad chemical priors while FT corrects local energetic errors with very little data. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | FT does not solve representational deficiencies such as lack of long-range electrostatics or spin; if the foundation lacks required physics for a target (e.g., charged-defect long-range fields), FT with small local datasets may be insufficient without augmenting the representation or including explicit electrostatic features. |
| recommended_best_practices | When tackling defect/dopant tasks: generate a small, targeted DFT set sampling the defect configuration space (NEB images, migration endpoints), fine-tune using multi-head replay to avoid catastrophic forgetting, and include dispersion/electrostatic corrections or augment model physics when long-range interactions are important. |

content.title: MPtrj dataset (Materials Project trajectories collection)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | MPtrj (training corpus) |
| name_full | MPtrj dataset (Materials Project trajectories collection) |
| brief_description | The primary pretraining dataset used for MACE-MP-0: ≈1.5M DFT configurations derived from Materials Project static calculations and structural optimizations, covering a wide range of inorganic crystals and some molecular components; labeled with PBE energies/forces/stresses (with some entries using Hubbard U). |
| citation_title |  |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Inorganic crystals across much of the periodic table (approx. 150k unique MP structures), small periodic unit cells (≈90% < 70 atoms), plus some molecular components; used to pretrain a foundation potential transferable to MOFs, catalysts and defects. |
| defect_types | MPtrj itself is largely composed of bulk/relaxed crystalline snapshots and MD/trajectory snapshots from Materials Project; it is not a targeted defect database. Defect-related examples in the paper come from fine-tuning/supplementary datasets rather than enumerated defect entries in MPtrj. |
| charge_state_handling | DFT labels are PBE; in Materials Project some calculations include Hubbard U for specific transition-metal + O/F compositions, leading to energy inconsistencies; MPtrj configurations do not systematically include explicit electron chemical potential labels or charged-defect corrections. |
| target_properties | Energy, forces, stresses (used to train ML potential which is then used to compute defect formation energies, activation barriers, NEBs, phonons, etc.). |
| representation_strategy_name | Dataset used to pretrain foundation MACE features (no special defect featurization inside dataset itself). |
| representation_strategy_description | Large, heterogeneous collection of DFT-relaxation snapshots and static calculations; serves as broad coverage pretraining corpus so that atom-centered MACE features learn general chemical/geometric priors. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Dataset is not defect-centered; contains many periodic bulk/unit-cell snapshots but not an explicit strategy of pristine-vs-defect delta encodings. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | N/A (dataset description). |
| graph_model_architecture | Used to train MACE models (see MACE entity). |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | This dataset is the pretraining source for the MACE-MP-0 foundation potential; internal features/embeddings arise from training on MPtrj. |
| data_regime_and_dataset | ≈1.5M configurations (rough count given), derived from Materials Project static and structure-optimization tasks; DFT level PBE with occasional Hubbard U; mostly small periodic unit cells. |
| transferability_evidence | The model pretrained on MPtrj generalizes to MOFs (QMOF) with MAE = 0.040 eV/atom and to many out-of-domain tasks after fine-tuning; UMAP analysis shows overlap in local environments between MPtrj training set and out-of-domain NEB defect images in specific tests. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Foundation trained on large MPtrj enables few-shot FT (5–100 points) to reach DFT-level accuracy for specific NEB/defect tasks, demonstrating efficiency of the foundation + FT workflow. |
| evaluation_protocol | Training/validation splits for the foundation fit are described in SI; the paper reports overall trained-model errors (energy and force MAEs) on validation/test splits but detailed defect-specific split strategies are in appendices/SI. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Paper discusses systemic data issues in MPtrj (Hubbard U inconsistencies, magnetic order variability) as sources of error but does not present defect-specific ablations comparing defect-only vs bulk-only pretraining. |
| performance_metrics | Size ≈1.5M configurations; foundation-model trained on MPtrj achieves energy MAE ≈18 meV/atom and force MAE ≈39 meV/Å (medium model). |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | Foundation trained on MPtrj gives a model able to reproduce phonon dispersions (benchmarked in SI); however, MPtrj lacks explicit datasets targeted at phonon-scattering-by-defects or thermal-conductivity degradation, so direct training for defect-induced thermal transport is not demonstrated. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Authors argue breadth/diversity of MPtrj is sufficient to produce transferable atomic-environment priors captured by MACE, enabling out-of-domain simulations and efficient FT for defects and catalysis. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | MPtrj contains inconsistent application of Hubbard U for certain transition metals with O/F that introduces energetic discontinuities; magnetic-order variability across entries for the same material can contribute energy scatter (some materials vary by >100 meV/atom across magnetic orders), which may degrade defect-prediction accuracy in affected chemistries. |
| recommended_best_practices | When building/using foundation models for defect physics, curate/avoid inconsistent electronic-structure labels (Hubbard U), include representative charged/defect configurations or plan targeted fine-tuning, and consider adding explicit long-range electrostatics if charged defects or dilute screening are central to the target tasks. |

metadata.title: Machine-learned impurity level prediction for semiconductors: the example of Cd-based chalcogenides
metadata.abstract: The ability to predict the likelihood of impurity incorporation and their electronic energy levels in semiconductors is crucial for controlling its conductivity, and thus the semiconductor’s performance in solar cells, photodiodes, and optoelectronics. The difficulty and expense of experimental and computational determination of impurity levels makes a data-driven machine learning approach appropriate. In this work, we show that a density functional theory-generated dataset of impurities in Cd-based chalcogenides CdTe, CdSe, and CdS can lead to accurate and generalizable predictive models of defect properties. By converting any semiconductor + impurity system into a set of numerical descriptors, regression models are developed for the impurity formation enthalpy and charge transition levels. These regression models can subsequently predict impurity properties in mixed anion CdX compounds (where X is a combination of Te, Se and S) fairly accurately, proving that although trained only on the end points, they are applicable to intermediate compositions. We make machine-learned predictions of the Fermi-level-dependent formation energies of hundreds of possible impurities in 5 chalcogenide compounds, and we suggest a list of impurities which can shift the equilibrium Fermi level in the semiconductor as determined by the dominant intrinsic defects. Machine learning predictions for the dominating impurities compare well with DFT predictions, revealing the power of machine-learned models in the quick screening of impurities likely to affect the optoelectronic behavior of semiconductors.

content.title: Base set of defect-site descriptors (period/group, defect-site index, neighbor counts)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Base defect-site feature vector |
| name_full | Base set of defect-site descriptors (period/group, defect-site index, neighbor counts) |
| brief_description | A small, defect-centered numeric encoding used for every impurity+site datapoint that records the impurity element period and group, a numeric defect-site index (encoding substitutional/interstitial site identity), and the number of Cd and X (Te/Se/S) nearest neighbors at that site. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Cd-based chalcogenides: CdTe, CdSe, CdS, plus mixed-anion alloys CdTe0.5Se0.5 and CdSe0.5S0.5 (models trained on the first three and tested on mixed-anion compounds). |
| defect_types | Single-point defects only: substitutional dopants at Cd site (M_Cd) and X site (M_X), interstitials (M_i) at different interstitial positions (neutral/Cd-site/X-site variants), native vacancies and antisites (for intrinsic defect energetics). No defect complexes or Frenkel pairs were modeled. |
| charge_state_handling | Does not itself encode charge; used alongside other features (see oxidation-state entry). ML targets include charged-defect transition levels but the base vector only identifies site and coordination numerically. |
| target_properties | Used as part of feature sets to predict neutral-state formation enthalpy (ΔH) and charge transition levels ε(q1/q2); downstream E^f(E_F) vs Fermi level curves and screening (dominating impurities). |
| representation_strategy_name | Defect-centered tabular/site-indexed feature vector (base) |
| representation_strategy_description | A compact tabular representation centered on the defect site: elemental identity encoded by period/group, discrete numeric defect-site index (0=M_Cd,1=M_X,0.5=neutral interstitial, 0.25/0.75 for interstitials biased to Cd/X site), and integer counts of Cd and X neighbors. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Defect-centered: encodes only local site identity and coordination; used together with additional element/unit-cell-derived descriptors rather than encoding full supercell geometry. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Local environment captured coarsely via number of Cd and X neighbors (integer counts). No explicit radial/angular basis, no cutoff radius reported beyond implicit coordination shells from site identification; species information in base vector is categorical/ordinal (period/group indices and neighbor counts). |
| graph_model_architecture | none (tabular descriptors + classical regressors: Random Forest, Kernel Ridge, LASSO). |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | none |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Used across the datasets in the paper (PBE and HSE data). Base descriptors included for all computed datapoints (PBE ΔH dataset: 989 points; PBE ε dataset: 2550 points; HSE ε dataset: 680 points). |
| transferability_evidence | Used as part of full feature sets when testing models trained on CdTe/CdSe/CdS and applied to out-of-sample mixed-anion compounds (CdTe0.5Se0.5 and CdSe0.5S0.5); contributed to the reported out-of-sample errors (see overall results). |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Learning curves show error decreases with more training data when using the base vector plus other descriptors; base vector alone yields worse performance (see ablation comparisons), so base vector is necessary but not sufficient for data-efficiency. |
| evaluation_protocol | Train/test splits done over the CdTe+CdSe+CdS pooled data with explicit out-of-sample evaluation on mixed-anion compounds; experiments included many random train draws (100 different models) to estimate mean and standard deviation; typical reported split used 90% training / 10% test for parity plots and RMSE estimates. |
| baselines_and_ablations | This base set is the mandatory core in all ablations; comparisons were made by adding elemental or unit-cell defect properties on top of it (see separate entries). |
| performance_metrics | Not predictive by itself; used within combined descriptor sets that achieved RMSEs reported elsewhere (e.g., ΔH combined descriptors test RMSE ~0.38 eV). |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | none |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Authors treat a compact numeric encoding of the defect site as a necessary anchor to relate elemental/unit-cell features to a specific defect geometry and coordination; the site-index and neighbor counts capture the primary local coordination differences among substitutional/interstitial sites. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Very coarse — does not encode continuous geometry, strain, atomic distances, angular information, or long-range electrostatics; insufficient alone to reach best accuracies. |
| recommended_best_practices | Use as a minimal defect-centered scaffold but augment with unit-cell-derived energetic/electronic descriptors and elemental properties for accurate predictions; include explicit charge-related features when predicting transition levels. |

| brief_description | A featurization composed solely of tabulated elemental properties of the impurity atom (M) such as period, group, first ionization energy, electronegativity, ionic radius, and other scalar chemical descriptors. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Applied to CdTe, CdSe, CdS and tested on mixed-anion variants; used as one of three main feature families. |
| defect_types | Same single-point defect types as in the study (substitutional M_Cd, M_X; interstitial M_i); elemental features only characterize the impurity species, not the site geometry. |
| charge_state_handling | No explicit charge-state features included in elemental-only set; for transition-level models the oxidation-state features (O1,O2) were added to enable charge-aware modeling (see separate entry). |
| target_properties | ΔH (neutral formation enthalpy) and ε(q1/q2) (charge transition levels). |
| representation_strategy_name | Elemental property fingerprint (tabular) |
| representation_strategy_description | Encodes continuous chemical attributes of the impurity atom (ionization energy, electronegativity, ionic radii, period, group) to capture chemical trends in defect energetics. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Not defect-centered by itself — must be combined with base site encoding to refer to a particular defect instance. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | No local environment radial/ angular detail; species info is continuous scalar properties rather than one-hot encoding. |
| graph_model_architecture | none |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | none |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Used across the PBE and HSE datasets; fed into models trained on CdTe/CdSe/CdS data (sizes as in Table I). |
| transferability_evidence | Elemental-only models performed worse on out-of-sample mixed-anion compounds compared to models including unit-cell defect features (out-of-sample RMSEs larger: e.g., ΔH RFR out-of-sample RMSE ~0.84 eV with elemental-only vs ~0.52 eV combined). |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Learning curves show elemental-only features give higher errors at all training sizes; combining with unit-cell features reduces needed data to reach a given RMSE. |
| evaluation_protocol | Same training/test splits; comparisons were made by training identical regressors on each descriptor family to evaluate importance. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Served as a baseline; ablation shows substantially worse performance than unit-cell or combined descriptors (Tables II and III). |
| performance_metrics | Example: For PBE ΔH using RFR: test RMSE = 0.65 eV (elemental-only) vs 0.38 eV (elemental+unit-cell); out-of-sample RMSE for CdTe0.5Se0.5 = 0.84 eV (elemental-only) vs 0.52 eV (combined). For ε(q/q-1), elemental-only RFR test RMSE = 0.34 eV vs combined = 0.30 eV. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | none |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Elemental properties carry useful chemical trend information but lack electronic/energetic context provided by explicit defect calculations, limiting predictive power. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Performs poorly for out-of-sample mixed compositions and lacks ability to capture host-dependent band-edge alignment effects. |
| recommended_best_practices | Combine elemental descriptors with cheap (unit-cell) computed defect electronic/energetic features to improve transferability and accuracy. |

content.title: Low-cost unit-cell defect calculation descriptors (energetic and electronic)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Unit-cell defect properties |
| name_full | Low-cost unit-cell defect calculation descriptors (energetic and electronic) |
| brief_description | Energetic and electronic quantities computed from a cheap 8-atom (Zinc Blende) unit-cell defect calculation for each impurity+site: formation enthalpy from unit cell (Cd-rich/intermediate/X-rich) and aligned valence/conduction band edges, used as features to improve ML predictions. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | CdTe, CdSe, CdS and mixed-anion tested; unit-cell defect calculations performed for the same impurity-site combinations as the supercell computations where available. |
| defect_types | Same single-point defect types (substitutional/interstitial) — unit-cell defect calculation performed for MCd, MX, or Mi in the 8-atom cell. |
| charge_state_handling | Unit cell calculations provide band-edge information; charged-defect correction and full-charge-state supercell corrections are handled in the DFT supercell calculations (Freysoldt) but the unit-cell features themselves are neutral-state energetic/electronic descriptors used by ML. |
| target_properties | ΔH and ε(q1/q2) prediction; unit-cell band edges show strong linear correlation with certain transition levels (+1/0, 0/-1). |
| representation_strategy_name | Low-cost unit-cell defect feature embedding |
| representation_strategy_description | Uses properties from an inexpensive 8-atom defect calculation: unit-cell formation enthalpy (Cd-rich/intermediate/X-rich) and the valence/conduction band edges (universally aligned via deep Cd 5s core), providing host electronic context and energetic proxy for full supercell behavior. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Defect-centered but computed in a small cell; acts as a compact surrogate for the larger supercell defect energetics. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Implicitly encodes local relaxation/energetics from the unit-cell DFT calculation; no explicit radial/angular basis disclosed; species present via actual DFT calculation. |
| graph_model_architecture | none |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | none |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Unit-cell features available for many points; highly correlated with supercell ΔH (\|r\| > 0.9 for ΔH) and with some transition levels (VB/CB edges \|r\| = 0.82/0.74 with +1/0 and 0/-1). Used across PBE and HSE modeling pipelines. |
| transferability_evidence | Inclusion of unit-cell features substantially improved out-of-sample performance on mixed-anion compounds compared to elemental-only features (Tables II–III); models with unit-cell features generalize better to CdTe0.5Se0.5 and CdSe0.5S0.5. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Adding unit-cell features reduced required training data to reach a target RMSE (learning curves show earlier saturation and lower asymptotic error when unit-cell features included). Example: ΔH test RMSE drops from ~0.65 eV (elemental-only) to ~0.45 eV (unit-cell-only) and to ~0.38 eV (combined). |
| evaluation_protocol | Compared in identical train/test/out-of-sample splits and over multiple random training draws; feature importance from Random Forest confirms unit-cell formation enthalpy is the top feature for ΔH prediction. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Ablation studies show unit-cell-only outperforms elemental-only; combined elemental+unit-cell gave best results. Feature importance analysis highlights unit-cell formation enthalpy and band-edge features. |
| performance_metrics | Example metrics: For PBE ΔH using RFR: training RMSE = 0.20 eV (unit-cell features), test RMSE = 0.45 eV; combined features test RMSE = 0.38 eV. For ε(q/q-1) test RMSE using RFR: unit-cell-only = 0.33 eV, combined = 0.30 eV. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | none |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Authors claim unit-cell defect properties capture key host-specific electronic structure (band edges) and energetic trends that are highly predictive for defect transition levels and formation enthalpies; they act as an inexpensive surrogate of supercell physics. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Unit-cell computations are cheaper but may not capture full supercell relaxation or long-range electrostatic/strain effects; some transition-levels differences between PBE and HSE remain and require additional handling. |
| recommended_best_practices | Compute low-cost unit-cell defect properties (formation enthalpy, aligned VB/CB edges) to include as features; combine with elemental descriptors for best transferability and accuracy. |

content.title: Explicit oxidation-state features (O1, O2) to encode charge transitions

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Oxidation-state charge feature |
| name_full | Explicit oxidation-state features (O1, O2) to encode charge transitions |
| brief_description | Two scalar features representing the impurity atom formal oxidation state (O1) and the host defect-site atom oxidation state (O2: +2 for Cd, -2 for Te/Se/S, 0 for interstitial), added so that O1-O2 equals the defect charge q and a single model can be trained for ε(q/q-1) across all q. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Applied for charge-transition modeling in CdTe, CdSe, CdS and tested on mixed-anion compounds. |
| defect_types | Single-point charged defects (substitutional/interstitial) across multiple integer charge states (+3..-3 in DFT supercells; ML targets ε(q/q-1) transitions). |
| charge_state_handling | Explicit charge-aware feature: O1 and O2 are added to descriptor sets to encode the expected charge q via O1-O2=q, enabling ML to learn ε(q/q-1) as one regression target rather than separate models per q; DFT computed charged-supercell energies used Freysoldt correction for physical charged-defect references. |
| target_properties | Charge transition levels ε(q1/q2) (all modeled transitions) and via these the Fermi-level-dependent formation energy E^f(q,E_F). |
| representation_strategy_name | Charge-aware oxidation-state encoding |
| representation_strategy_description | Encodes nominal oxidation states of impurity and site as scalar features so charge differences map to q; this lets models learn patterns across different charge transitions. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Defect-centered (applies to the impurity+site datapoint); ties directly to predicted charged-defect physics. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Oxidation states are scalars, not continuous electron-density features; no explicit long-range electrostatic descriptors included in ML input. |
| graph_model_architecture | none |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | none |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Used for ML of ε(q/q-1) across many PBE and HSE datapoints (see Table I for sizes); DFT charged calculations used for ground-truth with Freysoldt corrections. |
| transferability_evidence | Including oxidation-state features allowed training a single ε(q/q-1) model across multiple q and improved predictive generality; out-of-sample mixed-anion RMSE for ε with combined descriptors (including O1/O2) ~0.30–0.34 eV. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Encoding charge via oxidation states reduces number of distinct models to train and helps share information across charge states, improving sample efficiency relative to training separate models per transition. |
| evaluation_protocol | Models for ε(q/q-1) used pooled transition data and included O1/O2 in all descriptor sets; model performance reported for random splits and out-of-sample tests. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Authors contrasted training separate models per transition vs single model with O1/O2 and found the latter convenient; feature importance shows O1 (impurity oxidation state) is highly important for ε predictions. |
| performance_metrics | Using RFR with combined descriptors including O1/O2: test RMSE for ε(q/q-1) ~0.30 eV; out-of-sample RMSE ~0.33–0.34 eV (PBE-level). |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | none |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Encoding oxidation states informs ML of the integer charge transfer context and allows learning of transition-level trends across different q values, improving generalization. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Formal oxidation states are approximate and may not capture partial charge localization or long-range electrostatic screening; ML still depends on DFT corrections for charged-supercell effects. |
| recommended_best_practices | Include simple oxidation-state features when training unified models for charge transition levels; continue to apply proper charged-supercell corrections (Freysoldt) for DFT labels. |

content.title: Using lower-fidelity (PBE) transition levels as features and delta-learning to predict higher-fidelity (HSE) levels

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | PBE-as-descriptor and Delta-learning |
| name_full | Using lower-fidelity (PBE) transition levels as features and delta-learning to predict higher-fidelity (HSE) levels |
| brief_description | For scarce high-fidelity HSE data, the authors include PBE-computed ε(q1/q2) as an additional descriptor and/or train models on the difference δ = HSE - PBE (delta-learning), yielding substantially improved HSE prediction accuracy. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | HSE ε(q/q-1) modeling for CdTe, CdSe, CdS and mixed-anion compounds where only limited HSE data exist (HSE dataset ~680 points vs PBE ~2550). |
| defect_types | Single-point charged defects and the same transition levels (+2/+1 to -1/-2 for HSE subset). |
| charge_state_handling | PBE ε values include charged-defect information; delta-learning models the difference between HSE and PBE transition levels (which are charge-state aware), and predicted HSE = PBE + predicted δ. |
| target_properties | HSE-level ε(q/q-1) transition levels (higher-fidelity electronic defect levels). |
| representation_strategy_name | Cross-fidelity descriptor (PBE embedding) and delta-learning |
| representation_strategy_description | Adds the inexpensive/low-fidelity DFT prediction (PBE ε) as a numeric feature to ML models for HSE labels; alternatively, directly regress δ = HSE - PBE and combine with PBE to get HSE estimates. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Defect-centered: PBE prediction corresponds to the same impurity+site instance (so used as a per-datapoint scalar embedding). |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | PBE ε is a scalar per transition and implicitly summarizes local and host-dependent electronic structure within the lower-fidelity theory. |
| graph_model_architecture | none (applied with Random Forest regression and compared to KRR and LASSO). |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | This is an example of leveraging a lower-fidelity computed embedding rather than ML pretraining; not a neural foundation model. |
| data_regime_and_dataset | HSE ε dataset small (~680 points); PBE ε available for many more (~2550). Including PBE as a descriptor reduced test and out-of-sample RMSE for HSE from ~0.60 eV (without PBE) down to ~0.23 eV (with PBE); delta-learning gave test RMSE ~0.20–0.22 eV (Table IV). |
| transferability_evidence | Including PBE boosts generalization to out-of-sample mixed-anion compounds: example out-of-sample RMSE for HSE with PBE descriptor ≈ 0.20–0.22 eV; PBE and HSE ε are highly correlated (>0.95) which underlies success. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Delta-learning and adding PBE drastically reduce required HSE training data to reach a given error; error curves saturate earlier and at lower RMSE when PBE included. |
| evaluation_protocol | HSE models trained on the available HSE subset from CdTe/CdSe/CdS and evaluated on held-out tests and out-of-sample mixed compositions; comparisons made between models with and without PBE as descriptor and δ-learn models. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Ablation shows including only PBE as sole descriptor yields comparable performance to richer descriptor sets with PBE; delta-learning of δ gave lowest test/out-of-sample RMSEs among methods tested. |
| performance_metrics | Representative numbers: HSE ε RFR test RMSE without PBE ~0.61 eV, with PBE ~0.23 eV; δ-learn (RFR) test RMSE ~0.20 eV; out-of-sample RMSEs similarly reduced to ~0.20–0.26 eV (Table IV, Fig. 6). |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | none |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Because PBE and HSE ε are strongly correlated, PBE provides a powerful, low-cost embedding that transfers information about defect level trends; delta-learning captures systematic shifts between fidelities. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Relies on availability of a correlated low-fidelity theory (here PBE); if PBE-HSE correlation is weaker for other materials or defect types, the approach may be less effective. Some HSE outliers (Cu and Sn interstitials) degrade RMSE until removed. |
| recommended_best_practices | When high-fidelity labels are scarce, include lower-fidelity predictions as features or apply delta-learning; validate correlation between fidelities and check for outlier defect chemistries where systematic offsets fail. |

content.title: Random Forest / Kernel Ridge / LASSO regressors trained on combined elemental + unit-cell + base descriptors (with charge features) for defect energetics and transition levels

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Overall ML pipeline (RFR/KRR/LASSO with combined descriptors) |
| name_full | Random Forest / Kernel Ridge / LASSO regressors trained on combined elemental + unit-cell + base descriptors (with charge features) for defect energetics and transition levels |
| brief_description | A supervised learning pipeline using tabular defect-centered descriptors (base + elemental + unit-cell; plus oxidation states and optionally PBE ε) fed into classical regressors (Random Forest Regression, Kernel Ridge Regression with Gaussian kernel, and LASSO), with Random Forest performing best for out-of-sample screening. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Applied to CdTe, CdSe, CdS training set and tested on mixed-anion CdTe0.5Se0.5 and CdSe0.5S0.5; HSE models used smaller subsets. |
| defect_types | Single-point substitutional/interstitial/ vacancy/antisite defects; per-datapoint modeling of impurity+site (no complexes). |
| charge_state_handling | DFT labels included explicit charged-supercell calculations (+3 to -3) with Freysoldt corrections; ML models predict charge transition levels ε and use oxidation-state features to capture q-dependence; final E^f(E_F) curves assembled from ML ΔH and ε predictions to classify dominating impurities. |
| target_properties | Neutral formation enthalpy ΔH, charge transition levels ε(q1/q2), and derived Fermi-level-dependent formation energy E^f(E_F); used for screening dominating impurities that can shift equilibrium Fermi level. |
| representation_strategy_name | Tabular defect-centered descriptor + classical regressor pipeline |
| representation_strategy_description | Concatenate base site indices, elemental descriptors, unit-cell defect features, and charge/oxidation-state scalars into a single feature vector per defect instance; train Random Forest / KRR / LASSO to regress ΔH or ε. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Defect-centered (each feature vector corresponds to a specific impurity at a specific site); unit-cell computation gives a local reference rather than full-supercell geometry. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Local geometry represented only via site index and neighbor counts plus unit-cell DFT relaxation results; no explicit radial/angular basis or rotational equivariance used. |
| graph_model_architecture | none |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | No neural pretraining used; PBE predictions used as cross-fidelity embeddings for HSE modeling/delta-learning. |
| data_regime_and_dataset | PBE ΔH dataset: 989 computed points across 1827 possible combinations (~54% coverage); PBE ε dataset: 2550 points (~23% of 10962 possible transitions); HSE ε dataset: 680 points (~9.3% of 7308). |
| transferability_evidence | Explicit out-of-sample test on mixed-anion compounds (not present in training): ΔH combined-descriptor test RMSE ~0.38 eV (test) and out-of-sample ~0.52–0.57 eV; ε combined-descriptor RFR test RMSE ~0.30 eV and out-of-sample ~0.30–0.34 eV. Classification of whether impurity 'dominates' intrinsic defects: ML agrees with DFT in >95% of cases (false pos+neg <5%). |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Learning curves show RMSE improves with training size and begins to saturate; ~50% of PBE ΔH data gives ΔH test RMSE ~0.40 eV and out-of-sample ~0.55 eV. For HSE, adding PBE as descriptor reduces HSE RMSE substantially, supporting cross-fidelity data-efficiency. |
| evaluation_protocol | Models trained on pooled CdTe+CdSe+CdS data (often 90% training /10% test), uncertainties estimated from 100 random train draws; explicit out-of-sample evaluation on intentionally unseen mixed-anion compounds; feature importance reported from Random Forest; no graph/neural cross-validation reported. |
| baselines_and_ablations | Systematic comparisons between three descriptor families (elemental-only, unit-cell-only, combined) and three regressors (RFR, KRR, LASSO) show: unit-cell features >> elemental-only; combined best; RFR best for out-of-sample screening though KRR sometimes slightly better on test set; LASSO worst generally. Including PBE as descriptor or delta-learning significantly improves HSE predictions. |
| performance_metrics | Key reported RMSEs (eV): PBE ΔH (RFR, combined) test RMSE = 0.38 eV, out-of-sample ~0.52–0.57 eV; PBE ε(q/q-1) (RFR, combined) test RMSE = 0.30 eV, out-of-sample ~0.30–0.34 eV; HSE ε with PBE descriptor (RFR) test RMSE ≈ 0.23 eV, out-of-sample ≈ 0.20–0.26 eV; δ-learn (RFR) test RMSE ≈ 0.20 eV (Table II–IV). Classification (dominating impurity) agreement: >95% concordance with DFT (false pos+neg <5%). |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | none — paper does not model phonon scattering, scattering rates, or lattice thermal conductivity degradation. |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | The combination of elemental and unit-cell defect properties captures both chemical trends and host electronic/energetic context (e.g., band-edge alignment) that determine defect levels; Random Forest feature importances confirm the unit-cell formation enthalpy and impurity oxidation state as top predictors for ΔH and ε respectively. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | Does not include explicit long-range electrostatic descriptors beyond unit-cell band-edges; limited HSE data constrains high-fidelity predictions; some HSE outliers (Cu, Sn interstitials) cause higher RMSE until excluded; no treatment of defect complexes or phonon-related transport properties; unit-cell surrogates may miss supercell relaxation effects. |
| recommended_best_practices | Use combined elemental + unit-cell defect descriptors as a strong baseline; include oxidation-state features for charge transitions; apply Freysoldt corrections for DFT charged labels; use PBE predictions as auxiliary features or delta-learn to predict scarce high-fidelity labels; validate transferability with out-of-sample mixed-composition tests and report uncertainties via ensemble methods. |

metadata.title: Modified band alignment method to obtain hybrid functional accuracy from standard DFT: Application to defects in highly mismatched III-V:Bi alloys
metadata.abstract: This paper provides an accurate theoretical defect energy database for pure and Bi-containing 111-V (111-V:Bi) materials and investigates efficient methods for high-throughput defect calculations based on corrections of results obtained with local and semi-local functionals. Point defects as well as nearest-neighbor and second-nearest-neighbor pair defects were investigated in charge states ranging from -5 to 5. Ga-V:Bi systems (GaP:Bi, GaAs:Bi, and GaSb:Bi) were thoroughly investigated with significantly slower, higher fidelity hybrid Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof (HSE) and significantly faster, lower fidelity local density approximation (LDA) calculations. In both approaches spurious electrostatic interactions were corrected with the Freysoldt correction. The results were verified against available experimental results and used to assess the accuracy of a previous band alignment correction. Here, a modified band alignment method is proposed in order to better predict the HSE values from the LDA ones. The proposed method allows prediction of defect energies with values that approximate those from the HSE functional at the computational cost of LDA (about 20x faster for the systems studied here). Tests of selected point defects in In-V :Bi materials resulted in corrected LDA values having a mean absolute error (MAE) = 0.175 eV for defect levels vs. HSE. The method was further verified on an external database of defects and impurities in CdX (X=S, Se, Te) systems, yielding a MAE = 0.194 eV. These tests demonstrate the correction to be sufficient for qualitative and semi-quantitative predictions, and may suggest transferability to many semiconductor systems without significant loss in accuracy. Properties of the remaining In-V :Bi defects and all Al-V :Bi defects were predicted with the use of the modified band alignment method.

content.title: Modified Band Alignment correction (MBA)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | MBA |
| name_full | Modified Band Alignment correction (MBA) |
| brief_description | An empirical, band-gap-dependent correction to align defect charge-transition levels and formation energies from low-fidelity (LDA/GGA/PBE) calculations to hybrid (HSE) accuracy by applying an electrostatic-potential-derived shift plus a single fitted linear-in-gap term (β) and a constant formation-energy offset (γ). |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_systems | Primary: zincblende III-V dilute bismides (Ga-V:Bi: GaP/GaAs/GaSb; In-V:Bi; Al-V:Bi). Also tested on CdX (X = S, Se, Te) chalcogenides (from Ref. [46]). Multiple hosts used for training and testing. |
| defect_types | Point defects (substitutional Bi on III and V sites, vacancies, antisites) and pair/complex defects (nearest- and second-nearest-neighbor pairs). Charges analyzed ranged -5 to +5 (stable states mainly ±2 or ±3); pair defect complexes included. |
| charge_state_handling | Explicit charge labels q are used in formation energy formulas; Fermi level E_F treated as variable; Freysoldt (FNV) electrostatic correction applied to charged-supercell energies; MBA projection includes q-dependent terms and an empirical constant γ to correct formation energies. |
| target_properties | Defect formation energies, charge-state transition (defect) levels referenced to VBM, binding energies of defect pairs. |
| representation_strategy_name | Band-alignment-based numerical correction (MBA) |
| representation_strategy_description | Start from LDA/GGA defect charge-transition energies E^d; add an average electrostatic-potential shift E_shift (from pristine LDA vs HSE), then apply a band-gap-scaled linear correction: E_corr^d = E^d + E_shift + β((1-δ)E_g - E^d) (δ set to 0), and project to formation energies with an additional constant γ; β and γ are fitted empirically on a training set. |
| defect_centering_or_reference | Uses pristine (undefected) reference: alignment of average electrostatic potential of pure cell between low- and high-fidelity calculations; not a local structural descriptor, but references defect energies to a pristine host baseline. |
| local_environment_descriptor_details | Not applicable — MBA is not a local atomic descriptor but a scalar correction applied to computed defect energies/levels; no neighbor cutoff or angular/radial basis reported. |
| graph_model_architecture | None |
| pretraining_or_foundation_embeddings | None |
| data_regime_and_dataset | Parameters (β = -0.14, γ = 0.839 eV, δ = 0) fitted on Ga-V:Bi dataset (188 stable defect levels for Ga-V:Bi training set). Validated on In-V:Bi (198 point-defect formation energies calculated with both LDA and HSE) and on an external CdX dataset of 656 PBE→HSE charge-transition levels from Ref. [46]. Full produced database: 2673 defect formation energies (mix of direct HSE and LDA+MBA). |
| transferability_evidence | Fitted on Ga-V:Bi and applied without refit to In-V:Bi: MBA defect-level MAE = 0.175 eV (ME ≈ -0.009 eV) vs HSE; formation-energy MAE = 0.384 eV. Applied to CdX (PBE→HSE) data: defect-level MAE = 0.194 eV (ME ≈ -0.006 eV). These show significant accuracy gains vs BA and direct LDA/PBE and demonstrate reasonable transfer across similar semiconductor chemistries and across semi-local functionals. |
| data_efficiency_evidence | Authors report that re-optimizing MBA parameters with as few as ~10 points produces noticeable improvement; MBA has only one (β) (for levels) and one (γ) (for formation energies) major fitted parameters, indicating high data efficiency compared to ML that requires larger HSE+LDA training sets. |
| evaluation_protocol | Parameters optimized by minimizing RMSE on Ga-V:Bi training data; validation performed on held-out In-V:Bi dataset (explicitly computed with both LDA and HSE) and on external CdX dataset. Parity plots, MAE/RMSE/ME and precision/recall/F1 for stability/classification used for assessment. No use of graph splits — evaluation is across material systems (train on Ga-V:Bi, test on In-V:Bi and CdX). |
| baselines_and_ablations | Direct LDA/GGA baseline and standard Band Alignment (BA) correction (constant E_shift) used as baselines. MBA reduces MAE relative to BA (e.g., Ga-V:Bi defect levels MAE BA=0.226 eV -> MBA=0.182 eV). Ablations include setting δ = 0 (simpler 1-parameter correction) justified by information criteria; sensitivity to needing reoptimization for other crystal structures/supercell sizes tested. |
| performance_metrics | Ga-V:Bi (defect levels): LDA MAE = 0.439 eV -> BA MAE = 0.226 eV -> MBA MAE = 0.182 eV; (formation energies at E_F = 0): LDA MAE = 1.612 eV -> BA MAE = 0.904 eV -> MBA MAE = 0.370 eV (with γ chosen to set ME=0). In-V:Bi (test): defect levels MBA MAE = 0.175 eV; formation energies MBA MAE = 0.384 eV. CdX test (656 levels): MBA MAE = 0.194 eV. RMSE and ME statistics given in Table I of paper. |
| phonon_or_thermal_transport_link | None |
| interpretation_or_mechanistic_claims | Authors argue the dominant discrepancy between local/semi-local and hybrid defect levels is a band-alignment/band-gap effect (hence a constant + band-gap-dependent linear term suffices). MBA addresses systematic overestimation near bottom of gap after BA by adding a gap-scaled term. Remaining errors attributed to LDA/GGA inability to capture charge-density reorganization (especially q=0) and localization/Jahn-Teller effects. |
| failure_modes_and_limitations | MBA cannot correct q = 0 formation energies through band-alignment projection (intrinsic limitation); it can mispredict stability/classification when LDA lacks certain charge-state transitions (outliers where LDA/BA/MBA predict different stable charge states than HSE); parameters may require reoptimization for different crystal structures, supercell sizes, or significantly different chemistries; somewhat less effective for very low band gap materials but still improved ME/MAE. |
| recommended_best_practices | Compute E_shift from average electrostatic potential of pristine cell with at least one HSE primitive calculation; apply FNV electrostatic corrections consistently; fit MBA β (and γ for formation energies) on a small representative set (authors show ~10 points already useful) when switching to different crystal structures/supercell sizes; include spin-orbit coupling and consistent supercell size to improve transferability; use MBA as a fast multifidelity route before expensive HSE calculations. |

artifacts.description: Phenomenon: ML models for defect-influenced properties (formation energies, PES topology, charge transition levels, charge-dependent forces/phonons) fail when multiple defect charge states are fit jointly from geometry alone. Mechanism claim (inference): for a fixed atomic geometry, the mapping to energy/forces/IFCs is non-injective across charge states because the electronic state changes without a unique geometric signature. Therefore, adding an explicit net-charge conditioning variable (as a token/embedding) is the dominant representational requirement for multi-charge modeling; model capacity or angular features alone will not substitute. This theory is about identifiability, not just optimization.

paper-6906cba8c92984514089f2d909f633de2b.displayLabel: Multi-fidelity Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Charged Point Defects

s2Metadata.title: Multi-fidelity Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Charged Point Defects
s2Metadata.abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) can now reproduce the energy, forces and stresses of bulk materials with high accuracy compared to first-principles calculations. The description of imperfections, where coordination environments and electron counts deviate from those found in pristine reference structures, remains a challenge. We find that the current generation of foundation MLIPs do not describe the defect physics of the semiconductor Sb2Se3. We introduce global defect charge embeddings that distinguish the bonding characteristics of different charge states. We further employ a multi-fidelity approach that combines low-cost (semi-local exchange-correlation functional) reference data with high-quality (non-local hybrid functional) energies and forces that describe well the subtleties of the defect energy landscape. The resulting defect-capable force fields can find stable structural configurations and predict defect thermodynamics in quantitative agreement with direct quantum mechanical calculations, at a fraction of the computational cost.

paper-1ac0e91f059034f5d62532a10cdeabc099.displayLabel: Machine-learning potential for phonon transport in AlN with defects in multiple charge states

s2Metadata.title: Machine-learning potential for phonon transport in AlN with defects in multiple charge states
s2Metadata.abstract:
Understanding phonon transport properties in defect-laden AlN is important for their device applications. Here, we construct a machine-learning potential to describe phonon transport with accuracy in pristine and defect-laden AlN, following the template of Behler-Parrinello-type neural network potentials (NNPs) but extending them to consider multiple charge states of defects. The high accuracy of our NNP in predicting second- and third-order interatomic force constants is demonstrated through calculations of phonon bands, three-phonon anharmonic, phonon-isotope and phonon-defect scattering rates, and thermal conductivities. In particular, our NNP accurately describes the difference in phonon-related properties among various native defects and among different charge states of the defects. They reveal that the phonon-defect scattering rates induced by VN3+ are the largest, followed by VAl3−, and that VN1+ is the least effective scatterer. This is further confirmed by the magnitude of the respective depressions of the thermal conductivity of AlN. Our findings reveal the significance of the contribution from structural distortions induced by defects to the elastic scattering rates. The present work shows the usefulness of our NNP scheme to cost-efficiently study phonon transport in partially disordered crystalline phases containing charged defects.
 
 
 
 
 Published by the American Physical Society
 2025

content.title: 2 Theory Statements
Joint multi-charge CTL bound requires explicit charge conditioning

content.text: FORK: In joint training across charge states, explicit charge conditioning dominates over geometry-only learning. For a single-host charged-defect dataset spanning ≥5 integer charge states, any geometry-only MLIP (no charge token/scalar/embedding provided to the model) will NOT achieve thermodynamic transition-level MAE ≤ 0.05 eV on a held-out set; adding an explicit net-charge input will achieve MAE ≤ 0.05 eV. NUMERIC THRESHOLDS: ≥5 charge states; CTL MAE bound 0.05 eV. NEGATIVE PREDICTION: doubling backbone parameter count (±10%) without charge input will NOT break the 0.05 eV MAE bound.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Charge-conditioned MACE with a learnable global charge embedding reproduced HSE06 thermodynamic transition levels within ~0.015 eV (max deviation ≤0.02 eV claimed) while also reproducing ground-state geometries (RMSD ≤ 0.05 Å), indicating that explicit charge conditioning enables high-precision charge-dependent energetics/CTLs in one model.  <paper entityId="paper-6906cba8c92984514089f2d909f633de2b39840f" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="286256203" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Wang et al., 2026</paper>

- Foundation bulk-trained MLIPs without explicit charge conditioning systematically failed for charged-defect PESs in Sb2Se3, with defect-minimum RMSD typically ~0.2–0.4 Å and incorrect PES topology, consistent with the claim that geometry-only bulk-trained representations collapse charge-dependent landscapes.  <paper entityId="paper-6906cba8c92984514089f2d909f633de2b39840f" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="286256203" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.3">Wang et al., 2026</paper>

content.title: Charge token must be injected before message passing to separate charge-dependent minima

content.text: FORK: conditioning must act on the representation, not only as a post-hoc energy shift. If the charge input is provided only as a geometry-independent additive scalar energy head (post-message-passing) and NOT injected into node features before message passing, the model will NOT achieve defect-minimum structural RMSD ≤ 0.10 Å across ≥5 charge states; injecting charge into per-atom embeddings before message passing WILL achieve RMSD ≤ 0.10 Å. NUMERIC THRESHOLDS: RMSD 0.10 Å; ≥5 charge states. NEGATIVE PREDICTION: the post-hoc-only charge shift model will produce RMSD ≥ 0.20 Å for at least 2 of the charge states.
**Supporting evidence:**

- In the charge-embedded Sb2Se3 model, charge embedding is added to atomic embeddings at initialization and propagated through message passing, and the resulting model achieves ground-state RMSD ≤ 0.05 Å across charge states, supporting the necessity of conditioning the learned interactions, not merely adding a constant offset.  <paper entityId="paper-6906cba8c92984514089f2d909f633de2b39840f" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="286256203" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Wang et al., 2026</paper>

- Bulk-trained (charge-agnostic) foundations yield too-flat PESs and incorrect forces/relaxed minima (RMSD ~0.2–0.4 Å), consistent with the view that correct minima require charge-conditioned interactions.  <paper entityId="paper-6906cba8c92984514089f2d909f633de2b39840f" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="286256203" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.3">Wang et al., 2026</paper>

content.title: Predictions
2 Likely outcomes

content.text:
- On Sb2Se3-like charged vacancy datasets, replacing separate-per-charge models with one joint model that includes a charge conditioning input will reduce average CTL MAE by ≥0.10 eV relative to a geometry-only joint model at matched parameter count.
- If charge conditioning is injected pre-message-passing, the number of distinct relaxed minima found across charge states will increase by ≥2 (counted by SOAP clustering at r=5 Å) compared to a geometry-only model, because charge-dependent basins become separable.

content.title: 2 Unknown outcomes

content.text:
- A single scalar charge density input (Q_sys-style) will fail the CTL MAE ≤0.05 eV criterion on the same dataset where a categorical embedding passes; if it passes, the theory’s claim about representational separation (scalar vs embedding) is weakened.
- A very-long-range coordinate transformer (no explicit charge input) will still fail CTL MAE ≤0.05 eV across ≥5 charges; if it succeeds, the identifiability premise is falsified.

content.title: Conflicting & Unaccounted Evidence
2 Negative experiments

content.text:
- Fork test (decisive): train geometry-only joint-charge model vs charge-conditioned joint-charge model on the same dataset; if geometry-only achieves CTL MAE ≤0.05 eV, this theory is refuted.
- Fork test (architectural): charge-only-posthoc head vs charge-injected-pre-message-passing; if posthoc-only reaches RMSD ≤0.10 Å across all charges, this theory is refuted.

content.title: 1 Unaccounted for

content.text: - A charge-aware Behler–Parrinello NNP using only a global scalar Q_sys achieved DFT-like κ and phonon properties for charged vacancies in AlN, suggesting that in some single-host regimes a scalar may suffice, contrary to the implied need for richer embeddings in all cases.  <paper entityId="paper-1ac0e91f059034f5d62532a10cdeabc099d55396" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="272831919" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Dou et al., 2024</paper>

artifacts.description: Phenomenon: MLIPs and energy models show strong systematic errors when used outside the training regime (larger supercells, different hosts), especially when trained only on defect-containing cells. Mechanism claim (inference): the dominant transfer error is a host-baseline energy misattribution (and corresponding force/curvature softening) that does not cancel unless the representation or evaluation explicitly subtracts a matched pristine reference or includes host data. Therefore, for data-scarce defect sets, the best representation strategy is not 'learn E_f directly from defective cell', but 'learn total energy robustly and compute formation energies by matched defect–pristine differences', or explicitly train on both pristine and defect configurations to avoid host bias.
