paper-8aa035ef08ed201759dd58972ea075fd88.displayLabel: Machine learning Hamiltonian enables scalable and accurate defect calculations: the case of oxygen vacancies in amorphous SiO2

s2Metadata.title: Machine learning Hamiltonian enables scalable and accurate defect calculations: the case of oxygen vacancies in amorphous SiO2
s2Metadata.abstract: Point defects critically influence the properties of materials and devices, yet density functional theory (DFT) remains computationally demanding for defect supercell calculations. Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) offer high efficiency but require extensive datasets. MLIPs trained only on defect configurations in small supercells exhibit systematic energy errors in larger supercells, demonstrating limited transferability. Here, we present a machine learning Hamiltonian (MLH) model-based method for calculating total energies and atomic forces in defect supercells with linear-scaling computational cost, enabling efficient structural relaxation and accurate formation energy predictions. We take oxygen vacancies in amorphous SiO$_2$ as an example and train the MLH model on defect configurations in 95-atom supercells, with the training data derived from 120 self-consistent field calculations and 12 structural relaxations. The MLH model enables efficient structural relaxations for host (defect-free) and defect systems in larger supercells, avoiding the systematic energy errors observed in MLIPs. The cancellation of energy errors between host and defect systems yields accurate formation energy predictions, with deviations from DFT below 50 meV. The proposed method holds significant potential for defect simulations in complex materials.

paper-f388e9fb0255a8b285ca76a2ad9b1f6713.displayLabel: Can a deep-learning model make fast predictions of vacancy formation in diverse materials?

s2Metadata.title: Can a deep-learning model make fast predictions of vacancy formation in diverse materials?
s2Metadata.abstract: The presence of point defects, such as vacancies, plays an important role in materials design. Here, we explore the extrapolative power of a graph neural network (GNN) to predict vacancy formation energies. We show that a model trained only on perfect materials can also be used to predict vacancy formation energies (Evac) of defect structures without the need for additional training data. Such GNN-based predictions are considerably faster than density functional theory (DFT) calculations and show potential as a quick pre-screening tool for defect systems. To test this strategy, we developed a DFT dataset of 530 Evac consisting of 3D elemental solids, alloys, oxides, semiconductors, and 2D monolayer materials. We analyzed and discussed the applicability of such direct and fast predictions. We applied the model to predict 192 494 Evac for 55 723 materials in the JARVIS-DFT database. Our work demonstrates how a GNN-model performs on unseen data.

content.title: 2 Theory Statements
Supercell scaling failure of defect-only local energy decomposition

content.text: FORK: defect-only local MLIPs break under supercell scaling while reference-difference energy models do not. If a local per-atom-decomposed MLIP is trained on ≤600 defect-containing configurations from a fixed small supercell and WITHOUT any pristine/host-only training structures, then when evaluated on pristine host supercells with ≥2× atom count, it will NOT achieve mean absolute host energy error ≤ 100 meV/atom; it will exceed 500 meV/atom. Conversely, an energy model used only via ΔE = E(defect) − E(pristine) will achieve host error ≤ 100 meV/atom under the same 2× scaling. NUMERIC THRESHOLDS: training size ≤600; scaling ≥2× atoms; host error bounds 100 and 500 meV/atom. NEGATIVE PREDICTION: adding angle features or equivariance to the defect-only MLIP will NOT reduce host error below 100 meV/atom without adding pristine data.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Allegro-style local MLIP trained on a small defect-only dataset exhibited severe systematic host-energy bias when applied to host supercells (reported ≈1180 meV/atom host error), demonstrating the defect-only decomposition failure mode.  <paper entityId="paper-8aa035ef08ed201759dd58972ea075fd88ce66dc" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="287249268" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.2">Dai et al., 2026</paper>

- MLH (Hamiltonian-based) trained on 600 defect-related structures transferred to larger supercells and achieved defect formation-energy MAE 16–45 meV up to 383 atoms, consistent with the idea that representations that preserve a consistent host baseline (via electronic structure prediction) avoid catastrophic host bias under scaling.  <paper entityId="paper-8aa035ef08ed201759dd58972ea075fd88ce66dc" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="287249268" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Dai et al., 2026</paper>

content.title: Pretrained bulk energy models transfer to defects only via differencing, not direct defect regression

content.text: FORK: with bulk-pretrained weights, formation-energy transfer is driven by energy differencing, not direct defect featurization. For vacancy formation energies in diverse chemistries using a bulk-pretrained energy-per-atom model applied to unrelaxed defective cells, computing E_f via E(defect) − E(perfect) + μ will NOT achieve MAE ≤ 0.7 eV unless a global bias correction is applied; with a single global shift (one scalar) the MAE WILL be ≤ 1.0 eV but will NOT be ≤ 0.7 eV. NUMERIC THRESHOLDS: 0.7 eV and 1.0 eV MAE. NEGATIVE PREDICTION: fine-tuning on ≤50 defect labels will NOT push MAE below 0.7 eV if defect structures remain unrelaxed at inference.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Pretrained ALIGNN energy-per-atom model transferred from perfect bulk training to vacancy formation energies with overall MAE 1.51 eV, improved to 1.00 eV with a global scissor-shift, indicating a persistent systematic bias and that even with correction performance remains ~1 eV scale rather than sub-0.7 eV.  <paper entityId="paper-f388e9fb0255a8b285ca76a2ad9b1f6713188345" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="261593198" artifactId="extraction-result-3#uuid-e3.0">Choudhary et al., 2022</paper>

- The same study used unrelaxed defective structures for ALIGNN inference while DFT vacancy energies were relaxed, providing a concrete failure mode (geometry mismatch) that supports the negative prediction that small fine-tuning will not cross a tight MAE threshold if inference geometries remain unrelaxed.  <paper entityId="paper-f388e9fb0255a8b285ca76a2ad9b1f6713188345" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="261593198" artifactId="extraction-result-3#uuid-e3.0">Choudhary et al., 2022</paper>

content.title: Predictions
2 Likely outcomes

content.text:
- In defect-only local-MLIP training with ≤600 structures, adding just 50 pristine/bulk configurations to the training set will reduce pristine-host energy bias by ≥400 meV/atom on ≥2× larger supercells (measured on the same test set).
- For bulk-pretrained vacancy models, relaxing the defective structure with any force-accurate potential before inference will reduce MAE by ≥0.3 eV relative to unrelaxed inference, even without changing the energy model.

content.title: 2 Unknown outcomes

content.text:
- If a modern equivariant local MLIP (same training regime: ≤600 defect-only) achieves host error ≤100 meV/atom on ≥2× supercells without pristine data, then the 'host-baseline misattribution' mechanism is incomplete.
- If a bulk-pretrained energy model plus a single global shift reaches MAE ≤0.7 eV on unrelaxed defects, then the claimed ceiling is false.

content.title: Conflicting & Unaccounted Evidence
2 Negative experiments

content.text:
- Fork test: defect-only MLIP vs defect–pristine differencing energy model under ≥2× supercell scaling; if defect-only MLIP host error ≤100 meV/atom, theory is refuted.
- Fork test: bulk-pretrained ALIGNN differencing with one global shift; if MAE ≤0.7 eV on the 508 vacancy benchmark using unrelaxed geometries, theory is refuted.

content.title: 1 Unaccounted for

content.text: - MLH achieves extremely small formation-energy MAE (16–45 meV) with only 600 structures, but it is not a simple energy-differencing approach; it uses Hamiltonian prediction and electronic structure, which may represent a different mechanism than pristine-reference subtraction alone.  <paper entityId="paper-8aa035ef08ed201759dd58972ea075fd88ce66dc" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="287249268" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Dai et al., 2026</paper>

artifacts.description: Phenomenon: ML models for defect/dopant energetics show poor out-of-distribution (OOD) transfer across host chemistries when they ingest the full defective supercell as an absolute object. Theory: the dominant source of OOD failure is that the model must implicitly learn and subtract a host-dependent baseline energy manifold (host size/chemistry/strain) before learning the comparatively small defect perturbation. Therefore, representations that explicitly encode the defect as a Δ (defect minus pristine, or defect-local subgraph paired with pristine-local subgraph) will outperform full-supercell absolute encodings on cross-host transfer and few-shot adaptation. Conversely, models trained on full defective supercells without explicit pristine reference will NOT transfer unless the new defect class/chemistry is substantially represented in training (as observed for impurities/alloys/complexes).

paper-d5896724a45e69301ff13a77e2787adf84.displayLabel: Accelerating defect predictions in semiconductors using graph neural networks

s2Metadata.title: Accelerating defect predictions in semiconductors using graph neural networks
s2Metadata.abstract: First-principles computations reliably predict the energetics of point defects in semiconductors but are constrained by the expense of using large supercells and advanced levels of theory. Machine learning models trained on computational data, especially ones that sufficiently encode defect coordination environments, can be used to accelerate defect predictions. Here, we develop a framework for the prediction and screening of native defects and functional impurities in a chemical space of group IV, III–V, and II–VI zinc blende semiconductors, powered by crystal Graph-based Neural Networks (GNNs) trained on high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) data. Using an innovative approach of sampling partially optimized defect configurations from DFT calculations, we generate one of the largest computational defect datasets to date, containing many types of vacancies, self-interstitials, anti-site substitutions, impurity interstitials and substitutions, as well as some defect complexes. We applied three types of established GNN techniques, namely crystal graph convolutional neural network, materials graph network, and Atomistic Line Graph Neural Network (ALIGNN), to rigorously train models for predicting defect formation energy (DFE) in multiple charge states and chemical potential conditions. We find that ALIGNN yields the best DFE predictions with root mean square errors around 0.3 eV, which represents a prediction accuracy of 98% given the range of values within the dataset, improving significantly on the state-of-the-art. We further show that GNN-based defective structure optimization can take us close to DFT-optimized geometries at a fraction of the cost of full DFT. The current models are based on the semi-local generalized gradient approximation-Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional but are highly promising because of the correlation of computed energetics and defect levels with higher levels of theory and experimental data, the accuracy and necessity of discovering novel metastable and low energy defect structures at the PBE level of theory before advanced methods could be applied, and the ability to train multi-fidelity models in the future with new data from non-local functionals. The DFT-GNN models enable prediction and screening across thousands of hypothetical defects based on both unoptimized and partially optimized defective structures, helping identify electronically active defects in technologically important semiconductors.

content.title: 2 Theory Statements
Δ-reference encoding flips OOD transfer from multi-eV failure to sub-eV at ≤100 labels

content.text: FORK: Explicit defect Δ-to-pristine encoding (paired pristine+defect graphs with a subtraction readout) dominates over absolute defective-supercell encoding for cross-host transfer. NUMERIC THRESHOLD: when fine-tuning on ≤100 labeled examples from a new defect category (impurities OR alloys OR complexes), Δ-encoding will achieve test RMSE ≤ 0.70 eV, while absolute full-supercell encoding will NOT go below 1.50 eV. NEGATIVE PREDICTION: absolute encoding will not reach RMSE ≤ 0.70 eV under the ≤100-label regime even with identical architecture depth and cutoffs.
**Supporting evidence:**

- ALIGNN trained only on native defects transfers poorly: tested on impurities/alloys/complexes RMSEs 2.17/2.68/2.98 eV, indicating absolute defective-supercell encoding without explicit pristine reference does not generalize across defect categories/chemistries.  <paper entityId="paper-d5896724a45e69301ff13a77e2787adf8486d2dc" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="261696474" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Rahman et al., 2023</paper>

- Adding 50% of the new dataset to training reduces those RMSEs to 0.36/0.70/0.18 eV, showing that representation+model can succeed once the baseline shifts are learned with substantial in-domain examples—consistent with missing explicit Δ baseline subtraction being the bottleneck.  <paper entityId="paper-d5896724a45e69301ff13a77e2787adf8486d2dc" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="261696474" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Rahman et al., 2023</paper>

- Vacancy formation via energy-difference using a pretrained bulk energy-per-atom ALIGNN model (defect and pristine predicted separately) demonstrates transfer from pristine to vacancies without defect-specific training (MAE 1.51 eV, 1.00 eV after global shift), consistent with the benefit of explicitly computing a Δ energy rather than learning absolute defect energies from scratch.  <paper entityId="paper-f388e9fb0255a8b285ca76a2ad9b1f6713188345" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="261593198" artifactId="extraction-result-3#uuid-e3.0">Choudhary et al., 2022</paper>

content.title: Angle-rich encodings improve in-domain RMSE but do NOT fix category transfer

content.text: FORK: Adding explicit 3-body angle features (line-graph) primarily reduces in-domain error but does not rescue cross-category OOD transfer. NUMERIC THRESHOLD: on Dataset1 (native ZB defects), an angle-rich model (ALIGNN-like) will achieve RMSE ≤ 0.20 eV while a distance-only model (CGCNN-like) will NOT beat 0.30 eV; however, for transfer from native→impurities with zero impurity labels, angle-rich encoding will NOT achieve RMSE ≤ 1.50 eV (it will exceed 1.50 eV). NEGATIVE PREDICTION: angle-rich models will not reduce the native→impurity zero-shot error below 1.50 eV despite large in-domain gains.
**Supporting evidence:**

paper-6906cba8c92984514089f2d909f633de2b.displayLabel: Multi-fidelity Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Charged Point Defects

s2Metadata.title: Multi-fidelity Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Charged Point Defects
s2Metadata.abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) can now reproduce the energy, forces and stresses of bulk materials with high accuracy compared to first-principles calculations. The description of imperfections, where coordination environments and electron counts deviate from those found in pristine reference structures, remains a challenge. We find that the current generation of foundation MLIPs do not describe the defect physics of the semiconductor Sb2Se3. We introduce global defect charge embeddings that distinguish the bonding characteristics of different charge states. We further employ a multi-fidelity approach that combines low-cost (semi-local exchange-correlation functional) reference data with high-quality (non-local hybrid functional) energies and forces that describe well the subtleties of the defect energy landscape. The resulting defect-capable force fields can find stable structural configurations and predict defect thermodynamics in quantitative agreement with direct quantum mechanical calculations, at a fraction of the computational cost.

paper-d5896724a45e69301ff13a77e2787adf84.displayLabel: Accelerating defect predictions in semiconductors using graph neural networks

s2Metadata.title: Accelerating defect predictions in semiconductors using graph neural networks
s2Metadata.abstract: First-principles computations reliably predict the energetics of point defects in semiconductors but are constrained by the expense of using large supercells and advanced levels of theory. Machine learning models trained on computational data, especially ones that sufficiently encode defect coordination environments, can be used to accelerate defect predictions. Here, we develop a framework for the prediction and screening of native defects and functional impurities in a chemical space of group IV, III–V, and II–VI zinc blende semiconductors, powered by crystal Graph-based Neural Networks (GNNs) trained on high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) data. Using an innovative approach of sampling partially optimized defect configurations from DFT calculations, we generate one of the largest computational defect datasets to date, containing many types of vacancies, self-interstitials, anti-site substitutions, impurity interstitials and substitutions, as well as some defect complexes. We applied three types of established GNN techniques, namely crystal graph convolutional neural network, materials graph network, and Atomistic Line Graph Neural Network (ALIGNN), to rigorously train models for predicting defect formation energy (DFE) in multiple charge states and chemical potential conditions. We find that ALIGNN yields the best DFE predictions with root mean square errors around 0.3 eV, which represents a prediction accuracy of 98% given the range of values within the dataset, improving significantly on the state-of-the-art. We further show that GNN-based defective structure optimization can take us close to DFT-optimized geometries at a fraction of the cost of full DFT. The current models are based on the semi-local generalized gradient approximation-Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional but are highly promising because of the correlation of computed energetics and defect levels with higher levels of theory and experimental data, the accuracy and necessity of discovering novel metastable and low energy defect structures at the PBE level of theory before advanced methods could be applied, and the ability to train multi-fidelity models in the future with new data from non-local functionals. The DFT-GNN models enable prediction and screening across thousands of hypothetical defects based on both unoptimized and partially optimized defective structures, helping identify electronically active defects in technologically important semiconductors.

paper-1ac0e91f059034f5d62532a10cdeabc099.displayLabel: Machine-learning potential for phonon transport in AlN with defects in multiple charge states

s2Metadata.title: Machine-learning potential for phonon transport in AlN with defects in multiple charge states
s2Metadata.abstract:
Understanding phonon transport properties in defect-laden AlN is important for their device applications. Here, we construct a machine-learning potential to describe phonon transport with accuracy in pristine and defect-laden AlN, following the template of Behler-Parrinello-type neural network potentials (NNPs) but extending them to consider multiple charge states of defects. The high accuracy of our NNP in predicting second- and third-order interatomic force constants is demonstrated through calculations of phonon bands, three-phonon anharmonic, phonon-isotope and phonon-defect scattering rates, and thermal conductivities. In particular, our NNP accurately describes the difference in phonon-related properties among various native defects and among different charge states of the defects. They reveal that the phonon-defect scattering rates induced by VN3+ are the largest, followed by VAl3−, and that VN1+ is the least effective scatterer. This is further confirmed by the magnitude of the respective depressions of the thermal conductivity of AlN. Our findings reveal the significance of the contribution from structural distortions induced by defects to the elastic scattering rates. The present work shows the usefulness of our NNP scheme to cost-efficiently study phonon transport in partially disordered crystalline phases containing charged defects.
 
 
 
 
 Published by the American Physical Society
 2025

content.title: 2 Theory Statements
Without charge conditioning, a joint-charge MLFF will NOT separate charge-specific minima below 0.10 Å RMSD

content.text: FORK: A single joint MLFF conditioned on global defect charge (categorical embedding) dominates over a charge-agnostic joint MLFF trained on pooled multi-charge data. NUMERIC THRESHOLD: for a fixed defect and five charge states, charge-conditioned MLFF will yield ground-state RMSD ≤ 0.05 Å for each charge state, while charge-agnostic pooled MLFF will NOT achieve RMSD ≤ 0.10 Å for at least 3 of 5 charge states. artifacts.description: Cross-host transfer fails primarily because full-supercell pooling forces the network to learn absolute host energy baselines and band-alignment offsets that vary strongly with chemistry; this drowns the defect signal. Representations that explicitly reference the pristine host (E_defect − E_pristine or explicit Δ-features) compress the learning problem to a localized perturbation, yielding large gains in transfer and data efficiency. The fork is that (A) transfer is limited by missing physics/long-range interactions versus (B) transfer is limited by an avoidable target/representation mismatch (absolute-vs-delta). This theory commits to (B): defect-reference subtraction dominates.

paper-f388e9fb0255a8b285ca76a2ad9b1f6713.displayLabel: Can a deep-learning model make fast predictions of vacancy formation in diverse materials?

s2Metadata.title: Can a deep-learning model make fast predictions of vacancy formation in diverse materials?
s2Metadata.abstract: The presence of point defects, such as vacancies, plays an important role in materials design. Here, we explore the extrapolative power of a graph neural network (GNN) to predict vacancy formation energies. We show that a model trained only on perfect materials can also be used to predict vacancy formation energies (Evac) of defect structures without the need for additional training data. Such GNN-based predictions are considerably faster than density functional theory (DFT) calculations and show potential as a quick pre-screening tool for defect systems. To test this strategy, we developed a DFT dataset of 530 Evac consisting of 3D elemental solids, alloys, oxides, semiconductors, and 2D monolayer materials. We analyzed and discussed the applicability of such direct and fast predictions. We applied the model to predict 192 494 Evac for 55 723 materials in the JARVIS-DFT database. Our work demonstrates how a GNN-model performs on unseen data.

paper-8aa035ef08ed201759dd58972ea075fd88.displayLabel: Machine learning Hamiltonian enables scalable and accurate defect calculations: the case of oxygen vacancies in amorphous SiO2

s2Metadata.title: Machine learning Hamiltonian enables scalable and accurate defect calculations: the case of oxygen vacancies in amorphous SiO2
s2Metadata.abstract: Point defects critically influence the properties of materials and devices, yet density functional theory (DFT) remains computationally demanding for defect supercell calculations. Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) offer high efficiency but require extensive datasets. MLIPs trained only on defect configurations in small supercells exhibit systematic energy errors in larger supercells, demonstrating limited transferability. Here, we present a machine learning Hamiltonian (MLH) model-based method for calculating total energies and atomic forces in defect supercells with linear-scaling computational cost, enabling efficient structural relaxation and accurate formation energy predictions. We take oxygen vacancies in amorphous SiO$_2$ as an example and train the MLH model on defect configurations in 95-atom supercells, with the training data derived from 120 self-consistent field calculations and 12 structural relaxations. The MLH model enables efficient structural relaxations for host (defect-free) and defect systems in larger supercells, avoiding the systematic energy errors observed in MLIPs. The cancellation of energy errors between host and defect systems yields accurate formation energy predictions, with deviations from DFT below 50 meV. The proposed method holds significant potential for defect simulations in complex materials.

paper-4b74d83d81741f903cabe558c2e506347f.displayLabel: Point defect formation at finite temperatures with machine learning force fields

s2Metadata.title: Point defect formation at finite temperatures with machine learning force fields
s2Metadata.abstract: Point defects dictate the properties of many functional materials. The standard approach to modelling the thermodynamics of defects relies on a static description, where the change in Gibbs free energy is approximated by the internal energy. This approach has a low computational cost, but ignores contributions from atomic vibrations and structural configurations that can be accessed at finite temperatures. We train a machine learning force field (MLFF) to explore dynamic defect behaviour using Te+1i and V+2Te in CdTe as exemplars. We consider the different entropic contributions (e.g., electronic, spin, vibrational, orientational, and configurational) and compare methods to compute the defect free energies, ranging from a harmonic treatment to a fully anharmonic approach based on thermodynamic integration. We find that metastable configurations are populated at room temperature and thermal effects increase the predicted concentration of Te+1i by two orders of magnitude — and can thus significantly affect the predicted properties. Overall, our study underscores the importance of finite-temperature effects and the potential of MLFFs to model defect dynamics at both synthesis and device operating temperatures.

content.title: 2 Theory Statements
Delta-energy representation crosses the 1.0 eV OOD barrier with ≤10% target-host labels

content.text: Fork: (delta-to-pristine energy target + shared weights across defect and pristine) beats (absolute defective-supercell formation energy regression) for OOD host transfer. If a model is trained on Dataset 1 (native defects) and adapted to Dataset 2 (impurities) with only 10% of Dataset 2 labeled points, then a delta-to-pristine training target (predict E_defect and E_pristine and subtract, or predict ΔE directly) will achieve impurity formation-energy RMSE ≤ 0.60 eV, while an otherwise-matched absolute-E^f model will NOT reach RMSE < 1.00 eV. Negative prediction: the absolute-E^f model will not cross 1.00 eV RMSE at 10% labels.
**Supporting evidence:**

- ALIGNN trained on native defects (Dataset 1) fails catastrophically on impurities (Dataset 2) with RMSE 2.17 eV, implying that naive absolute-supercell regression does not transfer across defect chemistry without in-domain labels.  <paper entityId="paper-d5896724a45e69301ff13a77e2787adf8486d2dc" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="261696474" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Rahman et al., 2023</paper>

content.title: Defect-only local MLIPs exhibit supercell-size energy drift above 50 meV/atom unless trained with explicit host references

content.text: Fork: (training includes pristine/host configurations or explicit host-reference subtraction) prevents supercell-size drift, versus (defect-only training) causes systematic host-energy bias. For atom-centered local MLIPs trained only on defect supercells of size ≤100 atoms, the mean absolute host energy error on pristine host supercells of size ≥200 atoms will NOT fall below 50 meV/atom; adding ≥100 pristine-host configurations to training will reduce that host energy error to ≤5 meV/atom. Negative prediction: defect-only training cannot reach <50 meV/atom host error at larger size.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Allegro-style local MLIP trained on defect-only small-supercell data shows large systematic host-energy bias when applied to host supercells and larger supercells (reported ≈1180 meV/atom host error), consistent with strong size-transfer failure without host reference coverage.  <paper entityId="paper-8aa035ef08ed201759dd58972ea075fd88ce66dc" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="287249268" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.2">Dai et al., 2026</paper>

The current models are based on the semi-local generalized gradient approximation-Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional but are highly promising because of the correlation of computed energetics and defect levels with higher levels of theory and experimental data, the accuracy and necessity of discovering novel metastable and low energy defect structures at the PBE level of theory before advanced methods could be applied, and the ability to train multi-fidelity models in the future with new data from non-local functionals. The DFT-GNN models enable prediction and screening across thousands of hypothetical defects based on both unoptimized and partially optimized defective structures, helping identify electronically active defects in technologically important semiconductors.

content.title: 2 Theory Statements
Single charge-conditioned model beats per-q models for IFC-driven phonon predictions once ≥3 charge states are present

content.text: Fork: explicit charge conditioning (single model with charge input) dominates versus separate-per-q models. When training an ML potential intended to reproduce charge-dependent harmonic phonon spectra (or 2nd-order IFCs) for a defect across ≥3 charge states, a single charge-conditioned model will achieve phonon frequency MAE ≤ 0.15 THz on the highest optical branch, while a set of separate-per-q models trained on the same total number of structures will NOT achieve MAE < 0.30 THz. Negative prediction: the per-q ensemble will not cross 0.30 THz MAE under fixed total data budget.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Charge-aware Behler–Parrinello NNP with a global charge scalar (Q_sys) enabled accurate phonon spectra and κ in AlN across multiple defect charge states, motivated by non-uniqueness of mapping coordinates→energy across charges.  <paper entityId="paper-1ac0e91f059034f5d62532a10cdeabc099d55396" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="272831919" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Dou et al., 2024</paper>

- Global charge embedding in a MACE-based model is reported to be necessary: removing charge embedding collapsed charge-state separation and failed to identify correct charged-defect minima in Sb2Se3, supporting the claim that structure-only descriptors cannot disambiguate charge-dependent PESs.  <paper entityId="paper-6906cba8c92984514089f2d909f633de2b39840f" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="286256203" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Wang et al., 2026</paper>

content.title: Global-charge conditioning is necessary for accurate charged-defect PES topology: RMSD success threshold 0.10 Å

content.text: Fork: with explicit global charge conditioning, the model learns distinct charge-state PES basins; without it, charge basins collapse. For a fixed defect and five charge classes, a charge-conditioned equivariant MLFF will achieve relaxed ground-state structures with RMSD ≤ 0.10 Å to DFT in ≥90% of charge states, while an otherwise identical model without charge conditioning will NOT achieve RMSD ≤ 0.10 Å in more than 50% of charge states. Negative prediction: unconditioned model fails the majority criterion.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Charge-conditioned MACE model in Sb2Se3 reports ground-state RMSD ≤ 0.05 Å across charge states and ablation without charge embedding fails to separate charge states and misidentifies minima.  <paper entityId="paper-6906cba8c92984514089f2d909f633de2b39840f" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="286256203" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Wang et al., 2026</paper>

- Foundation bulk-trained MLIPs without charge-state descriptors systematically failed on charged-defect PESs with typical RMSD ~0.2–0.4 Å, supporting the necessity of explicit charge handling beyond structure-only bulk priors.  <paper entityId="paper-6906cba8c92984514089f2d909f633de2b39840f" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="286256203" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.3">Wang et al., 2026</paper>

content.title: Predictions
2 Likely outcomes

content.text:
- For a 3–5 charge-state defect phonon benchmark, charge-conditioned training yields optical-branch MAE ≤0.15 THz, while per-q models stay ≥0.30 THz at equal total N.
- Across 5 charge classes, charge-conditioned MLFF will meet RMSD ≤0.10 Å for ≥90% of charge states on a new host; unconditioned will not exceed 50%.

content.title: 2 Unknown outcomes

content.text:
- Replacing categorical charge embeddings with a continuous charge-density feature (q/V) will worsen performance for transition levels unless discretized into ≤7 bins; if continuous outperforms, this theory’s claim about categorical necessity is wrong.
- Adding explicit LR Coulomb terms with learned charges will remove the advantage of global charge conditioning; if it does, the mechanism is electrostatics rather than conditioning.

content.title: Conflicting & Unaccounted Evidence
2 Negative experiments

content.text:
- Fork test: per-q separate models match the conditioned model’s phonon MAE (≤0.15 THz) at equal total data—refutes necessity of conditioning for IFC targets.
- Fork test: unconditioned model reaches >50% RMSD success ≤0.10 Å on a new host—refutes the claimed generality of charge-conditioning necessity.

content.title: 1 Unaccounted for

content.text: - ALIGNN charged-defect handling via separate models per charge state can still achieve formation-energy RMSEs ~0.23–0.30 eV on the zincblende dataset, indicating per-q models can work for scalar energetics even without explicit charge features; this theory focuses on phonons/IFCs rather than scalar E^f only.  <paper entityId="paper-d5896724a45e69301ff13a77e2787adf8486d2dc" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="261696474" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Rahman et al., 2023</paper>

artifacts.description: For defect-influenced property prediction across many host materials, the dominant failure mode is that full-defective-supercell representations force the model to learn a large host-energy background and then subtract it implicitly, which collapses out-of-distribution transfer. A representation that explicitly forms a defect-local, delta-to-pristine encoding (energy/embedding differences between defective and pristine structures, or a defect-centered subgraph plus a pristine reference) should sharply improve cross-host transfer and data efficiency. This is not a claim that “local is better”; it commits that the *explicit subtraction* is the key mechanism, and that without it, transfer errors remain eV-scale even with angular features.

paper-d5896724a45e69301ff13a77e2787adf84.displayLabel: Accelerating defect predictions in semiconductors using graph neural networks

s2Metadata.title: Accelerating defect predictions in semiconductors using graph neural networks
s2Metadata.abstract: First-principles computations reliably predict the energetics of point defects in semiconductors but are constrained by the expense of using large supercells and advanced levels of theory. Machine learning models trained on computational data, especially ones that sufficiently encode defect coordination environments, can be used to accelerate defect predictions. Here, we develop a framework for the prediction and screening of native defects and functional impurities in a chemical space of group IV, III–V, and II–VI zinc blende semiconductors, powered by crystal Graph-based Neural Networks (GNNs) trained on high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) data. Using an innovative approach of sampling partially optimized defect configurations from DFT calculations, we generate one of the largest computational defect datasets to date, containing many types of vacancies, self-interstitials, anti-site substitutions, impurity interstitials and substitutions, as well as some defect complexes. We applied three types of established GNN techniques, namely crystal graph convolutional neural network, materials graph network, and Atomistic Line Graph Neural Network (ALIGNN), to rigorously train models for predicting defect formation energy (DFE) in multiple charge states and chemical potential conditions. We find that ALIGNN yields the best DFE predictions with root mean square errors around 0.3 eV, which represents a prediction accuracy of 98% given the range of values within the dataset, improving significantly on the state-of-the-art. We further show that GNN-based defective structure optimization can take us close to DFT-optimized geometries at a fraction of the cost of full DFT. The current models are based on the semi-local generalized gradient approximation-Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional but are highly promising because of the correlation of computed energetics and defect levels with higher levels of theory and experimental data, the accuracy and necessity of discovering novel metastable and low energy defect structures at the PBE level of theory before advanced methods could be applied, and the ability to train multi-fidelity models in the future with new data from non-local functionals. The DFT-GNN models enable prediction and screening across thousands of hypothetical defects based on both unoptimized and partially optimized defective structures, helping identify electronically active defects in technologically important semiconductors.

paper-8aa035ef08ed201759dd58972ea075fd88.displayLabel: Machine learning Hamiltonian enables scalable and accurate defect calculations: the case of oxygen vacancies in amorphous SiO2

s2Metadata.title: Machine learning Hamiltonian enables scalable and accurate defect calculations: the case of oxygen vacancies in amorphous SiO2
s2Metadata.abstract: Point defects critically influence the properties of materials and devices, yet density functional theory (DFT) remains computationally demanding for defect supercell calculations. Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) offer high efficiency but require extensive datasets. MLIPs trained only on defect configurations in small supercells exhibit systematic energy errors in larger supercells, demonstrating limited transferability. Here, we present a machine learning Hamiltonian (MLH) model-based method for calculating total energies and atomic forces in defect supercells with linear-scaling computational cost, enabling efficient structural relaxation and accurate formation energy predictions. We take oxygen vacancies in amorphous SiO$_2$ as an example and train the MLH model on defect configurations in 95-atom supercells, with the training data derived from 120 self-consistent field calculations and 12 structural relaxations. The MLH model enables efficient structural relaxations for host (defect-free) and defect systems in larger supercells, avoiding the systematic energy errors observed in MLIPs. The cancellation of energy errors between host and defect systems yields accurate formation energy predictions, with deviations from DFT below 50 meV. The proposed method holds significant potential for defect simulations in complex materials.

paper-f388e9fb0255a8b285ca76a2ad9b1f6713.displayLabel: Can a deep-learning model make fast predictions of vacancy formation in diverse materials?

s2Metadata.title: Can a deep-learning model make fast predictions of vacancy formation in diverse materials?
s2Metadata.abstract: The presence of point defects, such as vacancies, plays an important role in materials design. Here, we explore the extrapolative power of a graph neural network (GNN) to predict vacancy formation energies. We show that a model trained only on perfect materials can also be used to predict vacancy formation energies (Evac) of defect structures without the need for additional training data. Such GNN-based predictions are considerably faster than density functional theory (DFT) calculations and show potential as a quick pre-screening tool for defect systems. To test this strategy, we developed a DFT dataset of 530 Evac consisting of 3D elemental solids, alloys, oxides, semiconductors, and 2D monolayer materials. We analyzed and discussed the applicability of such direct and fast predictions. We applied the model to predict 192 494 Evac for 55 723 materials in the JARVIS-DFT database. Our work demonstrates how a GNN-model performs on unseen data.

content.title: 2 Theory Statements
OOD-transfer threshold: delta-to-pristine beats full-supercell beyond 5 hosts

content.text: FORK: For cross-host defect formation-energy prediction, explicit delta-to-pristine featurization dominates over full-defective-supercell graphs once the training set spans ≥5 distinct host materials; the opposite fork is that full-supercell with angle features is sufficient. NUMERIC THRESHOLD: at ≥5 hosts in training and a leave-one-host-out test, a delta-to-pristine model will achieve test RMSE ≤0.60 eV, while a matched-capacity full-supercell ALIGNN-style model will NOT achieve RMSE ≤0.60 eV (it will be ≥1.00 eV). NEGATIVE prediction: full-supercell models will not break the 0.60 eV barrier under host-wise OOD splits without explicit subtraction/reference.
**Supporting evidence:**

- ALIGNN trained on native defects transfers extremely poorly to impurities/alloys/complexes without adding representative new data: RMSEs 2.17–2.98 eV, indicating that full-supercell graphs entangle host/defect effects and do not generalize across defect/chemistry shifts.  <paper entityId="paper-d5896724a45e69301ff13a77e2787adf8486d2dc" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="261696474" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Rahman et al., 2023</paper>

- Local MLIP (Allegro-style) trained on defect-only supercells shows massive systematic host-energy bias (~1180 meV/atom) when applied to host/larger cells, consistent with the hypothesis that models that must infer the host baseline implicitly fail without explicit reference cancellation.  <paper entityId="paper-8aa035ef08ed201759dd58972ea075fd88ce66dc" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="287249268" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.2">Dai et al., 2026</paper>

content.title: Angular features stop helping after defect-centered cutoff 6 Å in transfer regime

content.text: FORK: For transfer across host chemistries, once a defect-centered representation includes neighbors out to r = 6.0 Å, adding explicit 3-body angle features (ALIGNN line-graph style) degrades transfer because it overfits host-specific angular statistics; the opposite fork is that angles continue to improve transfer. NUMERIC THRESHOLD: with r ≥ 6.0 Å defect-centered neighborhoods, adding angles will NOT reduce OOD RMSE by ≥0.10 eV and will instead increase it by ≥0.05 eV. NEGATIVE prediction: angle-augmented encodings will worsen cross-host OOD performance at fixed neighborhood radius ≥6 Å.
**Supporting evidence:**

- ALIGNN’s advantage over CGCNN/MEGNET in in-distribution zincblende defects is large (0.15 eV vs 0.35–0.40 eV RMSE), consistent with angles helping when learning within a narrow structural family; this sets up the discriminative risk that the same inductive bias could harm cross-host transfer.  <paper entityId="paper-d5896724a45e69301ff13a77e2787adf8486d2dc" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="261696474" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Rahman et al., 2023</paper>

- Despite strong in-distribution performance, ALIGNN shows catastrophic transfer failures to impurities/alloys/complexes when trained on native defects only (2–3 eV RMSE), indicating that additional geometric expressivity does not automatically yield transferability and can encode host-specific patterns.  <paper entityId="paper-d5896724a45e69301ff13a77e2787adf8486d2dc" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="261696474" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Rahman et al., 2023</paper>

content.title: Predictions
2 Likely outcomes

content.text:
- Under host-wise OOD splits with ≥8 hosts, explicit delta-to-pristine representations will reduce defect-formation-energy RMSE by ≥0.5 eV relative to full-supercell graphs, bringing RMSE to ≤0.60 eV.
- For defect-centered neighborhoods with r ≥ 6 Å, removing angle features will improve OOD RMSE by at least 0.05 eV even if it slightly worsens in-distribution RMSE.

content.title: 2 Unknown outcomes

content.text:
- Delta-to-pristine will make impurity transfer nearly as good as in-host performance (gap ≤0.15 eV); if so, it would imply host-energy entanglement is the dominant failure mode rather than missing chemistry coverage.
- If a full-supercell model with explicit pristine-energy auxiliary head (predict E_host and E_defect jointly) matches delta-to-pristine transfer, then explicit subtraction is not required—multi-task decomposition would be sufficient.

content.title: Conflicting & Unaccounted Evidence
2 Negative experiments

content.text:
- If full-supercell ALIGNN achieves ≤0.60 eV leave-one-host-out RMSE without explicit reference subtraction, the main claim fails.
- If angle features at r ≥ 6 Å improve OOD RMSE by ≥0.10 eV, the claimed overfitting reversal fails.

content.title: 1 Unaccounted for

content.text: - The evidence does not include a direct head-to-head comparison of delta-to-pristine vs full-supercell on the same multi-host defect dataset; the theory extrapolates from transfer failures and host-bias observations.

A model that is not explicitly conditioned on net charge will collapse charge-separated PESs, producing wrong relaxations and wrong force-constant differences—fatal for phonon-defect scattering and κ degradation. The theory commits that a minimal global charge token (categorical embedding or scalar charge density) is sufficient to separate charge-dependent PESs in practice, and that training separate models per charge state is inferior in data efficiency below a dataset-size threshold when the goal is phonon/IFC accuracy.

paper-6906cba8c92984514089f2d909f633de2b.displayLabel: Multi-fidelity Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Charged Point Defects

s2Metadata.title: Multi-fidelity Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Charged Point Defects
s2Metadata.abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) can now reproduce the energy, forces and stresses of bulk materials with high accuracy compared to first-principles calculations. The description of imperfections, where coordination environments and electron counts deviate from those found in pristine reference structures, remains a challenge. We find that the current generation of foundation MLIPs do not describe the defect physics of the semiconductor Sb2Se3. We introduce global defect charge embeddings that distinguish the bonding characteristics of different charge states. We further employ a multi-fidelity approach that combines low-cost (semi-local exchange-correlation functional) reference data with high-quality (non-local hybrid functional) energies and forces that describe well the subtleties of the defect energy landscape. The resulting defect-capable force fields can find stable structural configurations and predict defect thermodynamics in quantitative agreement with direct quantum mechanical calculations, at a fraction of the computational cost.

paper-1ac0e91f059034f5d62532a10cdeabc099.displayLabel: Machine-learning potential for phonon transport in AlN with defects in multiple charge states

s2Metadata.title: Machine-learning potential for phonon transport in AlN with defects in multiple charge states
s2Metadata.abstract:
Understanding phonon transport properties in defect-laden AlN is important for their device applications. Here, we construct a machine-learning potential to describe phonon transport with accuracy in pristine and defect-laden AlN, following the template of Behler-Parrinello-type neural network potentials (NNPs) but extending them to consider multiple charge states of defects. The high accuracy of our NNP in predicting second- and third-order interatomic force constants is demonstrated through calculations of phonon bands, three-phonon anharmonic, phonon-isotope and phonon-defect scattering rates, and thermal conductivities. In particular, our NNP accurately describes the difference in phonon-related properties among various native defects and among different charge states of the defects. They reveal that the phonon-defect scattering rates induced by VN3+ are the largest, followed by VAl3−, and that VN1+ is the least effective scatterer. This is further confirmed by the magnitude of the respective depressions of the thermal conductivity of AlN. Our findings reveal the significance of the contribution from structural distortions induced by defects to the elastic scattering rates. The present work shows the usefulness of our NNP scheme to cost-efficiently study phonon transport in partially disordered crystalline phases containing charged defects.
 
 
 
 
 Published by the American Physical Society

paper-f594d0f1e05d8292d376f2aa2e45cea8cd.displayLabel: Accelerating point-defect simulations using data-driven and machine learning approaches

s2Metadata.title: Accelerating point-defect simulations using data-driven and machine learning approaches
s2Metadata.abstract: Point defects in solid-state materials are now routinely simulated using large supercell structures, requiring efficient quantum mechanical solutions. Data-driven and machine learning (ML) models trained on computational data can enable rapid defect property predictions and high-throughput screening. In this article, we provide an overview of prominent efforts to accelerate defect simulations using these approaches. We begin by discussing the motivations for data-driven techniques in defect modeling, and describe efforts over the past decade to use descriptor-based models for rapid screening of defect properties—most notably in oxides. In particular, we discuss case studies where surrogate models and interatomic potentials were trained on density functional theory (DFT) data, leading to predictions with quantum mechanical accuracies at a fraction of the cost. In addition to geometry relaxation and formation energy predictions, these interatomic potentials are capable of predicting phonon modes and vibrational free energies to yield defect energetics at finite temperatures—representing a key frontier for computational defect research. We finish with a discussion on how to connect these approaches and their outputs with experimental data, and provide an outlook on this burgeoning subfield. content.title: 2 Theory Statements
Charge-conditioning threshold for charged-defect structures

content.text: FORK: For a single host with charged vacancy PESs, adding an explicit global charge embedding yields DFT-ground-state geometries across charge states, whereas a charge-agnostic equivariant MLIP cannot. NUMERIC THRESHOLD: with ≥2000 training structures spanning ≥5 charge states, a charge-embedded model will achieve ground-state RMSD ≤0.10 Å for each charge state, while the same backbone without charge embedding will NOT achieve RMSD ≤0.10 Å for at least 3 of the 5 charge states (it will be ≥0.20 Å). NEGATIVE prediction: charge-agnostic models will fail the ≤0.10 Å criterion in most charge states even at the same data volume.
**Supporting evidence:**

- In Sb2Se3, a MACE backbone without global charge embedding failed to separate charge states and failed to identify correct defect structures; with charge embedding it achieved RMSD ≤0.05 Å and transition levels within 0.015 eV, showing explicit charge conditioning resolves charge-dependent PES non-uniqueness.  <paper entityId="paper-6906cba8c92984514089f2d909f633de2b39840f" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="286256203" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Wang et al., 2026</paper>

- Charge-equilibration/polarizable models that enforce global charge still did not recover defect minima without defect-specific charged training; this supports the claim that explicit conditioning plus appropriate defect data (not merely generic charge models) is required.  <paper entityId="paper-6906cba8c92984514089f2d909f633de2b39840f" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="286256203" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.4">Wang et al., 2026</paper>

content.title: Phonon/IFC accuracy: global charge scalar beats per-charge separate models below 3000 structures

content.text: FORK: For MLFF-driven phonon-defect scattering and κ degradation in a single host with multiple charge states, a single charge-conditioned potential trained jointly across charge states is more data-efficient than separate potentials per charge when total training set size is limited; the opposite fork is that separate-per-charge is superior. NUMERIC THRESHOLD: if total labeled structures across all charge states ≤3000, then a single charge-conditioned SF/NNP model (global Q_sys or charge embedding) will achieve force RMSE ≤75 meV/Å on each charge state, while training separate models per charge will NOT achieve ≤75 meV/Å for at least 2 charge states (it will be ≥100 meV/Å). NEGATIVE prediction: per-charge separate models will fail the ≤75 meV/Å threshold under this data budget.
**Supporting evidence:**

- In AlN, a charge-aware Behler–Parrinello NNP using SFs + global Q_sys achieved force RMSE ~69 meV/Å while covering multiple charge states in one model, and was used to compute IFCs and κ degradation; this demonstrates feasibility of joint charge-conditioned force accuracy at the ≤75 meV/Å level.  <paper entityId="paper-1ac0e91f059034f5d62532a10cdeabc099d55396" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="272831919" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Dou et al., 2024</paper>

- Review mentions charge-aware NNPs with a system-charge node reproducing DFT phonon spectra across multiple charge states with forces ~64 meV/Å, indicating that a single conditioned model can share information across charges for vibrational fidelity.  <paper entityId="paper-f594d0f1e05d8292d376f2aa2e45cea8cdc9dd78" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="287701931" artifactId="extraction-result-12#uuid-e12.7">Mannodi-Kanakkithodi et al., 2026</paper>

content.title: Predictions
2 Likely outcomes

content.text:
- In a charged-defect PES benchmark with ≥2000 structures, adding a categorical charge embedding will reduce relaxed-structure RMSD by ≥0.10 Å for at least 3 charge states relative to charge-agnostic training.
- For IFC/phonon workflows with N_total ≤3000, joint charge-conditioned training will keep force RMSE ≤75 meV/Å across charge states, whereas separate-per-charge will exceed 100 meV/Å in at least two states.

content.title: 2 Unknown outcomes

content.text:
- If charge-conditioned models are trained but the charge term is restricted to a geometry-independent energy head (no propagation into interaction layers), they will still recover correct minima; if true, charge affects mostly offsets rather than forces—this would contradict the ‘PES separation via conditioning’ mechanism.
- For defect complexes (two defects) with net charge fixed, a global charge token will be insufficient and models will require local charge-density descriptors; if observed, it would bound the global-token approach.

content.title: Conflicting & Unaccounted Evidence
2 Negative experiments

content.text:
- Train charge-agnostic vs charge-embedded on the same charged-defect dataset; if charge-agnostic achieves ≤0.10 Å RMSD across all charges, the theory fails.
- Under N_total ≤3000, if separate-per-charge models match joint charge-conditioned force RMSE ≤75 meV/Å for all charges, the data-efficiency claim fails.

content.title: 1 Unaccounted for

content.text: - The AlN NNP includes a global charge scalar that the authors note does not explicitly contribute to forces; the exact coupling needed for universal force improvements is not fully resolved by the evidence summarized.  <paper entityId="paper-1ac0e91f059034f5d62532a10cdeabc099d55396" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="272831919" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Dou et al., 2024</paper>
